points: Real founder of Delhi Sultanate authority; reorganized the Iqta system
Consolidated 'Chahalgani' (Group of Forty Turkish nobles); introduced silver 'Tanka' and copper 'Jital'; obtained recognition from the Caliph of Baghdad

phases.name: Razia Sultan
points: First and only woman ruler of the Delhi Sultanate; capable and just administrator
Tried to reduce the power of Turkish nobles; faced opposition due to gender; deposed after a short but remarkable rule

phases.name: Nasir-ud-din Mahmud (under Balban as Naib)
points: Real authority rested with Balban; central authority strengthened; control over nobles increased

phases.name: Ghiyas-ud-din Balban
points: Absolute monarchy; theory of Kingship 'Zill-e-Ilahi'; strict court etiquette (Sijda, Paibos); efficient spy system (Barid)
Successfully resisted Mongol invasions; strengthened frontier defence

phases.name: Kaikubad & Last Mamluks
points: Weak rulers; influence of nobles increased; disorder and factionalism; rise of slave aristocracy
Overthrown by Jalal-ud-din Khalji (1290 CE)

women.name: Razia Sultan
women.note: r. 1236–1240; first woman ruler of the Delhi Sultanate; capable, just and progressive.

events.title: Qutb-ud-din Aibak founds the Mamluk Dynasty
events.desc: Consolidation of Turkish rule in North India begins; construction of the Qutub Minar started.

events.title: Iltutmish consolidates the Sultanate
events.desc: Central authority strengthened; the Iqta system reorganised; the silver Tanka and copper Jital introduced.

events.title: Razia Sultan's reign
events.desc: The first woman ruler of the Sultanate; opposed by Turkish nobles and eventually deposed.

events.title: Balban's centralisation
events.desc: Absolute monarchy strengthened; strict court discipline enforced; successful defence against Mongol invasions.

events.title: Fall of the Mamluk Dynasty
events.desc: The last Mamluk ruler Kaiqubad/Kaikubad is overthrown; Jalal-ud-din Khalji founds the Khalji Dynasty.

people.name: Shams-ud-din Iltutmish
people.note: r. 1211–1236; real founder of the Sultanate's stable authority.

people.name: Ghiyas-ud-din Balban
people.note: r. 1266–1287; theory of 'Zill-e-Ilahi' (Shadow of God).

prelims: Iltutmish introduced the standard silver "Tanka" (175 grains) and copper "Jital" coinage of the Delhi Sultanate.
The elite aristocratic council of 40 Turkish slave nobles, known as Turkan-i-Chihalgani or "The Forty", was created by Iltutmish and later broken by Balban.
Razia Sultan was the daughter of Iltutmish and ruled from 1236 to 1240 CE, adopting the title "Sultan" and riding horses uncovered.
Balban enunciated the theory of divine kingship, claiming to be "Zill-i-Ilahi" (Shadow of God) and instituting the Persian court customs of Sajda (prostration) and Paibos (feet-kissing).
Balban created a separate military department called Diwan-i-Arz under Imad-ul-Mulk to strengthen the defense against Mongol raids.
Qutbuddin Aibak died in 1210 CE after falling from his horse while playing Chaugan (early form of polo) in Lahore.
The Mongol conqueror Genghis Khan reached the Indus river in 1221 CE in pursuit of Khwarizm prince Jalaluddin Mangbarani, but Iltutmish prudently denied refuge, saving Delhi.
mains: Evaluate the contributions of Shamsuddin Iltutmish as the "real founder and consolidator" of the Delhi Sultanate.
Analyze the political factors that led to the rise and tragic fall of Razia Sultan, highlighting the gender dynamics and the resistance of the Turkish nobility (Chihalgani).
Critically examine Ghiyasuddin Balban's Theory of Kingship, court ceremonies, and "Blood and Iron" policy in strengthening the prestige and authority of the Crown.
Examine the internal and external security challenges faced by the Mamluk sultans, with particular reference to the Mongol threat on the northwestern frontier.

Political Administration: Turkan-i-Chahalgani (The Forty): Powerful council of forty Turkish slave-officers created by Iltutmish to consolidate sultanate authority, later ruthlessly liquidated by Balban.
Iqta System: Institutionalized revenue assignment system where provincial governors (Iqtadars/Muqtis) collected taxes, maintained troops, and remitted surplus (Fawazil) to the central treasury.

Balban's Theory of Kingship: Absolute monarchical prestige claiming descent from mythical hero Afrasiyab; proclaimed kingship as Niyabat-i-Khudai (vice-regency of God) and monarch as Zill-i-Ilahi (shadow of God).

Court Protocol & Rigour: Instituted Persian court ceremonial of Sijda (prostration) and Paibos (kissing the monarch's feet); introduced the Persian spring festival of Nauroz; excluded non-Turks and low-born from high state offices.
Military: Diwan-i-Arz: Established as a separate military department by Balban under an independent minister (Ariz-i-Mamalik) to end corruption and enforce strict muster-roll inspections.
Mongol Frontier Defence: Iron curtain policy of fortresses along the North-West frontier (Lahore, Multan, Sunam, Samana) commanded by veteran generals like Sher Khan and Prince Muhammad.
Blood and Iron Policy: Severe military suppression of Mewati bandits, Katehr rebels, and Doab insurgents to secure trade corridors around Delhi.
Economy & Currency: Standardized Currency: Iltutmish introduced the standard silver Tanka (175 grains) and copper Jital, providing the monetary backbone of Delhi Sultanate trade for centuries.
Urbanization & Agrarian Inflow: Concentration of agricultural revenue in urban administrative centers stimulated specialized craft manufacture, metalworking, and paper usage.
Trade Corridors: Secured Overland Silk Route feeder tracks linking Lahore and Delhi with Central Asian and Persian merchant caravans (Karwanis).
Art & Architecture: Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque (Delhi): Earliest surviving congregational mosque of Delhi Sultanate, built by Qutb-ud-din Aibak using spolia from dismantled temples with corbelled arches.
Qutub Minar: 72.5m sandstone minaret commenced by Aibak (1199 CE) and completed by Iltutmish with Arabic calligraphy and fluted balconies.
Adhai Din Ka Jhopra (Ajmer): Early Indo-Islamic mosque built by Aibak featuring an ornate multi-arched screen.
Structural Innovations: Tomb of Iltutmish pioneered the squinch arch in India; Balban's Tomb (Mehrauli) represents the earliest true radiating arch (voussoirs) in Indian monumental architecture.
Literature & Culture: Tabaqat-i-Nasiri: Landmark Persian political history and court chronicle authored by Qazi Minhaj-us-Siraj, dedicated to Sultan Nasiruddin Mahmud.
Taj-ul-Ma'asir: Elaborate rhyming Persian prose chronicle of early Turkish conquests written by Hasan Nizami under Aibak and Iltutmish.
Sufi Confluence: Flourishing of Chishti Sufi order under Khwaja Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki and Baba Farid, establishing Delhi as a premier spiritual hub of Islam in South Asia.
Establishment & Consolidation (Iltutmish: Qutbuddin Aibak (r. 1206–1210 CE): Governor of Muhammad Ghori; ruled from Lahore; styled "Lakhbaksh" (giver of lakhs) for immense generosity; started construction of Qutb Minar (dedicated to Sufi saint Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki); died playing Chaugan (polo).

Shamsuddin Iltutmish (r. 1211–1236 CE): Regarded as the true consolidator of the Sultanate; shifted capital to Delhi; obtained formal investiture (Mansur) from the Abbasid Caliph of Baghdad (1229 CE); averted Mongol invasion by diplomatically refusing asylum to Jalaluddin Mangbarani pursued by Genghis Khan (1221 CE); completed Qutb Minar; instituted Turkan-i-Chihalgani (The Corpse of Forty Turkish slave-oligarchs); introduced pure silver Tanka (175 grains) and copper Jital.

Razia Sultan (r. 1236–1240 CE): First and only woman sovereign of the Delhi Sultanate; nominated by Iltutmish over incompetent sons; discarded purdah, donned male attire (Qaba and Kulah), rode elephants in battle; appointed Abyssinian slave Jamaluddin Yaqut as master of the royal stables (Amir-i-Akhur); provoked rebellion of Turkish Chihalgani nobles led by Altunia of Bhatinda; killed near Kaithal.
Ghiyasuddin Balban: Autocracy & Blood-an: Theory of Divine Kingship: Claimed descent from the mythical Persian hero Afrasiyab; proclaimed the Sultan to be the "Zill-i-Ilahi" (Shadow of God on Earth) and recipient of "Niyabat-i-Khudai" (Viceregency of God); introduced rigid Persian court etiquette: Sajda (prostration before the Sultan) and Paibos (kissing the Sultan's feet); celebrated the Persian spring festival of Nauroz.

Destruction of Chihalgani & Espionage: Systematically liquidated the treacherous "Forty" (Turkan-i-Chihalgani) nobles to eliminate rivals; instituted an omnipresent spy network (Barids) reporting directly to the Sultan.

Blood and Iron Policy: Mercilessly crushed Meo / Mewati dacoits around Delhi, clearing the forests and establishing police military outposts (Thanas); suppressed the rebellion of Tughril Khan in Bengal, impaling rebels on stakes along the market of Lakhnauti; created Diwan-i-Arz under Imad-ul-Mulk to check recurring Mongol incursions.

periods.title: Khalji Dynasty
periods.tagline: A Period of Expansion, Administrative Reforms, Economic Prosperity and Military Glory
periods.overview: The Khaljis were the first Turkic dynasty to hold power at Delhi that was not descended from the old Mamluk military elite, and under their second and by far most consequential ruler, Alauddin Khalji, the Sultanate reached a level of territorial extent, administrative reach, and sheer intrusive control over everyday economic life that none of its predecessors had approached. Alauddin's famous market reforms fixed the prices of essential goods across the empire and backed the policy with an intelligence and enforcement apparatus — the Barid and Munhiyan spy networks — sophisticated enough to make it stick, financing in turn a large, professionally maintained standing army capable of repeatedly repelling Mongol invasions and campaigning as far south as the Deccan. This was also a court of genuine cultural achievement: the poet and musician Amir Khusrau, closely associated with the Sufi saint Nizamuddin Auliya, became one of the era's most celebrated literary figures, while the Alai Darwaza and Siri Fort added a new architectural vocabulary to the Sultanate's built heritage. The dynasty's brief remaining span shows how quickly this level of centralised control could unravel without Alauddin's particular combination of ruthlessness and administrative rigor: Qutb-ud-din Mubarak Shah relaxed nearly every one of his father's controls within a few years, and the usurper Khusro Khan's short, unstable, and unpopular rule ended in 1320 when Ghazi Malik overthrew him, founding the Tughlaq dynasty that would inherit — and, in its own very different way, dramatically test — the machinery of Sultanate governance the Khaljis had built.

phases.name: Jalal-ud-din Firuz Khalji
points: Founder of the Khalji Dynasty; overthrew the Mamluks in 1290
Adopted a policy of conciliation; strengthened the state and won popularity

phases.name: Alauddin Khalji
points: Great conqueror & administrator; extended the empire from Gujarat to Bengal and from the Himalayas to the Deccan
Market reforms, revenue reforms, military reforms, strict law & order; highly centralised administration with a strong espionage network (Barid, Munhiyan)
Land revenue reforms (measurement & cash payment); price control of essential goods; abolition of intermediaries

phases.name: Qutb-ud-din Mubarak Shah Khalji
points: Soft-natured compared to Alauddin; took interest in pleasures and religion; gave freedom to nobles
Repealed many of Alauddin's strict policies; nobles regained power; leniency led to decline in central authority

phases.name: Khusro Khan
points: Converted to Islam and gained power; murdered Mubarak Shah and usurped the throne
Short and unpopular rule; overthrown by Ghazi Malik (founder of the Tughlaq Dynasty) in 1320

Political Administration: Jalal-ud-din: mild and conciliatory policy, gave importance to justice & welfare
Alauddin: highly centralised administration, strong espionage network, efficient revenue & military system, district administration under Shiqdar & Amil
Mubarak Shah: relaxed control over administration, gave high positions to favourites, nobles became powerful
Khusro Khan: depended on a few supporters, no strong administrative base
Economy: Alauddin's land revenue reforms and market reforms (price control of essential goods); state control over trade, grains & markets
Mubarak Shah repealed many of Alauddin's economic restrictions; prices rose again
Military: Alauddin: large standing army, branding of horses (Dag) & registration of soldiers (Chehra), regular cash payment; defeated the Mongols repeatedly
Mubarak Shah: army discipline declined, corruption increased
Religion: Jalal-ud-din: Sunni Muslim, tolerant towards Hindus
Alauddin: strict Sunni ruler; persecution of certain groups (especially Mongols); supported Islam
Mubarak Shah: more liberal & tolerant; interested in Sufism
Art & Architecture: Alai Darwaza (begun under Jalal-ud-din, completed under Alauddin), Alai Minar (unfinished), Siri Fort, Hauz-i-Alai
Literature & Culture: Persian was the court language under Alauddin; patronage to Amir Khusrau (poet, musician) and other scholars & Sufis
Imperial Expansion & Deccan Campaigns: Imperialist drive: Alauddin Khalji (r. 1296–1316 CE) murdered his uncle Jalaluddin at Kara (Prayagraj); assumed title "Sikandar-i-Sani" (Second Alexander); conquered Gujarat (1299; where eunuch military genius Malik Kafur was acquired for 1,000 dinars - Hazar Dinari), Ranthambore (1301; Jauhar of Rajput women led by Rani Ranga Devi described by Amir Khusrau), Chittor (1303; Rani Padmini legend recorded later in Malik Muhammad Jayasi's Padmavat), Malwa, and Jalor.

Deccan & Far South Expeditions: Malik Kafur led four lightning southern expeditions: Devagiri (Yadavas under Ramachandra), Warangal (Kakatiyas under Prataparudra, who surrendered the Koh-i-Noor diamond), Dvarasamudra (Hoysalas under Vira Ballala III), and Madurai (Pandyas); southern kingdoms were not directly annexed, but converted into tributary vassal states paying colossal war indemnities and annual tribute.
Economic Market Control & Price Fixation: Strategic rationale: Alauddin required a colossal, permanent standing army to defend against massive Mongol invasions (Qutlugh Khwaja, Targhi) and expand across India without exhausting state treasury funds; fixed retail prices of every commodity in Delhi.

Four specialized markets in Delhi: 1. Mandi (Grain market), 2. Sarai-i-Adl (Cloth, sugar, herbs, dry fruits, and manufactured goods), 3. Horses, cattle, and slaves market, 4. Miscellaneous general goods.

Market regulatory bureaucracy: Diwan-i-Riyasat (Commerce ministry headed by Malik Yaqut); Shahna-i-Mandi (Market Superintendent maintaining registers of merchants); Barids (intelligence officers) and Munhiyas (undercover child spies testing shopkeepers' weights); brutal punishments: flesh carved out of shopkeepers caught giving short weights.

Agrarian reforms: First Sultan to measure agricultural land (Masahat) using the Biswa standard; state revenue share fixed at 50% (half) of gross produce (Kharaj); direct tax collection eliminating village middlemen (Khuts, Muqaddams); imposed grazing tax (Charai) and house tax (Ghari).
Military Reforms: Standing army & direct cash pay: Paid soldiers directly in cash (Naqd) from royal treasury (234 Tankas annually for a regular cavalryman, plus 78 Tankas for a second horse - Do-Aspa).

Anti-corruption controls: Dagh system (branding royal marks on horses to prevent substitution with inferior ponies) and Chehra / Huliya system (detailed descriptive physical register of each soldier to prevent fraudulent proxy muster-rolls).

women.name: Malika-i-Jahan
women.note: Played an important role in administration during Alauddin's Deccan campaigns; other royal women influenced court politics through their connections.

events.title: Jalal-ud-din founds the Khalji Dynasty
events.desc: The Khaljis overthrow the Mamluks, ending the Slave Dynasty and beginning the first Turkic dynasty after them.

events.title: Alauddin Khalji's reign and reforms
events.desc: The empire reaches its maximum geographical extent under Alauddin, accompanied by market, revenue, and military reforms.

events.title: Defeat of Mongol invasions
events.desc: Alauddin Khalji repeatedly defeats Mongol incursions, strengthening the northwest frontier.

events.title: End of the Khalji Dynasty
events.desc: Khusro Khan's short, unpopular rule ends when he is overthrown by Ghazi Malik, who founds the Tughlaq Dynasty.

people.name: Alauddin Khalji
people.note: r. 1296–1316; greatest Khalji ruler; empire reached its maximum extent under him.

people.name: Amir Khusrau
people.note: Prominent at Alauddin's court; associated with the Sufi saint Nizamuddin Auliya.

people.name: Ziauddin Barani
people.note: Author of the Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi, a key primary source for the period.

prelims: Alauddin Khalji assumed the title "Sikandar-i-Sani" (Second Alexander) and struck coins bearing this epithet.
Alauddin Khalji was the first ruler of the Delhi Sultanate to introduce the Dagh (branding of horses) and Chehra (descriptive roll of soldiers) systems in the army.
In Alauddin's market control policy, the specialized central cloth and luxury goods market was called the "Sarai-i-Adl".
The market control machinery was overseen by the Shahna-i-Mandi (superintendent) and monitored by child secret spies called "Munhiyas".
Alauddin measured cultivable agricultural land based on the "Biswa" unit (Masahat system) and fixed the land revenue at 50% of the produce.
Malik Kafur (Hazar Dinari) led Alauddin's military expeditions into South India, defeating the Yadavas of Devagiri, Kakatiyas of Warangal, Hoysalas of Dwarasamudra, and Pandyas of Madurai.
The famous Persian epic poem Padmavat, recounting the siege of Chittor and Rani Padmini's Jauhar, was composed in Awadhi by Malik Muhammad Jayasi during the reign of Sher Shah Suri (1540 CE).
mains: Critically analyze the economic and market control measures introduced by Alauddin Khalji. Was it an egalitarian socialist experiment or a ruthless fiscal mechanism to sustain a massive standing army?
Examine Alauddin Khalji's agrarian policy with specific reference to land measurement (Masahat), revenue extraction, and the curtailment of hereditary rural intermediaries (Khuts and Muqaddams).
Discuss the geopolitical strategy behind Alauddin Khalji's southern campaigns led by Malik Kafur, analyzing why he chose indirect tributary vassalage rather than direct territorial annexation.
Evaluate the military reforms of Alauddin Khalji (Dagh, Chehra, cash salaries) in successfully repelling the repeated Mongol invasions of India.

periods.title: Tughlaq Dynasty
periods.tagline: A Period of Experimentation, Administrative Reforms, Economic Policies, Military Campaigns and Architectural Grandeur
periods.overview: No dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate better illustrates both the ambition and the fragility of medieval Indian statecraft than the Tughlaqs, whose ninety-four years span Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq's restoration of firm central authority, his son Muhammad bin Tughlaq's extraordinary run of large-scale administrative experiments, Firuz Shah Tughlaq's more cautious and genuinely welfare-oriented consolidation, and a final generation of weak rulers who watched the empire disintegrate around them. Muhammad bin Tughlaq in particular remains one of the most debated figures in Indian history: a ruler capable enough to extend the Sultanate to its greatest territorial reach — from Bengal to the Indus, from the Himalayas to the Deccan — and genuinely interested in learning and administrative reform, yet remembered above all for schemes that failed at enormous human and financial cost, including a forced mass relocation of Delhi's population to a new capital at Daulatabad and an ill-conceived token currency that collapsed when it could not be trusted. His successor Firuz Shah Tughlaq drew the obvious lesson, governing far more conservatively: reducing the tax burden, investing heavily in irrigation canals and new towns, and compiling an administrative code (the Fatawa-i-Firuz Shahi) that prioritised stability over ambition. That stability did not survive him. The later Tughlaqs proved unable to hold the empire together, provincial governors increasingly acted as independent rulers, and Timur's catastrophic invasion and sack of Delhi in 1398 delivered a blow from which the dynasty never recovered, clearing the way for the far more limited authority of the Sayyids.

phases.name: Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq
points: Founder of the Tughlaq Dynasty; re-established strong central authority
Built the Tughlaqabad Fort (1321 CE); controlled Mongol threats
Promoted agriculture and irrigation; strict revenue collection and law & order

phases.name: Muhammad bin Tughlaq
points: One of the ablest but most controversial rulers of India; extended the empire from Bengal to the Indus and from the Himalayas to the Krishna River
Bold and largely unsuccessful experiments: token currency, capital shift (Delhi to Daulatabad), Doab revenue increase, agricultural reforms, Khalisa land expansion
Promoted learning, scholars & intellectuals despite frequent revolts and discontent

phases.name: Firuz Shah Tughlaq
points: Strengthened administration; many welfare and public works projects
Reduction in land revenue; abolition of some harsh taxes; promotion of irrigation & canals
Compiled the 'Fatawa-i-Firuz Shahi'; established new towns and cities

phases.name: Later Tughlaqs
points: Weak & ineffective rulers; nobles became powerful; provinces became independent
Timur's invasion (1398 CE) shakes the empire; repeated revolts and invasions
Decline of central authority and disintegration of the Tughlaq Empire

Political Administration: Ghiyas-ud-din: centralised administration, strong monarch & disciplined army, reorganised Iqta system
Muhammad bin Tughlaq: highly centralised but harsh, introduced Diwan-i-Mustakhraj (revenue), stringent control over officials
Firuz Shah: well-organised bureaucracy, departmental administration, emphasis on written records
Later Tughlaqs: weak central authority, provinces acted independently, nobles became hereditary & powerful
Economy: Ghiyas-ud-din: land revenue main source, agriculture encouraged
Muhammad bin Tughlaq: Doab revenue increase (harsh), token currency experiment, Khalisa land expansion, trade & commerce encouraged
Firuz Shah: reduced land revenue, abolition of many taxes (jizya on Hindus abolished), encouraged agriculture, trade & crafts
Later Tughlaqs: economic instability, disruption of trade, heavy taxation by nobles
Military: Muhammad bin Tughlaq: large standing army, conquests in South India, Gujarat, Bengal
Firuz Shah: large but defensive army, focus on fortification
Later Tughlaqs: army weakened, unable to resist Timur
Architecture & Public Works: Muhammad bin Tughlaq: Jahanpanah City, Adilabad Fort (Daulatabad)
Firuz Shah: many cities – Firozabad, Firozpur, canals, gardens, madrasas, hospitals, Ashokan pillars installed
Later Tughlaqs: little construction, many earlier works neglected
Religion: Ghiyas-ud-din: Sunni Muslim, tolerant towards non-Muslims
Muhammad bin Tughlaq: Sunni Muslim, debated scholars of all religions
Firuz Shah: Sunni orthodox, patron of ulama, some conservative policies
Later Tughlaqs: intolerance increased, religious persecution in some areas
Muhammad bin Tughlaq's Controversial Exp: Intellectual contradictions: Highly erudite scholar of Arabic, Persian, mathematics, astronomy, philosophy, and medicine; described by contemporaries (Barani, Ibn Battuta) as a "mixture of opposites" and visionary ahead of his times.

Transfer of capital (1327 CE): Ordered shifting of royal court and population from Delhi to Devagiri (renamed Daulatabad in Maharashtra) to rule South India more centrally and secure defense against Mongols; immense human suffering along the 1500 km march; failure forced him to order the populace back to Delhi.

Token Currency Experiment (1329–1330 CE): Introduced brass and bronze coins (token currency) pegged at par with silver Tankas to address global silver shortages; failed catastrophically because the state failed to establish a monopoly over minting; every Hindu and Muslim house turned into a counterfeit mint; forced to redeem all worthless token coins with pure gold and silver coins from treasury.

Khurasan & Qarachil Expeditions: Recruited an army of 370,000 men paid one year's salary in advance for the Khurasan expedition, which was cancelled when Central Asian alliances collapsed; Qarachil expedition into the Kumaon Himalayas resulted in devastating army destruction due to monsoon landslides and guerrilla warfare.

Doab Taxation & Diwan-i-Kohi: Drastically hiked land revenue in the fertile Ganga-Yamuna Doab during a severe famine, causing peasant rebellion; later pioneered agricultural relief: established Diwan-i-Kohi (agricultural development department), provided state crop loans (Sondhar / Takkavi), and dug wells.
Firuz Shah Tughlaq's Welfare & Orthodoxy: Appeasement of Nobility & Ulema: Made the Iqta system and administrative offices hereditary; restored confiscated land endowments to Ulema; banned un-Islamic court practices; imposed Jizya on Brahmins for the first time as a separate tax.

Canal Networks & Agricultural Boom: Constructed 5 major irrigation canals (including Western Yamuna Canal and Satluj canal), irrigating extensive agricultural tracts in Haryana and Punjab; levied Haqq-i-Sharb (irrigation water cess at 1/10th of produce); planted 1,200 royal fruit orchards around Delhi.

Welfare Institutions & Urban Foundations: Established Diwan-i-Khairat (charity department for poor girls' marriages and orphans), Diwan-i-Bandagan (department for managing 180,000 royal slaves / Ghulam), and Dar-ul-Shafa (free state hospital in Delhi); founded new cities: Firozabad, Jaunpur (named after Muhammad bin Tughlaq / Jauna Khan), Hisar-Firoza, and Fatehabad; brought two Ashokan pillars from Topra (Haryana) and Meerut to Delhi.

women.name: Taj-ud-din Firuz Shah's queen(s)
women.note: Supported charitable works during Firuz Shah's reign; women from royal families took interest in religious & public works.

events.title: Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq founds the dynasty
events.desc: Re-establishes strong central authority in the Delhi Sultanate after the Khaljis; builds the Tughlaqabad Fort.

events.title: Capital shift to Daulatabad
events.desc: Muhammad bin Tughlaq's controversial transfer of the capital from Delhi to Daulatabad, one of several bold administrative experiments.

events.title: Firuz Shah Tughlaq's welfare reign
events.desc: Abolition of harsh taxes, major irrigation and public works, and the compilation of the Fatawa-i-Firuz Shahi.

events.title: Timur's invasion of Delhi
events.desc: Timur's devastating invasion shakes the weakened Tughlaq empire, accelerating its decline.

events.title: End of the Tughlaq Dynasty
events.desc: The fragmented Tughlaq empire gives way to the Sayyid Dynasty.

people.name: Muhammad bin Tughlaq
people.note: r. 1325–1351; extended the empire to its greatest extent but is best known for bold, largely failed experiments.

people.name: Firuz Shah Tughlaq
people.note: r. 1351–1388; noted for welfare measures and public works.

people.name: Ziauddin Barani
people.note: Author of the Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi; wrote 'Kiran-us-Sa'dain'.

prelims: Muhammad bin Tughlaq established a separate department of agriculture called "Diwan-i-Amir-Kohi" to encourage state-assisted cultivation and disburse Takkavi crop loans.
Muhammad bin Tughlaq issued token currency made of copper and brass, minted at parity with silver Tankas, between 1329 and 1330 CE.
Firuz Shah Tughlaq was the first Sultan of Delhi to impose Jizya on Brahmins as a distinct tax.
Firuz Shah Tughlaq created a specialized department called "Diwan-i-Bandagan" to look after the welfare and training of over 180,000 state slaves.
Firuz Shah Tughlaq constructed extensive canal networks in North India and levied an irrigation tax called "Haqq-i-Sharb" (10% of produce).
The two Ashokan monolithic pillars from Topra (Haryana) and Meerut (UP) were transported and re-erected in Delhi by Firuz Shah Tughlaq.
The Moroccan traveler Ibn Battuta visited India in 1334 CE during the reign of Muhammad bin Tughlaq, served as Qazi of Delhi, and wrote the travelogue Kitab-ur-Rihla.
mains: Critically evaluate the five administrative and economic experiments of Muhammad bin Tughlaq, assessing whether their failure was due to conceptual flaws or defective execution.
Compare and contrast the religious and administrative policies of Muhammad bin Tughlaq and Firuz Shah Tughlaq, with specific reference to their relations with the Ulema and the nobility.
Examine Firuz Shah Tughlaq's public works infrastructure (canals, urban foundations, hospitals, and charity departments), evaluating its long-term impact on the agrarian economy of North India.
Analyze the accounts of Ibn Battuta and Ziauddin Barani as primary sources for reconstructing the political psychology and administrative dynamics of the Tughlaq era.

quickFacts: Delhi (later Daulatabad during Muhammad bin Tughlaq)

periods.title: Sayyid Dynasty
periods.tagline: A Short-lived but Important Phase of Transition in the Delhi Sultanate
periods.overview: The Sayyid Dynasty is best understood as a period of genuine transition rather than a strong regime in its own right — a dynasty installed by circumstance (Timur's devastating 1398 invasion had left the Sultanate in ruins, and Khizr Khan, the governor Timur appointed at Multan, simply moved into the resulting power vacuum at Delhi) rather than by conquest or clear legitimacy, and one that never fully recovered the Sultanate's former reach. Even its most capable ruler, Mubarak Shah, managed only relative stability rather than expansion, reorganising administration and controlling the nobility with some success during his thirteen-year reign; his successors, Muhammad Shah and Alauddin Alam Shah, presided over a rapidly accelerating loss of central authority, with real power increasingly concentrated in the hands of powerful nobles like the Wazir Khwaja Jahan rather than the nominal Sultan. The thirty-seven-year dynasty's chief historical significance lies precisely in this weakness: it demonstrates just how far Sultanate authority had eroded after the Tughlaq collapse, and it set the stage — almost by default — for the ambitious Afghan noble Bahlul Lodi to simply walk into Delhi and seize it in 1451, founding the dynasty that would rule until Babur's invasion brought the entire Sultanate era to its end.

phases.name: Kizr Khan
points: Founder of the Sayyid Dynasty; appointed by Timur after his invasion (1398 CE)
Governor of Multan, later became Sultan of Delhi; tried to restore order and consolidated power
Established Sayyid Dynasty rule in Delhi in 1414 CE after Tughlaq decline

phases.name: Mubarak Shah
points: Most successful and capable ruler of the dynasty; reorganized administration and strengthened central authority
Controlled powerful nobles; encouraged agriculture; coins struck in his name
Relative stability and prosperity during his reign

phases.name: Muhammad Shah
points: Weak and ineffective ruler; administration fell into the hands of nobles
Rise of factionalism; royal authority declined; revolts by nobles and governors increased

phases.name: Alauddin Alam Shah
points: Puppet ruler in the hands of powerful nobles; real power rested with Khwaja Jahan (Wazir)
Central authority almost collapsed; decline of Sayyid power

phases.name: End of Sayyid Dynasty
points: Bahlul Lodi, a powerful Afghan noble, captured Delhi in 1451 CE and established Lodi rule, ending Sayyid rule

Political Administration: Kizr Khan: established Sayyid rule in Delhi, limited territory (mainly Delhi and surrounding areas), depended on old Tughlaq officials
Mubarak Shah: strengthened central administration, controlled powerful nobles, reorganized revenue collection
Muhammad Shah: lost control over nobles and provinces, factionalism increased, frequent revolts
Alauddin Alam Shah: no real power, controlled by nobles, Wazir Khwaja Jahan held real authority, administration in complete disorder
Economy: Kizr Khan: land revenue main source, agriculture slowly revived
Mubarak Shah: agriculture improved, trade and markets revived, currency system continued
Muhammad Shah: revenue system weakened, corruption increased
Alauddin Alam Shah: economic decline, irregular revenue collection, trade and agriculture affected
Religion: Ulama and Sufis remained influential across the dynasty; Islam remained the state religion; Persian language flourished in administration and literature
Origins & Timur's Shadow: Invasion of Timur (1398 CE): Timur's devastating sack of Delhi broke the backbone of the Tughlaq empire; appointed Khizr Khan (governor of Multan) as his viceroy in Punjab.

Foundation: Khizr Khan (r. 1414–1421 CE) occupied Delhi, founding the Sayyid Dynasty; claimed direct descent from Prophet Muhammad; ruled not as independent Sultan but as "Rayat-i-Ala" (Vassal of Timur and his successor Shah Rukh).
Political Instability & Decline: Successors: Mubarak Shah (r. 1421–1434 CE) suppressed rebellions in Mewat, Gwalior, and the Doab; founded the city of Mubarakabad on the Yamuna; patronized Yahya bin Ahmad Sirhindi, who authored the invaluable dynastic history Tarikh-i-Mubarak Shahi.

End of Dynasty: Succeeded by Muhammad Shah and Alauddin Alam Shah; Alam Shah voluntarily abdicated the throne in 1451 CE in favor of Bahlul Lodi, retiring peacefully to Badaun, enabling the peaceful transition to the Afghan Lodi dynasty.

events.title: Kizr Khan founds the Sayyid Dynasty
events.desc: Establishes Sayyid rule in Delhi following the decline of the Tughlaqs, after being appointed by Timur.

events.title: Mubarak Shah's reign
events.desc: The most capable Sayyid ruler brings relative stability and prosperity through stronger administration.

events.title: Bahlul Lodi captures Delhi
events.desc: The Afghan noble Bahlul Lodi ends Sayyid rule and establishes the Lodi Dynasty.

people.name: Kizr Khan
people.note: r. 1414–1421; appointed by Timur.

people.name: Mubarak Shah
people.note: r. 1421–1434; most capable Sayyid ruler.

people.name: Khwaja Jahan
people.note: Held real authority during the reign of Alauddin Alam Shah.

prelims: Khizr Khan founded the Sayyid dynasty in 1414 CE, ruling under the subordinate title "Rayat-i-Ala" acknowledging Timur and Shah Rukh.
The historical chronicle Tarikh-i-Mubarak Shahi, an essential contemporary source for the Sayyid period, was authored by Yahya bin Ahmad Sirhindi.
The last ruler of the Sayyid dynasty, Alauddin Alam Shah, peacefully abdicated the throne of Delhi in 1451 CE and retired to Badaun.
The Sayyid dynasty rulers claimed direct biological descent from the Prophet Muhammad, hence the name "Sayyid".
Mubarak Shah Sayyid founded the city of Mubarakabad along the banks of the Yamuna river.
mains: Assess the political condition of Northern India following Timur's invasion (1398 CE) and analyze how Khizr Khan established the Sayyid dynasty amidst regional fragmentation.
Evaluate the historical significance of Yahya Sirhindi's Tarikh-i-Mubarak Shahi in understanding the transition from the Tughlaqs to the Afghan Lodis.
Examine the internal rebellions in Mewat, the Doab, and Gwalior faced by the Sayyid rulers, explaining why the dynasty was unable to re-establish centralized Sultanate authority.

quickFacts: 1451 CE (Rise of Lodi Dynasty by Bahlul Lodi)

periods.title: Lodi Dynasty
periods.tagline: The Last Dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate — Political Instability, Regional Challenges and the Dawn of the Mughal Era
periods.overview: The Lodis close out the Delhi Sultanate's 320-year run, and their reign traces an arc that is almost a compressed replay of the whole Sultanate era: a founder who stabilises the state through conciliation rather than conquest, a strong middle ruler who genuinely reforms and expands it, and a final ruler whose harshness and poor judgment brings the entire structure down. Bahlul Lodi, the only Afghan (Pathan) dynasty to rule at Delhi, spent his reign consolidating rather than expanding, winning the loyalty of a fractious Afghan nobility through a deliberately conciliatory style of rule that let provincial governors retain considerable autonomy in exchange for stability. His son Sikandar Lodi then used that stability to genuinely reform the state — regularising land measurement and revenue collection, improving agriculture and trade, founding the city of Agra in 1504, and patronising Persian learning and culture — producing what many historians regard as the high point of Lodi governance. Ibrahim Lodi inherited a functioning state and, through a combination of arrogance, harsh treatment of the same nobility his grandfather had carefully conciliated, and an inability to read the growing threat from Kabul, managed to lose it entirely: defeated and killed at the First Battle of Panipat in 1526, his death did not just end the Lodi dynasty but the entire 320-year Delhi Sultanate, opening the era of Mughal rule that would dominate Indian history for the next three centuries.

phases.name: Bahlul Lodi
points: Founder of the Lodi Dynasty; elected as Sultan by nobles; followed a policy of conciliation
Provincial governors enjoyed considerable autonomy; strengthened Afghan control in North India
Extended control over Delhi, Punjab, Haryana and parts of UP; maintained peace and won the trust of nobles

phases.name: Sikandar Lodi
points: Able and administrative ruler; centralized administration; reorganized provinces and appointed able officers
Reforms in revenue (Gaj-i-Sikandari land measurement), agriculture and market system; regulation of prices of commodities
Promoted learning, literature and Persian culture; founded Agra in 1504 CE; strict in religious matters

phases.name: Ibrahim Lodi
points: Last ruler of the Lodi Dynasty; highly centralised but in a harsh manner; ignored the advice of nobles
Arrogant and authoritarian; alienated nobles by his harsh attitude; many nobles revolted against him
Faced the external challenge of Babur's rise in Afghanistan; defeated and killed by Babur at the First Battle of Panipat (1526 CE)

phases.name: End of the Lodi Dynasty
points: Defeat of Ibrahim Lodi by Babur in the First Battle of Panipat (1526 CE)
Establishment of the Mughal Empire in India; end of Afghan rule in Delhi

Political Administration: Bahlul Lodi: elected as Sultan by nobles, followed policy of conciliation, provincial governors enjoyed autonomy, strengthened Afghan control in North India
Ibrahim Lodi: highly centralised but in a harsh manner, ignored advice of nobles, many nobles revolted against him, weak control over provinces
Economy: Bahlul Lodi: land revenue the main source, agriculture encouraged

Sikandar Lodi: revenue system improved and regularized, measurement of land (Gaj-i-Sikandari), irrigation works developed, regulation of prices of commodities, promoted agriculture and trade, concern for welfare of peasants
Ibrahim Lodi: economy weakened due to rebellions, heavy expenditure on army, weak revenue collection in provinces
Military: Bahlul Lodi: strong Afghan cavalry, maintained a disciplined army
Sikandar Lodi: well-organized army, modern weapons used, frontier protection strengthened
Ibrahim Lodi: large army but poorly loyal, nobles did not support him in war
Architecture & Culture: Bahlul Lodi: built many mosques and tombs (e.g. Bahlul Lodi's Tomb)
Sikandar Lodi: promoted Persian language and literature, patron of scholars like Mubarak Shah and Alam Khan, built many mosques, madrasas and gardens (e.g. Sikandar Lodi's Tomb, Lodi Gardens)
Ibrahim Lodi: no major architectural works
First Afghan Empire in India: Afghan tribal confederacy ethos: Bahlul Lodi (r. 1451–1489 CE) established the First Afghan Empire in India; ruled on the principle of primus inter pares (first among equals), refusing to sit on an elevated throne in front of his Afghan tribal sardars; annexed the rival Sharqi Sultanate of Jaunpur (1479 CE), reuniting the central Gangetic plains with Delhi; issued the Bahloli copper coin.

Sikandar Lodi (r. 1489–1517 CE): Greatest Lodi ruler; transformed tribal Afghan monarchy into a centralized imperial despotism; founded the city of Agra (1504 CE) as his second capital and military headquarters against Rajput confederacies.

Measurement & Cultural patronage: Introduced standard measurement rod Gaz-i-Sikandari (32 digits / 39 inches) used up to Akbar's reign; composed Persian poetry under the pen-name "Gulrukhi"; had medical treatise Arghya-Roga translated from Sanskrit into Persian under the title Farhang-i-Sikandari; patron of classical music (Lahjat-i-Sikandar Shahi).
Ibrahim Lodi & The Battle of Panipat (15: Despotic clash with Afghan Sardars: Ibrahim Lodi (r. 1517–1526 CE) asserted unbending royal absolutism, humiliating senior Afghan grandees (asserting "a king has no relatives or clan"); provoked rebellions by his uncle Alam Khan Lodi and Daulat Khan Lodi (Governor of Punjab), who invited Babur (ruler of Kabul) to invade India.

First Battle of Panipat (21 April 1526): Babur's disciplined force of 12,000 men defeated Ibrahim Lodi's army of 100,000 soldiers and 1,000 elephants; Babur utilized field artillery (cannons under Ustad Ali and Mustafa) and the Ottoman Tulghuma tactical flanking system; Ibrahim Lodi died fighting on the battlefield (the only Delhi Sultan to perish in combat); marked the demise of the Delhi Sultanate and foundation of the Mughal Empire.

events.title: Bahlul Lodi founds the Lodi Dynasty
events.desc: The last dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate is established after the decline of the Sayyids; Afghan power in North India is consolidated.

events.title: Sikandar Lodi founds Agra
events.desc: Sikandar Lodi's efficient administration, revenue reforms and cultural patronage mark the high point of Lodi rule.

events.title: First Battle of Panipat
events.desc: Babur defeats and kills Ibrahim Lodi, ending the Delhi Sultanate and founding the Mughal Empire in India.

people.name: Sikandar Lodi
people.note: r. 1489–1517; able administrator; founded Agra (1504).

people.name: Ibrahim Lodi
people.note: r. 1517–1526; defeated and killed by Babur at Panipat.

prelims: The First Afghan Empire in India was established by Bahlul Lodi in 1451 CE.
Sikandar Lodi founded the city of Agra in 1504 CE and made it his capital in 1506 CE.
The standard land measurement rod "Gaz-i-Sikandari" of 32 units was introduced by Sikandar Lodi and continued into the Mughal era.
Sikandar Lodi composed Persian poems under the pen-name "Gulrukhi".
The Sanskrit musical treatise Lahjat-i-Sikandar Shahi and medical treatise Farhang-i-Sikandari were compiled under Sikandar Lodi's patronage.
The First Battle of Panipat took place on 21 April 1526, where Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi using firearms and the Tulghuma flanking strategy.
Ibrahim Lodi is the only Sultan of Delhi who died fighting on the battlefield.
mains: Analyze the transition of Afghan political theory of kingship from Bahlul Lodi's tribal egalitarianism ("first among equals") to Sikandar and Ibrahim Lodi's centralized absolutism.
Examine the political and administrative contributions of Sikandar Lodi, with specific reference to the foundation of Agra, the Gaz-i-Sikandari, and his cultural patronages.
Discuss the tactical, technological, and political factors that enabled Babur to defeat Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat (1526).

quickFacts: Delhi (later Agra founded by Sikandar Lodi in 1504)
1526 CE (Defeat by Babur in First Battle of Panipat)

periods.title: Vijayanagara Empire
periods.tagline: A Glorious Hindu Empire of South India — Defender of Dharma & Culture, Centre of Prosperity, Art, Literature and Trade
periods.overview: While the Delhi Sultanate and, later, the Mughals dominated North India, the Vijayanagara Empire built and sustained an equally significant, largely independent Hindu imperial power across the south for more than three centuries — founded in 1336 at Hampi partly, according to tradition, as a deliberate bulwark against the northward-then-southward push of Islamic conquest, and sustained through four successive dynasties (Sangama, Saluva, Tuluva, and Aravidu) until its eventual decline. The empire's undisputed peak came under Krishna Deva Raya of the Tuluva dynasty in the early 16th century, whose military successes against the Deccan Sultanates and the Gajapatis of Odisha coincided with an extraordinary flowering of temple architecture (the Vitthala Temple and its famous stone chariot among the most celebrated), Telugu and Kannada literature, and a genuinely cosmopolitan trading economy that drew Portuguese, Persian, and other foreign merchants to its ports. This was not a fragile or improvised state: it ran a sophisticated Nayaka administrative system for provincial governance, maintained a professional standing army, and supported an unusually visible tradition of royal women's patronage of temples and cultural institutions. Its end came suddenly and violently rather than through slow decline — a coalition of Deccan Sultanates inflicted a catastrophic defeat at the Battle of Talikota in 1565, sacking and permanently destroying the capital at Hampi — after which the empire survived only in greatly reduced form under the Aravidu dynasty until 1646, but its architectural and cultural legacy remained, and remains, one of South India's defining historical inheritances.

phases.name: Foundation – Sangama Dynasty
points: Founded by Harihara I & Bukka Raya I in 1336 CE; capital Hampi (Vijayanagara)
Established a strong Hindu empire to protect dharma from invasions
Organized administration and built a powerful army; prosperity in agriculture, trade, art and literature

phases.name: Saluva Dynasty
points: Saluva Narasimha seized power in 1485; strengthened central authority
Continued expansion and administrative reforms; built new forts and tanks; encouraged art, literature and temple construction

phases.name: Tuluva Dynasty (Golden Age)
points: Founded by Vira Narasimha under guidance of Tuluva generals; greatest ruler Krishna Deva Raya (1509–1529)
Empire reached its greatest extent; defeated Bahmani sultans, Gajapatis of Odisha and others
Age of prosperity, culture, literature and achievements

phases.name: Aravidu Dynasty
points: Capital shifted to Penukonda, later Chandragiri & Vellore; continued the legacy despite challenges
Faced pressure from the Deccan Sultanates; empire declined gradually

phases.name: End of Vijayanagara Empire
points: Defeated in the Battle of Talikota (1565 CE) by the Deccan Sultanates (Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmadnagar, Bidar, Berar)
Capital Hampi was destroyed and plundered; empire survived in reduced form under Aravidu rulers till 1646 CE

Political Administration: Sangama: well-organized administration, Nayaka system for provincial control, council of ministers and strong army
Saluva: centralized administration, reforms in revenue & military system, reduced power of old nobles
Tuluva: highly centralized & efficient administration, Amara-Nayaka system strengthened, strong espionage system, well organized army with cavalry, infantry, elephants & artillery
Aravidu: administration continued but weakened, power of Nayakas increased, frequent conflicts weakened central authority
Economy: Sangama: agriculture the main occupation, developed irrigation (tanks, canals), encouraged trade & crafts
Saluva: land revenue system improved, growth in trade (spices, horses, diamonds), state control on key commodities
Tuluva: prosperous economy, active foreign trade with Arabs, Persians, Portuguese, Chinese; export spices/textiles/precious stones, import horses/metals
Aravidu: economy affected by wars & invasions, decline in trade gradually, over-reliance on agriculture
Religion: Sangama: strong patronage to Hindu religion, reconstructed many temples, tolerant towards other religions
Tuluva: great supporter of Hinduism, built many grand temples (Vitthala, Hazara Rama), patronized saints & acharyas (Vyasa Tirtha), tolerant towards Islam & Christianity
Aravidu: continued temple patronage, growth of Bhakti movement, influence of saints & scholars continued
Art & Architecture: Sangama: built many temples, tanks & forts; Hampi became a beautiful city; blend of Dravidian & Indo-Islamic styles
Tuluva: golden age of architecture; Vitthala Temple, Lotus Mahal, Elephant Stables, Hazara Rama Temple; beautiful carvings, gopurams & sculptures
Aravidu: continued construction in smaller scale; temples at Tirupati, Srirangam, Kanchipuram
Genesis & Four Dynasties: Foundation (1336 CE): Founded on the banks of Tungabhadra by brothers Harihara I and Bukka I of the Sangama dynasty, under the spiritual guidance of sage Vidyaranya of the Sringeri Matha; four successive dynasties: 1. Sangama (1336–1485), 2. Saluva (1485–1505, founded by Saluva Narasimha), 3. Tuluva (1505–1570), 4. Aravidu (1570–1646, founded by Tirumala).

Krishnadevaraya (r. 1509–1529 CE): Pinnacle of Tuluva glory; defeated Sultan of Bijapur (conquered Raichur Doab 1520), subjugated Gajapatis of Odisha (conquered Udayagiri, Kondavidu); styled "Andhra Bhoja", "Abhinava Bhoja", and "Yavana-rajya-sthapana-acharya"; friendly ties with Portuguese Governor Albuquerque (secured monopoly over Arabian war-horses).
Administrative Institutions: Nayankara &: Nayankara System: Provincial military-feudal organization; territories assigned to military commanders termed Amara-Nayakas; in exchange for revenue extraction, Nayakas maintained a fixed quota of foot-soldiers, cavalry, and war-elephants for the King and remitted an annual cash tribute to the royal treasury; maintained substantial local administrative autonomy.

Ayagar System: Village self-governance; each village managed by a body of 12 hereditary village functionaries (Ayagars: headman/Gaunda, accountant/Karnam, blacksmith, carpenter, watchman, etc.); paid through tax-free land plots (Manyam) or a share of agricultural crops; eroded traditional Chola-style autonomous village assemblies.
Art, Architecture & Mahanavami Festival: Vijayanagara Architectural Style: Monumental Raya Gopurams (soaring entrance towers); Kalyana Mandapas (intricately carved marriage halls with monolithic musical pillars); hippogryph / yali rearing horse pillars; monuments at Hampi: Hazara Rama Temple (carved with continuous narrative Ramayana bas-reliefs), Vitthala Temple (famous stone chariot and 56 musical pillars).

Mahanavami Dibba: Massive stone stepped ceremonial platform; focal point of the 10-day state Mahanavami (Dussehra) festival where feudatory Nayakas paid annual homage, military parades were inspected, and animal sacrifices were performed.

Foreign Chroniclers: Nicolo de Conti (Italian, visited 1420 under Devaraya I); Abdur Razzaq (Persian envoy of Shah Rukh, 1443 under Devaraya II: "The city is such that eyes have not seen, nor ears heard of any place to equal it on earth"); Duarte Barbosa (1518); Domingo Paes (1520–22 under Krishnadevaraya); Fernao Nuniz (1535–37 under Achyuta Raya).
Battle of Talikota (1565) & Fall of Hamp: Rakshasi-Tangadi catastrophe: Regent Aliya Rama Raya played balance-of-power diplomacy among the Deccan Sultanates; provoked a united confederacy of four Deccan Sultanates (Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmednagar, Bidar); Rama Raya was captured and beheaded; the imperial metropolis of Hampi was systematically sacked, looted, and burned for six months; capital shifted south to Penukonda and Chandragiri under the Aravidu dynasty.

women.name: Queen Tirumalamba
women.note: Queen of Bukka Raya I; played an important role in royal and cultural activities.

women.name: Chinna Devi & Tirumala Devi
women.note: Queens of Krishna Deva Raya; helped in royal & cultural activities.

women.name: Women in society
women.note: Women were learned, respected & participated in religion, art, literature & social works; the Devadasi tradition supported art, music & dance.

events.title: Foundation of the Vijayanagara Empire
events.desc: Harihara I and Bukka Raya I found the empire at Hampi to protect dharma from northern invasions.

events.title: Reign of Krishna Deva Raya
events.desc: The empire's golden age: military success against the Bahmanis and Gajapatis, and a flowering of art, literature and architecture.

events.title: Battle of Talikota
events.desc: A coalition of Deccan Sultanates decisively defeats Vijayanagara; the capital Hampi is destroyed and plundered.

events.title: End of the Vijayanagara Empire
events.desc: The empire, reduced to Penukonda, Chandragiri and Vellore under the Aravidu dynasty, finally ends.

people.name: Harihara I & Bukka Raya I
people.note: Founded the empire in 1336 CE.

people.name: Krishna Deva Raya
people.note: r. 1509–1529; empire reached its greatest extent under him.

prelims: The Vijayanagara Empire was founded in 1336 CE on the southern banks of the Tungabhadra river by Harihara and Bukka under the inspiration of sage Vidyaranya.
Krishnadevaraya composed the epic Telugu treatise on statecraft, Amuktamalyada (story of Andal), and the Sanskrit drama Jambavati Kalyanam.
Krishnadevaraya's royal court was adorned by the "Ashtadiggajas" (eight great Telugu poets), including Allasani Peddana (Andhra Kavita Pitamaha) and Tenali Ramakrishna.
The Nayankara system in Vijayanagara was a military-feudal system where officers called Amara-Nayakas held land assignments in exchange for maintaining troops.
The Ayagar system was an administrative system where 12 hereditary officials governed village affairs in the Vijayanagara Empire.
The Persian ambassador Abdur Razzaq visited Vijayanagara in 1443 CE during the reign of Devaraya II, describing the seven concentric fortified rings of the city.

The Battle of Talikota (also known as the Battle of Rakshasi-Tangadi) took place on 23 January 1565, in which the combined armies of Bijapur, Ahmednagar, Golconda, and Bidar destroyed Vijayanagara power.
mains: Analyze the Nayankara and Ayagar administrative systems of the Vijayanagara Empire, comparing them with the Delhi Sultanate's Iqta system.
Examine the political, military, and cultural achievements of Krishnadevaraya, evaluating why his reign is considered the Golden Age of South Indian history.
Discuss the unique architectural and urban planning features of Hampi, with specific reference to the Vitthala Temple, Hazara Rama Temple, and the Mahanavami Dibba.
Evaluate the accounts of foreign travelers (Abdur Razzaq, Domingo Paes, Fernao Nuniz) in reconstructing the urban wealth, military pageantry, and society of Vijayanagara.

periods.title: The Deccan Sultanates
periods.tagline: Five Successor Sultanates of the Bahmani Kingdom — Ahmednagar, Bijapur, Berar, Golconda, and Bidar: Centers of Deccani Art, Architecture & Trade
periods.overview: Following the disintegration of the Bahmani Kingdom around 1490 CE, five independent sultanates emerged in the Deccan plateau: the Nizam Shahis of Ahmednagar, the Adil Shahis of Bijapur, the Imad Shahis of Berar, the Qutb Shahis of Golconda, and the Barid Shahis of Bidar. Despite frequent internecine wars and shifting alliances, the Deccan Sultanates formed a united front to defeat Vijayanagara at the pivotal Battle of Talikota (1565). They fostered a distinct Deccani culture synthesizing Persian, Turkish, and local Telugu, Kannada, and Marathi elements, creating architectural wonders like the Gol Gumbaz and Charminar before being annexed into the Mughal Empire under Aurangzeb.

phases.name: Disintegration of Bahmani Kingdom & Emergence of Five Sultanates
points: Malik Ahmad declared independence in Ahmednagar (Nizam Shahi dynasty) in 1490.
Yusuf Adil Shah established the Adil Shahi dynasty at Bijapur (1490).
Fathullah Imad-ul-Mulk founded the Imad Shahi dynasty in Berar (1490).
Sultan Quli Qutb-ul-Mulk proclaimed independence in Golconda (Qutb Shahi dynasty, 1512).
Qasim Barid founded the Barid Shahi dynasty in Bidar (1492–1528).

phases.name: Deccan Alliance & The Battle of Talikota
points: The Sultanates of Bijapur, Ahmednagar, Golconda, and Bidar forged a historic alliance against Vijayanagara ruler Aliya Rama Raya.
Battle of Talikota (Rakshasi-Tangadi, January 1565): The combined Sultanate artillery and cavalry decisively crushed Vijayanagara, leading to the destruction of Hampi.
Berar was subsequently annexed by Ahmednagar in 1574; Bidar was annexed by Bijapur in 1619.

phases.name: The Era of Malik Ambar & Cultural Flourishing
points: Regency of Chand Bibi defending Ahmednagar and Bijapur against Mughal incursions.
Malik Ambar (an Ethiopian / Habshi military genius and Prime Minister of Ahmednagar) pioneered guerrilla warfare (Bargir-giri) and the revenue assessment system (Ain-i-Dahsala equivalent).
Ibrahim Adil Shah II of Bijapur ('Jagadguru Badshah') composed the musical treatise Kitab-i-Navras in Dakhani Urdu, honoring Saraswati and Ganesha.
Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah built the iconic Charminar in Hyderabad (1591) to commemorate the eradication of plague.

phases.name: Mughal Conquest & Annexation
points: Shah Jahan's Treaties of 1636 forced Bijapur and Golconda to accept Mughal suzerainty and pay tributes.
Aurangzeb personally led imperial armies to conquer Bijapur (1686, capturing Sikandar Adil Shah) and Golconda (1687, capturing Abul Hasan Tana Shah after 8-month siege of Golconda Fort).

Administration & Military Innovations: Pioneered guerilla cavalry tactics (Bargir-giri / Ganimi Kava), later mastered by Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj.
Recruitment of Habshis (African elite soldiers/administrators like Malik Ambar) alongside Persian (Afaqi) and local Deccani nobles.
Extensive employment of Maratha revenue officers and cavalry commanders, laying the administrative groundwork for the Maratha state.
Deccani Art & Architecture: Gol Gumbaz (Bijapur): Mausoleum of Muhammad Adil Shah featuring the world's second-largest dome (unsupported by pillars) and acoustic whispering gallery.
Charminar & Mecca Masjid (Hyderabad): Grand Qutb Shahi granite and stucco monuments with minarets and arcades.
Mahmud Gawan Madrasa (Bidar): Three-storey Persian college with glazed tiles, minarets, and a 3,000-manuscript library.
Deccani Miniature Painting: Brilliant jewel-like colors, elongated figures, and Persian-Turkish-Vijayanagara fusion.
Economy & Trade: World-renowned diamond mining in Golconda (Kollur Mines produced Koh-i-Noor, Hope, and Darya-i-Noor diamonds).
Vibrant maritime trade through port of Machilipatnam and Konkan ports (Dabhol, Chaul) with Persian Gulf, Southeast Asia, and Europe (Dutch and English East India Companies).
Bahmani Empire & Mahmud Gawan: Foundation (1347 CE): Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah (Zafar Khan) revolted against Muhammad bin Tughlaq, founding the Bahmani Kingdom (capitals: Gulbarga, later Bidar); perpetual geopolitical conflict with Vijayanagara over the fertile Krishna-Tungabhadra (Raichur) Doab and Marathwada ports (Goa).

Mahmud Gawan (r. 1463–1481 CE as Prime Minister / Khwaja Jahan): Persian merchant-administrator; streamlined provincial governance by dividing the 4 bloated provinces (Tarafs) into 8 manageable districts; secured royal monopoly over artillery; constructed the world-famous three-storey Mahmud Gawan Madrasa at Bidar (Islamic college adorned with Persian tilework and 3,000-volume library); executed due to a forged treason letter planted by jealous rival Deccani nobles, leading to the collapse of Bahmani unity.
The Five Deccan Sultanates & Architectur: Five successor sultanates: 1. Bijapur (Adil Shahi dynasty, 1490–1686, founded by Yusuf Adil Shah), 2. Golconda (Qutb Shahi dynasty, 1512–1687, founded by Quli Qutb Shah), 3. Ahmednagar (Nizam Shahi dynasty, 1490–1633, founded by Malik Ahmad), 4. Berar (Imad Shahi dynasty, 1490–1574), 5. Bidar (Barid Shahi dynasty, 1492–1619).

Bijapur's architectural zenith: Gol Gumbaz (mausoleum of Muhammad Adil Shah) boasting the world's second largest dome (144-foot diameter) unsupported by pillars, and a legendary acoustic "Whispering Gallery" where soft murmurs echo 11 times; Ibrahim Rauza (tomb of Ibrahim Adil Shah II, "Jagadguru Badshah", author of musical treatise Kitab-i-Navras in Dakhani Urdu).

Golconda & Hyderabad: Founded by Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah, who built the iconic Charminar in 1591 CE in Hyderabad to commemorate the eradication of plague; Golconda diamond mines (Kollur mine yielding the Koh-i-Noor, Hope, and Darya-i-Noor diamonds).

Malik Ambar of Ahmednagar: Abyssinian prime minister; introduced guerrilla warfare (Bargir-giri) against Mughal armies; conducted scientific land revenue settlement based on actual crop measurement inspired by Todar Mal.

women.name: Chand Bibi
women.role: Regent of Bijapur & Warrior Queen of Ahmednagar
women.note: Famous for defending Ahmednagar fort against Mughal imperial armies under Prince Murad in 1595, wearing armor and personally overseeing defensive artillery.

women.name: Hayat Bakshi Begum
women.note: Influential Qutb Shahi diplomat and patron of mosques, caravanserais, and charitable institutions in Hyderabad; negotiated peace with Aurangzeb.

events.title: Tripartite Breakup of Bahmani Kingdom
events.desc: Ahmednagar, Bijapur, and Berar simultaneously declare independence from the Bahmani Sultanate.

events.title: Battle of Talikota (Rakshasi-Tangadi)
events.desc: The alliance of Bijapur, Ahmednagar, Golconda, and Bidar decisively defeats the Vijayanagara Empire.

events.title: Foundation of Hyderabad & Construction of Charminar
events.desc: Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah founds Hyderabad and constructs the four-minaret monument.

events.title: Mughal Annexation of Bijapur and Golconda
events.desc: Emperor Aurangzeb besieges and annexes Bijapur (1686) and Golconda (1687), ending Sultanate rule.

people.name: Malik Ambar
people.role: Prime Minister & Military Commander of Ahmednagar
people.note: Ethiopian-born statesman who introduced land revenue surveys, built modern Aurangabad (Fatehnagar), and repeatedly thwarted Mughal expansion.

people.name: Ibrahim Adil Shah II
people.note: Author of Kitab-i-Navras, patron of arts and architecture (Ibrahim Rauza), renowned for secular governance and syncretism.

prelims: The Bahmani Kingdom was founded in 1347 CE by Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah (Zafar Khan), with its initial capital at Gulbarga (Ahsanabad).
Mahmud Gawan, prime minister of the Bahmani Kingdom, built the monumental three-storey theological college (Madrasa) at Bidar in 1472 CE.
The Gol Gumbaz in Bijapur is the mausoleum of Muhammad Adil Shah, renowned for its massive single dome and acoustic Whispering Gallery.
Ibrahim Adil Shah II of Bijapur was titled "Jagadguru Badshah" and "Abla Baba" (friend of the poor) for his religious syncretism, authoring the musical classic Kitab-i-Navras.
The Charminar in Hyderabad was built in 1591 CE by Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah to commemorate the cessation of a devastating plague epidemic.
Malik Ambar, the prime minister of Ahmednagar, pioneered the "Bargir-giri" guerrilla warfare technique against the Mughals and reformed land revenue administration.
The legendary diamond mines that produced the Koh-i-Noor diamond were situated in the Golconda Sultanate (Kollur mines).
mains: Examine the administrative reforms and military modernization spearheaded by Mahmud Gawan in the Bahmani Sultanate, analyzing why his execution precipitated its disintegration.
Trace the rise and architectural contributions of the Five Deccan Sultanates, with special focus on Gol Gumbaz in Bijapur and the Charminar in Hyderabad.
Evaluate the political and military role of Malik Ambar in organizing Deccani resistance against Mughal imperial expansion in the 17th century.
Analyze the cultural and literary synthesis achieved under the Deccan Sultanates, specifically the development of Dakhani language and miniature painting traditions.

periods.title: The Mughal Empire
periods.tagline: A Great Empire that Unified India — Pillars of Administration, Culture, Art & Architecture; a Symbol of Syncretic Culture and Prosperity
periods.overview: The Mughal Empire is the single most consequential political entity in medieval Indian history, and its 331-year span — from Babur's 1526 victory at Panipat to the formal end of Mughal rule amid the 1857 Revolt — divides naturally into a rise, a golden age, and a long, contested decline that this page introduces before its individual emperors each get their own dedicated treatment elsewhere on this site. The rise runs through Babur's brief founding reign and Humayun's dramatic loss and fifteen-year recovery of the throne, before Akbar's forty-nine-year reign turns a fragile, contested kingdom into a genuinely durable empire through military conquest paired with unusually deliberate policies of religious tolerance (Sulh-i-Kul), administrative innovation (the Mansabdari and land-revenue systems), and cultural synthesis. The golden age that follows under Jahangir, and especially Shah Jahan, produces the Mughal Empire's most recognisable cultural legacy — above all the Taj Mahal — alongside continued prosperity and territorial stability. Aurangzeb's long, militarily successful but administratively and financially draining reign then marks the empire's greatest territorial extent and, simultaneously, the beginning of the strain that would undo it: reimposed religious taxation, decades of costly Deccan warfare against the rising Marathas, and a jagirdari crisis in land-revenue administration that his weaker 18th-century successors could never resolve. What survived past Aurangzeb's death in 1707 was less an empire than its idea — a nominal emperor increasingly controlled by nobles, regional powers, and eventually the British East India Company — but that idea, and the administrative and cultural framework the Mughals had built, would shape Indian governance and culture long after real Mughal power had disappeared.

phases.name: Babur
points: Founded the Mughal Empire in India after winning the Battle of Panipat (1526 CE); defeated Ibrahim Lodi
Battle of Khanwa (1527) and Ghaghra (1529); wrote 'Baburnama' (an autobiography); laid the foundation of a strong empire

phases.name: Humayun
points: Succeeded Babur; lost the empire to Sher Shah Suri (1540); took refuge in Persia
Recovered Delhi in 1555; died in 1556 after a fall from the library stairs

phases.name: Akbar the Great
points: Greatest of the Mughals; expanded empire & consolidated rule; abolished Jizya & Pilgrimage Tax
Introduced Sulh-i-Kul (universal peace); Navaratnas in his court; reforms in administration, revenue, military & judiciary; promoted art, culture, literature & secularism

phases.name: Jahangir
points: Known for love of art & nature; strengthened administration; encouraged painting and naturalistic art
Wrote 'Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri' (memoirs); justice-loving ruler

phases.name: Shah Jahan
points: Golden age of Mughal architecture; built the Taj Mahal, Red Fort, Jama Masjid, Shalimar Gardens
Strong administration; empire at its territorial peak; luxurious court and culture

phases.name: Aurangzeb Alamgir
points: Last strong Mughal emperor; large territorial expansion; reimposed Jizya; long Deccan wars weakened the empire
Strict Sunni Muslim; death in 1707 marks the beginning of rapid decline

phases.name: Decline
points: Weak successors; power struggle among Marathas, Sikhs, Jats, Rohillas & regional states
Economic decline; British East India Company became dominant; last Mughal Bahadur Shah II; 1857: end of Mughal rule

Political Administration: Babur: centralised rule, divided empire into provinces, trusted nobles
Akbar: efficient central administration, Mansabdari system, Subah-Sarkar-Pargana system, record keeping
Jahangir: continued Akbar's system, strong bureaucracy, imperial authority at its peak
Shah Jahan: highly centralised, increased control but more dependence on nobles
Aurangzeb: centralisation continued but weakened later
Economy: Babur: booty from victories, agriculture encouraged
Akbar: land revenue system (Zabt), Todar Mal's bandobast, promotion of trade & crafts
Jahangir: trade & industry flourished, expansion of markets, increase in revenue
Shah Jahan: prosperity & wealth high, growth of handicrafts, textiles, trade
Aurangzeb: heavy expenditure on wars, economic strain, decline in trade in later period
Religion: Akbar: policy of Sulh-i-Kul (universal peace), abolished Jizya, Din-i-Ilahi
Jahangir & Shah Jahan: generally tolerant, followed policies broadly similar to Akbar
Aurangzeb: reimposed Jizya, orthodox Sunni ruler
Art, Architecture & Culture: Akbar: blend of Indian, Persian & Central Asian styles, Fatehpur Sikri, Agra Fort
Jahangir: painting at its best, naturalistic art
Shah Jahan: golden age of architecture — Taj Mahal, Red Fort, Jama Masjid
Aurangzeb: less focus on art & architecture
Mughal Miniature Paintings & Architectur: Mughal Miniature Evolution: Humayun brought Persian masters Mir Sayyid Ali and Abdus Samad from Safavid Tabriz. Akbar established the royal Tasvir Khana, overseeing vast collaborative manuscripts (Hamzanama on cloth, Razmnama Persian translation of Mahabharata). Jahangir shifted the atelier towards supreme naturalism, individual royal portraiture, halos, and scientific animal/botanical studies by Ustad Mansur ('Siberian Crane', 'Zebra'). Shah Jahan introduced formal imperial durbars with radiant lapis and burnished gold leaf borders.

Indo-Islamic Architectural Masterpieces: Synthesized Persian arcuate engineering (true arch, bulbous double dome, Charbagh quadripartite garden layout) with indigenous Indian stone carving, trabeate brackets, and jali lattices. Exemplified by Humayun's Tomb (precursor to Taj Mahal), Akbar's red sandstone Fatehpur Sikri (Buland Darwaza, Panch Mahal), Itmad-ud-Daulah's tomb (introducing extensive white marble pietra dura inlay), and Shah Jahan's Taj Mahal (the jewel of symmetrical Indo-Islamic architecture).
Mughal Institutional Matrix & Composite: Imperial state apparatus: Bureaucratic centralization balanced with regional diversity; royal sovereign as "Zill-i-Ilahi" (Shadow of God) governing under the moral ethos of Sulh-i-Kul (universal peace); administrative hierarchy from Subah (province) to Sarkar (district) and Pargana (sub-district).

Mansabdari & Jagirdari interdependence: Civil and military administration integrated through the Mansabdari system; Mansabdars paid via temporary revenue assignments (Jagirs), preventing feudal landed entrenchment through periodic transfers every 3–4 years.

Composite architectural and artistic heritage: Synthesis of Persian, Central Asian, and indigenous Indian traditions in architecture (Charbagh, red sandstone, white marble, double dome, pietra dura) and miniature painting (Mughal atelier fusing Persian delicacy with Indian vitality).

women.name: Nur Jahan
women.note: Influential queen during Jahangir's reign; involved in administration, coinage, architecture & charity work.

women.name: Jahanara Begum
women.note: Daughter of Shah Jahan; patron of arts, built 'Sarais', involved in trade & welfare.

women.name: Zeb-un-Nissa
women.note: Scholar, poetess (wrote in Persian); daughter of Aurangzeb.

events.title: First Battle of Panipat
events.desc: Babur defeats Ibrahim Lodi, founding the Mughal Empire in India.

events.title: Akbar's accession
events.desc: Akbar becomes emperor at age 13 and goes on to consolidate and expand the empire into its golden age.

events.title: Aurangzeb's reign
events.desc: The empire reaches its greatest territorial extent but is weakened by prolonged Deccan wars and reimposed Jizya.

events.title: Death of Aurangzeb
events.desc: Marks the beginning of rapid Mughal decline amid weak successors and regional power struggles.

events.title: End of Mughal rule
events.desc: The Revolt of 1857 and its suppression bring a formal end to Mughal rule in India.

people.name: Shah Jahan
people.note: r. 1628–1658; builder of the Taj Mahal.

prelims: The Mughal administrative province was called a "Subah", headed by a Subahdar, while financial administration was independently directed by the provincial Diwan.
Under the Mughal Jagirdari system, the land whose revenue was reserved directly for the imperial treasury was called "Khalisa", whereas land assigned to Mansabdars was termed "Jagir".
The revenue assessment manual and administrative encyclopaedia of Akbar's empire, Ain-i-Akbari, was authored by Abul Fazl as the third volume of the Akbarnama.
The bilingual silver coin carrying the Sanskrit translation "Avyaktamekam" alongside Arabic Kalima was minted by Mahmud of Ghazni, not the Mughals; the standard Mughal silver coin was the Rupiya.
The custom of "Jharokha Darshan" (daily appearance on the palace balcony) was introduced by Akbar to build personal rapport with common subjects.
Mughal miniature paintings reached their peak of naturalism and portraiture under Jahangir, while architectural monumentality peaked under Shah Jahan.
The Battle of Tukaroi (1575) resulted in the annexation of Bengal and Bihar into the Mughal Empire by Akbar.
mains: Critically evaluate the structural relationship between the Mansabdari system and the Jagirdari system in sustaining the fiscal and military power of the Mughal Empire.
Analyze the evolution of the concept of sovereignty in the Mughal state from Babur to Akbar and Aurangzeb.
Discuss the composite cultural synthesis (Ganga-Jamuni Tehzeeb) achieved under Mughal rule in the realms of language, music, painting, and architecture.

quickFacts: Agra, Fatehpur Sikri, Lahore, Delhi, Shahjahanabad

periods.title: Babur
periods.tagline: The First Mughal Emperor — A Timurid Prince, Warrior, Writer and Visionary
periods.overview: Babur's five-year reign in India is almost startlingly brief for a man remembered as the founder of one of history's great empires — a reminder that the Mughal Empire's later grandeur was not preordained but built, quite precariously, on a single military campaign by an exiled Central Asian prince with nothing left to lose. Descended from both Timur and Genghis Khan, Babur had already been driven out of his ancestral kingdom of Farghana and lost Samarkand more than once before Afghan nobles discontented with the Delhi Sultanate's Ibrahim Lodi invited him into India — an invitation he answered decisively at the First Battle of Panipat in 1526, where his relatively small but tactically sophisticated force (using the Tulughma flanking manoeuvre, mobile artillery, and cart fortifications learned from Ottoman and Central Asian warfare) destroyed Ibrahim Lodi's vastly larger army. Securing that victory took two more years of hard fighting — against the formidable Rajput confederacy under Rana Sanga at Khanwa in 1527, and against Afghan resistance at Chanderi and Ghaghra — before Babur could turn to actually governing rather than conquering, a task his brief remaining years and largely personal, uninstitutionalised style of rule left mostly unfinished. What he did leave behind mattered enormously anyway: a foothold in North India that his son Humayun would nearly lose entirely, the Persianate court culture and garden architecture (the Charbagh style) that later Mughal emperors would develop into their signature aesthetic, and the Baburnama, an unusually candid and literary royal memoir that remains one of the great primary sources for understanding how the Mughal Empire actually began.

phases.name: Early Life & Background
points: Born 14 February 1483 in Andijan (Fergana Valley, present-day Uzbekistan); great-great-grandson of Timur (Tamerlane) and Genghis Khan
Lost his father at a young age; became ruler of Farghana at age 12; lost Samarkand several times but gained rich experience in wars and administration; spent years in exile

phases.name: Invasion of India
points: Invited by Daulat Khan Lodi and Alam Khan (discontented nobles of the Delhi Sultanate) to fight Ibrahim Lodi
Crossed the Indus in November 1524 with an army of about 12,000–15,000; reached Punjab, captured Lahore (1524) and Dipalpur; advanced towards Delhi

phases.name: First Battle of Panipat
points: Faced Ibrahim Lodi's army (about 100,000 soldiers and 1,000 elephants)
Babur used superior strategy: Tulughma (flanking attack), Araba (cart fortification), matchlocks & artillery
Ibrahim Lodi was killed; Babur won a historic victory and captured Delhi & Agra

phases.name: Conquest & Control
points: Captured Delhi (April 1526) and Agra (May 1526)
Defeated Rajput ruler Rana Sanga of Mewar in the Battle of Khanwa (16 March 1527)
Defeated Afghan chiefs Mahmud Lodi in the Battle of Chanderi (1528) and the Afghan confederacy in the Battle of Ghaghra (1529); established firm control over North India

phases.name: Last Years & Death
points: Spent his last years consolidating his rule; died on 26 December 1530 in Agra at the age of 47
Buried in Aram Bagh, Agra (his own garden)

Administration: Personal rule; no elaborate bureaucracy like later Mughals; advisors and military commanders helped in governance
Divided the empire into provinces (subahs) and smaller units; appointed governors (khalifas) and officials
Followed Islamic principles and Timurid traditions in justice; maintained a standing army and loyal Turkish-Mongol cavalry
Economy: No formal revenue system; relied on land revenue and personal control
Supported farming and encouraged irrigation in key regions; connected India with Central Asia and beyond through trade routes
Continued the use of existing coins; issued coins in his name in later years
Military: Central Asian style of warfare (cavalry, archers, matchlocks); used artillery and firearms (advanced for his time)
Strategic use of war elephants and cavalry; the Tulughma (flanking movement) and Araba (cart fortification) systems were decisive at Panipat and Khanwa
Culture & Intellectual Life: A learned and literary emperor; wrote the 'Baburnama' (autobiography) in Chagatai Turkish (later translated into Persian and English)
Patronized Persian and Central Asian scholars, poets and artists; introduced Persianate culture and traditions in India
Loved gardens, nature, poetry and calligraphy; laid the foundation for the Mughal artistic tradition; introduced the Charbagh style of garden architecture (e.g. Aram Bagh in Lahore)
Central Asian Heritage & Military Innova: Lineage and early career: Zahiruddin Muhammad Babur was a Timurid prince of Fergana; descended from Timur on father's side and Genghis Khan on mother's side; seized Kabul in 1504 CE after losing Samarkand twice.

Tactical revolution in Indian warfare: Introduced gunpowder artillery and field matchlocks (Tufang) to North India, directed by Ottoman master-gunners Ustad Ali Quli and Mustafa Rumi; deployed the Ottoman tactical formation (Rumi device / Araba carts tied together with rawhide ropes) combined with the central Asian flanking maneuver (Tulghuma) to encircle hostile armies.
Four Decisive Battles: 1. First Battle of Panipat (21 April 1526): Decisively crushed Ibrahim Lodi, breaking the Delhi Sultanate.

2. Battle of Khanwa (16 March 1527 near Bharatpur): Crushed the formidable Rajput confederacy led by Rana Sanga of Mewar; Babur declared the war a Jihad, broke his wine goblets, swore total abstinence, and assumed the triumphant title "Ghazi".
3. Battle of Chanderi (1528): Besieged and captured Chanderi from Rajput ruler Medini Rai, resulting in Rajput women committing Jauhar.

4. Battle of Ghagra (1529): Fought on the Ghagra river (Bihar/UP) against the allied Afghan forces under Mahmud Lodi and Sultan Nusrat Shah of Bengal; secured Mughal hegemony across the entire Gangetic plains from Kabul to Bihar.
