Literary & Aesthetic Genius: Autobiography (Tuzuk-i-Baburi / Baburnama): Composed in his mother-tongue Chagatai Turkic; celebrated worldwide for unvarnished frankness, acute naturalist observations of Indian flora, fauna, climate, geography, fruits (mango, melons), and psychological portraits of contemporaries; translated into Persian by Abdur Rahim Khan-i-Khanan during Akbar's reign.

Charbagh Garden Design: Pioneered the formal symmetrical Persian four-quadrant garden (Charbagh) layout with raised stone pathways and intersecting running water channels; laid out Aram Bagh (Ram Bagh) at Agra.

women.name: Qutlugh Nigar Khanum
women.note: Played a significant role in his life and court; well-educated and supported literary and cultural activities. Though her direct political role was limited, her presence strengthened the royal household and cultural environment.

events.title: Birth of Babur
events.desc: Born in Andijan; descended from Timur and Genghis Khan through the Chagatai line.

events.title: Invasion of India
events.desc: Invited by discontented Afghan nobles, Babur advances from Kabul via Panipat, capturing Lahore and Punjab.

events.title: First Battle of Panipat
events.desc: Babur defeats and kills Ibrahim Lodi using the Tulughma flanking tactic, artillery and cart fortifications, founding the Mughal Empire.

events.title: Battle of Khanwa
events.desc: Babur defeats the Rajput confederacy under Rana Sanga of Mewar, securing Mughal control of North India.

events.title: Battles of Chanderi and Ghaghra
events.desc: Babur defeats the Afghan chief Mahmud Lodi and an Afghan confederacy, consolidating control over North India.

events.title: Death of Babur
events.desc: Babur dies in Agra; succeeded by his son Humayun.

people.name: Babur
people.note: r. 1526–1530; author of the Baburnama.

people.name: Ibrahim Lodi
people.role: Last Sultan of the Delhi Sultanate
people.note: Defeated and killed by Babur at Panipat, 1526.

people.name: Rana Sanga
people.note: Defeated by Babur at the Battle of Khanwa, 1527.

prelims: Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi in the First Battle of Panipat on 21 April 1526, using Ottoman Araba cart lines and Tulghuma flanking tactics.
Babur assumed the title of "Ghazi" after defeating Rana Sanga of Mewar at the Battle of Khanwa in 1527.
Babur's autobiography, the Tuzuk-i-Baburi (Baburnama), was originally written in Chagatai Turkic and later translated into Persian by Abdur Rahim Khan-i-Khanan.
Babur introduced the symmetrical Persian four-fold garden layout (Charbagh) into India, creating the Aram Bagh at Agra.
The two master Ottoman artillery experts who directed Babur's cannons were Ustad Ali Quli and Mustafa Rumi.
The Battle of Ghagra (1529) was the first major battle in India fought simultaneously on land and in river waters, in which Babur defeated the allied Afghan chiefs.
Babur was initially buried in the Aram Bagh at Agra before his mortal remains were relocated to the Bagh-e-Babur in Kabul according to his will.
mains: Evaluate the military innovations introduced by Babur in Indian warfare, with special reference to field artillery, gunpowder, and the Tulghuma tactical system.
Assess the historical, literary, and naturalist value of Babur's autobiography, the Baburnama, as a primary source for early 16th-century Indian geography, flora, and society.
Analyze the geopolitical consequences of the Battle of Khanwa (1527), examining why it was far more decisive than the First Battle of Panipat in consolidating Mughal supremacy.

periods.title: Humayun
periods.tagline: The Second Mughal Emperor — Restorer of the Empire, Patron of Culture, Learning & Architecture
periods.overview: If Babur's reign shows how the Mughal Empire could be won, Humayun's shows just as clearly how easily it could have been lost — and the fact that it was not, despite a full decade and a half of exile, is arguably the single most important twist in early Mughal history. Inheriting the throne at Babur's death in 1530, Humayun faced immediate challenges from his own brothers and, more seriously, from the brilliant Afghan administrator-general Sher Shah Suri, who inflicted decisive defeats at Chausa (1539) and Kannauj (1540) and drove Humayun out of India entirely. What followed was not merely survival but genuine transformation: fifteen years in Persian exile, sheltered by the Safavid ruler Shah Tahmasp I, exposed Humayun to Persian court culture, art, and administrative practice in ways that would deeply influence Mughal aesthetics for generations. When Sher Shah's Sur dynasty collapsed into infighting after his death, Humayun seized the opportunity, returned with Persian military support, defeated the Sur successors, and reclaimed Delhi and Agra in 1555 — only to die the following year after a fall from his library stairs, leaving the restored empire to his thirteen-year-old son Akbar. Humayun's own reign, then, produced comparatively little in the way of conquest or institution-building; its real legacy is that the empire survived at all, and that it returned carrying a stronger current of Persian cultural influence, most visibly embodied in Humayun's own tomb in Delhi — the first great Mughal garden-tomb and the direct architectural ancestor of the Taj Mahal.

phases.name: Accession & Early Years
points: Became emperor after Babur's death on 26 December 1530; faced challenges from his brothers (Kamran, Askari, Hindal); spent initial years securing the empire

phases.name: Challenges & Loss of Empire
points: Strong Afghan challenge under Sher Shah Suri; defeated at Chausa (1539); defeated at Kannauj/Bilgram (1540); lost Delhi & Agra, went into exile

phases.name: Exile & Persian Years
points: Took refuge in Sindh, Rajasthan and finally Persia; received help from Shah Tahmasp I of Iran; stayed in Persia for about 15 years, learning Persian culture, Shia ideas, art, etiquette and administration

phases.name: Reconquest of India
points: With Persian military support, returned to India; defeated Sikandar Suri at Machhiwara (Punjab) in 1555; recaptured Delhi (23 July 1555) and Agra; gradually restored Mughal rule in North India

phases.name: Last Years & Death
points: Spent last year consolidating his rule; died on 24 January 1556 in Delhi after a fall from the stairs of his library at Purana Qila; buried in Humayun's Tomb, Delhi (first garden-tomb in India)

Political Administration: Tried to maintain his father Babur's administrative system; appointed competent nobles in provinces; could not centralise authority strongly due to constant struggles
Economy: Revenue system continued as before; encouraged trade and commerce; promoted agriculture, dug canals and restored wells in some areas
Military: Inherited a strong army from Babur; used artillery and firearms; defeats due to Afghan strategy and lack of stability; reorganized the army with Persian help during exile
Art, Architecture & Culture: Great patron of Persian culture, literature, art and architecture; introduced Persian artists, calligraphers and scholars in India
Built Humayun's Tomb in Delhi (designed by Mirak Mirza Ghiyas) — first garden tomb in India; loved books and astrology; established a large library at Purana Qila
Foreign Relations: Good relations with Safavid ruler Shah Tahmasp I of Persia; received military and financial help during exile
Fratricidal Divisions & Afghan Resurgenc: Inherited weaknesses: Nasiruddin Humayun (r. 1530–1540 and 1555–1556 CE) divided his vast, unassimilated empire among his three disloyal brothers according to Timurid tradition: Kamran received Kabul and Kandahar, Askari received Sambhal, and Hindal received Alwar/Mewat; undermined central treasury and unified military command.

Duel with Sher Khan Suri: Confronted the strategic Afghan genius Sher Khan; suffered catastrophic routs at the Battle of Chausa (1539, where Humayun escaped drowning in the Ganga with the help of water-carrier Nizam) and the Battle of Bilgram / Kannauj (1540), forcing Humayun into a 15-year harrowing exile in Sindh, Rajasthan, and Persia.
Exile in Safavid Persia & Restoration (1: Safavid alliance: Welcomed by Shah Tahmasp I of Safavid Persia; received Persian troops in exchange for ceding Kandahar and embracing Shia rituals; brought illustrious Persian master painters Mir Sayyid Ali and Abdus Samad back to India, founding the Mughal School of Miniature Painting.

Restoration & Death: Recaptured Lahore and Delhi in 1555 CE following the collapse of the Sur successors (defeating Sikandar Suri at the Battle of Sirhind); founded the city of Dinpanah in Delhi; died tragically in January 1556 after tumbling down the steep stone stairs of his library (Sher Mandal) in Delhi; historian Stanley Lane-Poole remarked: "Humayun tumbled through life, and tumbled out of it."
Humayun's Tomb (Prototypical Masterpiece: Architectural landmark: Commissioned in 1565 CE by his senior widow Biga Begum (Haji Begum); designed by Persian architect Mirak Mirza Ghiyas; first monumental garden-tomb (Charbagh) on the Indian subcontinent; first monument to feature a colossal double-dome of white marble, red sandstone cladding, and octagonal Hasht-Bihisht chambers; direct stylistic progenitor of the Taj Mahal.

women.name: Haji Begum (Humayun's sister)
women.note: Played a key role during the crisis; managed affairs and supported Humayun in exile.

women.name: Gulbadan Begum
women.note: Wrote the Humayun-nama, an important primary source for this period.

events.title: Humayun's accession
events.desc: Succeeds Babur as the second Mughal emperor, immediately facing challenges from his brothers.

events.title: Defeats at Chausa and Kannauj
events.desc: Sher Shah Suri decisively defeats Humayun, who loses Delhi and Agra and goes into exile.

events.title: Persian exile
events.desc: Humayun spends fifteen years in exile, receiving refuge and military support from the Safavid ruler Shah Tahmasp I.

events.title: Reconquest of Delhi
events.desc: With Persian support, Humayun defeats the Suri successors and recaptures Delhi and Agra, restoring Mughal rule.

events.title: Death of Humayun
events.desc: Humayun dies after a fall from his library stairs at Purana Qila; his son Akbar becomes emperor at age 13.

people.name: Sher Shah Suri
people.note: Defeated Humayun and ruled North India 1540–1545.

people.name: Shah Tahmasp I
people.note: Provided refuge and military support to Humayun in exile.

prelims: Humayun was decisively routed by Sher Shah Suri at the Battle of Chausa (1539) and the Battle of Bilgram/Kannauj (1540), driving him into exile.
Humayun regained the throne of Delhi in 1555 CE by defeating Sikandar Suri at the Battle of Sirhind.
Humayun brought master Persian miniature painters Mir Sayyid Ali and Abdus Samad to India, laying the foundation of the Mughal atelier.
Humayun built the fortress city of Dinpanah on the banks of the Yamuna in Delhi.
Humayun died in 1556 CE from injuries sustained after falling down the staircase of the Sher Mandal library building in Purana Qila.
Humayun's Tomb in Delhi was designed by the Persian architect Mirak Mirza Ghiyas and commissioned by his widow Haji Begum (Biga Begum).
The Humayun-Nama, an intimate biographical account of Humayun's life and court, was composed in Persian by his sister Gulbadan Begum.
mains: Examine the internal and external factors that caused the collapse of Humayun's empire in 1540 CE, evaluating his personal character and political miscalculations.
Assess the architectural significance of Humayun's Tomb in Delhi, explaining how it served as a transitional model and structural prototype for the Taj Mahal.
Discuss the cultural impact of Humayun's exile at the Safavid court of Persia on the evolution of Mughal art, architecture, and court etiquette.

quickFacts: 24 January 1556, Delhi; buried in Humayun's Tomb

periods.title: The Sur Interregnum
periods.tagline: A Turbulent Decade and a Half that Saw the Decline of the Sur Empire and the Re-emergence of the Mughals under Humayun
periods.overview: The fifteen years between Humayun's two reigns are sometimes treated as a mere gap in Mughal history, but the Sur Interregnum they cover deserves attention on its own terms: Sher Shah Suri, the Afghan general who defeated and exiled Humayun, used his brief five-year reign to build an administrative model — a standardised land-revenue survey and assessment system, the Grand Trunk Road with regularly spaced sarais for travellers, a reliable postal network, and a stable currency — sophisticated enough that the Mughals would later adopt substantial parts of it wholesale once they returned to power. His son Islam Shah Suri largely continued this efficient administration for another eight years, but the dynasty's fatal weakness became apparent immediately after his death in 1553: without either founder's combination of military authority and administrative vision, the Sur state fractured almost instantly into competing claimants and factional infighting, with no successor able to command the loyalty Sher Shah had built. It was this rapid disintegration — not any renewed Mughal military strength — that let Humayun walk back into Delhi in 1555 with comparatively modest Persian assistance, a reminder that good administration alone, without a stable mechanism for succession, could not guarantee a dynasty's survival any more than military conquest alone could.

phases.name: Sher Shah Suri
points: Occupied Delhi in 1540 after defeating Humayun at Chausa (1539) and Kannauj (1540); founded the Sur Empire
Able and just ruler; died on 22 May 1545 (accidental death)

phases.name: Islam Shah Suri
points: Succeeded Sher Shah; expanded & consolidated the empire; efficient administrator; died on 19 November 1553 (natural death)

phases.name: Internal Struggles
points: Weak successors led to factionalism — Adil Shah, Ibrahim Shah, Sikandar Shah and others; nobles fought for power; empire lost strength

phases.name: Humayun's Return
points: Took advantage of Sur disunity; with help of Persian Shah Tahmasp, re-entered Delhi on 23 July 1555; re-established Mughal rule

phases.name: Humayun's Death
points: Died on 24 January 1556 after falling from the stairs of his library at Purana Qila, Delhi; Akbar became emperor at age 13

Political Administration: Sher Shah: established the Sur Empire, strong central authority, divided the empire into provinces (Sarkars) and districts (Parganas)
Islam Shah: consolidated the empire, maintained law & order, efficient bureaucracy
Period of instability (1553–1555): weak rulers, factionalism among nobles, loss of central control
Economy: Sher Shah: land revenue system (Zabt), measurement of land, fixed revenue demand
Islam Shah: continued revenue reforms, encouraged agriculture, trade & industry
Instability period: revenue system neglected, jagirdars became powerful, economic decline
Administration & Infrastructure: Sher Shah built roads (e.g. Grand Trunk Road, Sonargaon to Peshawar), constructed sarais at regular intervals, improved communications, introduced standard weights and measures, a well-organized postal system (Dak Chowkis), Patta (record of rights) & Qabuliyat (agreement)
Sher Shah Suri's Administrative Zenith: Rise from Farid to Sultan: Born Farid Khan in Sasaram (Bihar); awarded the title "Sher Khan" after slaying a tiger single-handedly; established the Second Afghan Empire (r. 1540–1545 CE).

Hierarchical administrative structure: Empire divided into 47 territorial divisions called Sarkars; each Sarkar administered by two royal officers: Shiqdar-i-Shiqdaran (law, order, and criminal justice) and Munsif-i-Munsifan (revenue assessment and civil disputes); each Sarkar was subdivided into several Parganas headed by a Shiqdar (executive), Amin/Munsif (revenue), Fotadar (treasurer), and two Karkuns (Persian and Hindi record scribes).
Pioneering Agrarian & Currency Reforms: Rai system of crop measurement: Land scientifically measured using a standard rope Gaz-i-Sikandari; cultivable soil classified into three grades based on fertility: Good, Middling, and Bad; average yield calculated and state revenue fixed at 1/3rd of produce, payable in cash or kind.

Patta and Qabuliyat: Instituted written title deeds (Patta) issued by the state specifying the peasant's land holdings and assessed tax, while the cultivator signed an agreement deed of acceptance (Qabuliyat); eliminated fraudulent extortion by corrupt revenue officers.

Standardized Imperial Coinage: Reformed monetary chaos by introducing standard tri-metallic coinage: pure silver Rupiya (178 grains of high-purity silver, which served as the direct ancestor of modern Indian currency) and copper Dam (380 grains; exchange ratio 1 Rupiya = 64 Dams).
Communications, Highway Infrastructure &: Sadak-e-Azam (Grand Trunk Road): Re-engineered and paved the ancient imperial highway from Sonargaon (Bengal) through Delhi and Lahore to Peshawar (Indus river) spanning over 2,500 km; lined with shady trees, fruit orchards, and freshwater wells.

Sarais (Caravanserais) & Postal Dak: Constructed 1,700 fortified roadside inns (Sarais) every two kos (approx 6 km), providing separate food, water, and lodging for Hindus and Muslims; functioned as state post-houses (Dak-Chowkis) where horses were kept for rapid message transmission.

Mausoleum at Sasaram: Magnificent octagonal red sandstone tomb built in the middle of a vast artificial lake at Sasaram (Bihar), representing the transition from Sultanate architectural massiveness to Mughal aesthetic grace; died in 1545 CE during the siege of Kalinjar fort due to an accidental explosion of a gunpowder magazine.

women.name: Women in this period
women.note: Very little direct mention of prominent women in the sources for the Sur period; women generally lived in purdah; the era was comparatively peaceful under Sher Shah and Islam Shah.

events.title: Sher Shah Suri founds the Sur Empire
events.desc: After defeating Humayun at Chausa and Kannauj, Sher Shah occupies Delhi and establishes efficient, model administration.

events.title: Sher Shah's administrative reforms
events.desc: Construction of the Grand Trunk Road, a standardized revenue system, and a postal network become a model later adopted by the Mughals.

events.title: Sur factionalism
events.desc: Weak successors after Islam Shah's death lead to noble infighting and the collapse of central control.

events.title: Humayun recaptures Delhi
events.desc: Taking advantage of Sur disunity, and with Persian support, Humayun re-enters Delhi, ending the Sur Interregnum.

people.name: Sher Shah Suri
people.note: r. 1540–1545; model of good governance.

people.name: Islam Shah Suri
people.note: r. 1545–1553; consolidator.

prelims: Sher Shah Suri introduced the standard silver coin called "Rupiya" (178 grains) and copper coin called "Dam" (380 grains), with an exchange ratio of 1 Rupiya = 64 Dams.
The system of "Patta" (deed of title) and "Qabuliyat" (deed of agreement) for peasant land revenue settlement was introduced by Sher Shah Suri.
Under Sher Shah, the empire was divided into Sarkars, each headed by a Shiqdar-i-Shiqdaran (law and order) and Munsif-i-Munsifan (revenue).
Sher Shah rebuilt the ancient highway from Sonargaon (Bengal) to Peshawar, known as the "Sadak-e-Azam", later named the "Grand Trunk Road" by Lord Auckland.
Sher Shah constructed 1,700 roadside Sarais (inns) that also functioned as royal postal exchange stations (Dak-Chowkis).
The magnificent octagonal tomb of Sher Shah Suri, standing in the centre of a large artificial water tank, is located at Sasaram (Bihar).
Sher Shah Suri died in 1545 CE during the siege of Kalinjar Fort (Bundelkhand) when a store of gunpowder exploded accidentally.
mains: Critically examine the administrative, agrarian, and monetary reforms of Sher Shah Suri, evaluating why historians describe him as the "fore-runner of Akbar".
Analyze the infrastructure, trade, and communication achievements of Sher Shah Suri with special reference to the Sadak-e-Azam and the Sarai postal network.
Assess the architectural features of Sher Shah's Tomb at Sasaram and the Qila-i-Kuhna Mosque in Purana Qila, Delhi.

quickFacts: Chausa (1539), Kannauj (1540), Death of Sher Shah (1545), Death of Islam Shah (1553), Humayun's Return (1555)

periods.title: Akbar the Great
periods.tagline: Founder of a United & Tolerant India — Builder of Empire, Promoter of Unity, Patron of Culture, Pioneer of Good Governance
periods.overview: Akbar's forty-nine-year reign is where the Mughal Empire stops being a fragile, twice-nearly-lost conquest and becomes a genuinely durable, well-governed state — and the scale of what he actually built, starting from the throne he inherited as a thirteen-year-old under regent Bairam Khan, is difficult to overstate. Militarily, Akbar's conquests brought Malwa, Gujarat, Bengal, Rajasthan, Kashmir, and Sindh under direct Mughal control, transforming a patchwork inheritance into a genuinely unified empire; administratively, his Mansabdari system of ranked nobility and the Dahsala land-revenue system devised by Raja Todar Mal (built on careful measurement and assessment of actual agricultural output rather than arbitrary demand) gave that empire a bureaucratic backbone sophisticated enough to survive for centuries. What sets Akbar apart from every other conqueror of comparable scale, though, is his deliberate, sustained experimentation with religious and cultural policy: abolishing the Jizya tax on non-Muslims and the pilgrimage tax, hosting interfaith debates at the Ibadat Khana in his new capital of Fatehpur Sikri, forming marriage alliances with Rajput houses that gave Hindu nobility real positions of power and trust, and eventually proposing Din-i-Ilahi, a personal ethical path drawing on multiple traditions — never a state religion, and followed only by a small circle at court, but a genuinely unusual gesture from a 16th-century emperor. The result was a composite Mughal court culture — blending Persian, Central Asian, and Indian artistic, architectural, and administrative traditions — sturdy and legitimate enough that his successors, whatever their individual differences, could build directly on his foundations rather than having to refight the basic questions of how the empire should be run.

phases.name: Accession
points: Became emperor at the age of 13 after Humayun's death; Bairam Khan acted as regent; defeated Hemu at the Second Battle of Panipat (1556)

phases.name: Consolidation
points: Captured Delhi & Agra; eliminated threats from Sikandar Sur (1557) and other Afghan chieftains; made Bairam Khan retire (1560); started direct rule

phases.name: Expansion
points: Conquered Malwa (1561), Gujarat (1572), Bengal (1576), Rajasthan/Amber (1562), Marwar (1568), Bikaner/Jaisalmer (1570), Sindh (1591), Kashmir (1586)
Defeated Mughals in Kabul & Qandahar (1581); annexed vast new territories

phases.name: Administrative & Ideological Innovations
points: Introduced Sulh-i-Kul (universal peace); abolished Jizya (1564); started Din-i-Ilahi (1582)
Regularized administration and revenue system (Dahsala system by Todar Mal); strengthened central authority

phases.name: Last Years
points: Consolidated empire and ensured stability; patronized art, culture, literature and learning; died on 27 October 1605 at Agra

Political Administration: Established centralized administration; Mansabdari System (graded ranking of nobles, 10 to 10,000); Jagirdari System (land assignments in lieu of salary)
Abolished the practice of transferring jagirs in revenue-rich areas only; established an efficient intelligence system; improved provincial administration — Subah, Sarkar, Pargana system
Economy: Land Revenue System – Dahsala System (introduced by Todar Mal); measurement of land – Zabt System; classification of land and crops; fixed revenue demand – 1/3rd of average produce
Encouraged agriculture, irrigation, trade and crafts; developed infrastructure — roads, sarais, bridges
Religion: Policy of Sulh-i-Kul – peace with all; abolished Jizya (1564) and Pilgrimage Tax; held Ibadat Khana discussions (from 1575) with scholars of different religions
Promoted Sulh (ethical monotheism); established Din-i-Ilahi (1582) — a spiritual path based on truth, morality and service
Society: Promoted social harmony and integration; abolished slavery (except prisoners of war); encouraged inter-caste and inter-faith relations
Rajput policy — matrimonial alliances, high positions for Rajputs; won hearts of people through justice and welfare measures
Art, Architecture & Learning: Blended Indian, Persian and Central Asian styles; built Fatehpur Sikri, Agra Fort (renovated), Lahore Fort; patronized miniature painting — Mughal School of Painting
Encouraged literature in Persian, Sanskrit, Hindi, Arabic; translated the Mahabharata (Razmnama), Ramayana, Atharvaveda, Upanishads, Bible etc. into Persian; founded Maktabs and Madrasas
Consolidation & Rajput Matrimonial Polic: Accession & Regency: Crowned at Kalanaur (Punjab) at age 13 (1556 CE); regency of Bairam Khan (Khan-i-Khanan); defeated Hemu (Hemu Vikramaditya) at the Second Battle of Panipat (5 November 1556); ended Petticoat Government (Maham Anaga) in 1562 CE.

Rajput Conciliation Policy: Married Harkha Bai (Jodha Bai / Mariam-uz-Zamani), daughter of Raja Bharmal of Amber (1562 CE); inducted Rajput princes into highest imperial ranks (Raja Bhagwant Das, Raja Man Singh, Todar Mal); conquered Chittor (1568; siege resisted by Jaimal and Patta) and Ranthambore; Maharana Pratap resisted heroically, fighting the epic Battle of Haldighati (18 June 1576; Mughal army commanded by Raja Man Singh).
Mansabdari System & Military Hierarchy: Institutional structure: Universal administrative, civil, and military cadre introduced in 1571 CE; every officer assigned a numerical rank (Mansab) ranging from 10 to 10,000 (highest reserved for princes).

Zat and Sawar duality: Introduced dual ranks in 1595–96 CE: Zat indicated the officer's personal status, hierarchical standing, and basic salary; Sawar determined the number of mounted horsemen (cavalry troops) the officer was obligated to maintain for state service.

Dagh and Chehra: Revived the branding of horses (Dagh) and descriptive rolls of troopers (Chehra); classified troops into Dah-Bisti (2 horses per trooper); payment made either in cash (Naqdi) or through revenue assignments of land (Jagir).
Todar Mal's Dahsala (Zabt) Land Revenue: Ain-i-Dahsala (1580 CE): Formulated by finance minister Raja Todar Mal; average yield of each crop and its average market price over the past 10 years (1570–1580) were scientifically calculated; state revenue share fixed at one-third (33.3%) of average produce, payable in cash.

Land classification into 4 categories: 1. Polaj (annually cultivated land, never left fallow), 2. Parauti (land left fallow for 1 or 2 years to regain fertility), 3. Chachar (land left fallow for 3 to 4 years), 4. Banjar (uncultivated wasteland for 5 or more years).

Measurement & Offices: Replaced rope measurement with bamboo rods joined with iron rings (Tanab / Bamboo jarib); introduced the Ilahi Gaz (41 digits / 33 inches). Pargana officers: Amalguzar (revenue collector), Qanungo (keeper of village revenue records), Patwari (village accountant).
Religious Evolution: Ibadat Khana to Sul: Early reforms: Abolished pilgrimage tax on Hindus (1563 CE) and repealed Jizya (1564 CE).

Ibadat Khana (House of Worship, 1575 CE): Erected at Fatehpur Sikri; initially for debates among Sunni Muslim scholars; later opened in 1578 CE to representatives of all faiths: Purushottam and Devi (Hinduism), Dastur Meherji Rana (Zoroastrianism / Parsi), Harivijaya Suri and Vijayasena Suri (Jainism - awarded title Jagadguru), Father Rudolf Acquaviva and Antonio Monserrate (Jesuit Portuguese Christianity).

Mahzarnama (Infallibility Decree, September 1579): Drafted by Sheikh Mubarak (father of Abul Fazl and Faizi); proclaimed Akbar as the "Imam-i-Adil" (supreme arbiter in religious disputes), empowering him to choose any interpretation of Islamic law consistent with public welfare.

Sulh-i-Kul & Din-i-Ilahi (Tauhid-i-Ilahi, 1582 CE): Ethos of universal peace, toleration, and harmony (Sulh-i-Kul); launched Din-i-Ilahi as an ethical-spiritual fellowship promoting reason, self-restraint, and devotion to the Emperor without dogma, holy book, or priestly class; only 18 prominent courtiers joined, including Raja Birbal.
Art, Literature & Fatehpur Sikri: Fatehpur Sikri Capital: Founded in 1571 CE near shrine of Sufi saint Shaikh Salim Chishti; built Buland Darwaza (lofty 176-foot triumphal gateway commemorating Gujarat conquest 1572), Panch Mahal (five-storey pyramidal colonnaded palace), Diwan-i-Khas (with central carved pillar bracket), Jodha Bai's Palace.

Navaratnas & Literary translations: Court adorned by Nine Gems (Abul Fazl, Faizi, Tansen, Birbal, Todar Mal, Man Singh, Abdur Rahim Khan-i-Khanan, Fakir Aziao-Din, Mullah Do-Piyaza); Abul Fazl authored Akbarnama and Ain-i-Akbari; Maktab Khana (translation bureau) translated Mahabharata into Persian as Razmnama (illustrated by Daswant and Basawan), Ramayana, and Rajatarangini.

women.name: Mariam-uz-Zamani (Harkha Bai)
women.note: Hindu Rajput princess; influential in court, patron of charity & trade activities.

women.name: Salima Sultan Begum
women.note: Daughter of Sher Shah; author of the Humayun-nama; respected by Akbar.

women.name: Ruqaiya Sultan Begum
women.note: Educated and cultured; maintained correspondence.

women.name: Jodha Bai (Harkha Bai)
women.note: Akbar's chief consort; promoted religious harmony.

women.name: Other royal women
women.note: Played important roles in administration, charity, diplomacy and cultural patronage; though women did not hold formal political power, they had significant influence in court & society.

events.title: Second Battle of Panipat
events.desc: The young Akbar, guided by Bairam Khan, defeats Hemu and secures the throne.

events.title: Abolition of Jizya
events.desc: Akbar abolishes the Jizya tax on non-Muslims, part of his broader policy of religious tolerance.

events.title: Conquest of Gujarat and Bengal
events.desc: Major territorial expansion consolidates Mughal control over key trading regions.

events.title: Ibadat Khana established
events.desc: A 'House of Worship' at Fatehpur Sikri where Akbar holds interfaith religious discussions.

events.title: Din-i-Ilahi founded
events.desc: Akbar introduces a spiritual path for a select few followers, based on truth, morality and service — never a state religion.

events.title: Death of Akbar
events.desc: Akbar dies at Agra, leaving behind a strong, stable and inclusive empire.

people.name: Akbar the Great
people.note: r. 1556–1605; widely regarded as the greatest Mughal emperor.

people.name: Bairam Khan
people.note: Guided the young Akbar through the empire's early consolidation.

people.name: Raja Todar Mal
people.note: Devised the Dahsala/Zabt land revenue system.

people.name: Abul Fazl
people.note: Author of the Akbarnama and Ain-i-Akbari.

prelims: Akbar introduced the Mansabdari system based on the twin ranks of "Zat" (personal status and salary) and "Sawar" (cavalry quota required to maintain).
The "Ain-i-Dahsala" system of land revenue, introduced in 1580 CE, was engineered by Akbar's finance minister Raja Todar Mal.
Under Akbar's revenue system, land was classified into four categories: Polaj (regularly cultivated), Parauti (fallow 1–2 yrs), Chachar (fallow 3–4 yrs), and Banjar (fallow 5+ yrs).
Akbar established the Ibadat Khana (Hall of Prayer) at Fatehpur Sikri in 1575 CE for inter-faith religious debates.
The "Mahzarnama" (Infallibility Decree) was issued in 1579 CE, declaring Akbar the supreme arbiter (Imam-i-Adil) in religious disputes.
Akbar abolished the pilgrimage tax in 1563 CE and the Jizya tax on non-Muslims in 1564 CE.
The Buland Darwaza at Fatehpur Sikri was built by Akbar in 1601 CE to commemorate his conquest of Gujarat.
mains: Critically evaluate the administrative and military structure of the Mansabdari system, discussing how the dual Zat and Sawar ranks functioned.
Trace the intellectual and religious evolution of Akbar from orthodoxy to the Ibadat Khana debates, the Mahzarnama, and the philosophy of Sulh-i-Kul.
Analyze the features and economic impact of Todar Mal's Dahsala (Zabt) system on the agrarian economy of the Mughal Empire.
Examine Akbar's Rajput policy, highlighting the diplomatic balance of matrimonial alliances, military induction, and religious toleration in building an all-India empire.

quickFacts: Second Battle of Panipat (1556), Gujarat (1572), Haldighati (1576)*

periods.title: Jahangir
periods.tagline: The Fourth Mughal Emperor — Connoisseur of Art & Nature, Just and Tolerant Ruler
periods.overview: Jahangir inherits from his father Akbar an empire already well-administered and largely at peace, and his twenty-two-year reign is best understood as a continuation and refinement of that stability rather than a new departure — a period in which the Mughal court could afford to turn its attention toward art, natural history, and justice rather than consolidation or conquest. His introduction of the 'Chain of Justice', a literal chain hung outside his palace that any subject could ring to appeal directly to the emperor, exemplifies the personal, almost theatrical style of just kingship he cultivated, while his genuine passion for natural history produced some of the most naturalistic and closely observed painting in the entire Mughal tradition. The most consequential development of his reign, though, was neither artistic nor administrative but marital: his marriage to Nur Jahan in 1611 gradually made her an extraordinarily powerful political actor in her own right — issuing farmans (royal orders) in her own name, a privilege almost unheard of for a Mughal woman, and effectively co-governing alongside (and at times overshadowing) her husband, particularly as Jahangir's health declined. His reign also marks the empire's first serious institutional contact with England, granting the East India Company trading rights at Surat in 1608 and hosting the ambassador Sir Thomas Roe from 1615 to 1619 — a relationship that would, over the following two and a half centuries, prove far more consequential to Indian history than anyone at Jahangir's court could have anticipated.

phases.name: Accession
points: Acceded to the throne on 24 October 1605 after the death of Akbar; faced rebellion of his son Khusrau (1606 CE) which was suppressed; married Jagat Gosain (1607), daughter of Raja Man Singh

phases.name: Consolidation & Early Years
points: Consolidated the empire and continued Akbar's policies; strengthened nobility through the Mansabdari system; patronised arts, culture and literature

phases.name: Major Events & Developments
points: Granted a charter to the English East India Company (1608) to establish a factory at Surat; Prince Khusrau rebelled again (1612) but was defeated and blinded
Nur Jahan became a powerful influence after their marriage (1611); Jahangir invaded Kangra (1615) and incorporated it; Sir Thomas Roe, English ambassador, visited the court (1615–19)

phases.name: Later Years
points: Spent more time in pleasure, art and nature; continued peace and prosperity in the empire; administration remained efficient though with increasing influence of the Nur Jahan group

phases.name: Death
points: Died on 28 October 1627 at Lahore; succeeded by his son Shah Jahan; buried in Shahdara (Lahore) in a magnificent tomb

Political Administration: Maintained strong central authority and the mansabdari system; efficient revenue administration continued; emphasis on justice and welfare of subjects
Justice & Reforms: Introduced the 'Chain of Justice' to ensure people could directly appeal to the king; appointment of able ministers and officials; continued land revenue system and mansabdari system; focus on welfare of subjects and fair taxation
Religion: Followed the policy of Sulh-i-Kul (universal peace) of Akbar; personally inclined towards Sufism; promoted tolerance and religious harmony
Art, Architecture & Culture: Flourishing of Mughal painting; naturalism and portraiture reached its peak; development of gardens (Shalimar Bagh, Kashmir); patronised literature in Persian; wrote the Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri (autobiography)
Foreign Relations: Friendly relations with England; charter to the English East India Company (1608); contacts with Persia, Ottoman Empire, Europe; Sir Thomas Roe's embassy (1615–19) was an important event
Consolidation & The Golden Chain of Just: Accession & Twelve Edicts: Nuruddin Muhammad Jahangir (r. 1605–1627 CE) installed the famous Zanjir-i-Adl (Golden Chain of Justice) linking the Shah Burj of Agra Fort to a stone post on the Yamuna bank, equipped with 60 golden bells for direct access by any oppressed subject; issued 12 imperial decrees (Dastur-ul-Amal) prohibiting arbitrary transit cesses (Tamgha), house confiscation, and animal slaughter on certain days.

Rebellion of Prince Khusrau (1606): Eldest son Prince Khusrau revolted with blessings of fifth Sikh Guru, Guru Arjan Dev; Khusrau was captured and blinded; Guru Arjan Dev was executed at Lahore, creating an enduring rift between the Mughal state and the Sikh Panth.
Diplomacy & European Contacts: Mewar Settlement (1615 CE): Concluded an honorable peace treaty with Rana Amar Singh of Mewar negotiated by Prince Khurram (Shah Jahan); Rana was exempt from personal attendance at court and sent crown prince Karan Singh as Mansabdar of 5,000; Chittor fort restored on condition it would not be fortified.

British East India Company Embassies: Captain William Hawkins (1608–1611, received 400 Mansab, styled "English Khan") and Sir Thomas Roe (1615–1619, ambassador of King James I of England); Roe secured imperial farmans granting English trading factories at Surat, Cambay, and Ahmedabad.
Nur Jahan Junta & Artistic Splendor: Nur Jahan (Mehr-un-Nisa): Married Jahangir in 1611 CE; assumed title "Nur Mahal" then "Nur Jahan" (Light of the World); formed the powerful court faction (Junta) consisting of herself, her father Mirza Ghiyas Beg (Itmad-ud-Daula), brother Asaf Khan, and Prince Khurram; royal coins struck jointly in her name; issued imperial farmans.

Mughal Miniature Painting Zenith: Jahangir was a consummate aesthetic connoisseur (boasted in his autobiography Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri that he could identify the brushstrokes of individual artists on a single portrait); specialized in naturalist studies of birds, animals, flowers, and individual portraiture; master court artists: Ustad Mansur (Wunder of the Age / Nadir-ul-Asr, famed for painting the Siberian crane, Dodo, and Bengal Florican), Abul Hasan (Nadir-uz-Zaman), Bishandas, Manohar, and Govardhan.

Itmad-ud-Daula's Tomb (Agra): Built by Nur Jahan (1622–1628 CE); first monument built entirely of white marble inlaid with extensive delicate Pietra Dura (semi-precious stone inlays forming floral arabesques), serving as the stylistic transition from red sandstone to Shah Jahan's marble architecture.

women.name: Nur Jahan (Mehr-un-Nisa)
women.note: Exercised great influence on administration, politics and military decisions; issued farmans in her own name; patron of arts, architecture and culture.

women.name: Jagat Gosain
women.note: Wife of Jahangir; other women also influenced court culture.

events.title: Jahangir's accession
events.desc: Ascends the throne after Akbar's death and continues most of his father's policies.

events.title: Rebellions of Prince Khusrau
events.desc: Jahangir's son rebels twice; the second rebellion ends with Khusrau's defeat and blinding.

events.title: Charter to the English East India Company
events.desc: Jahangir grants trading rights, allowing the English to establish a factory at Surat.

events.title: Marriage to Nur Jahan
events.desc: Nur Jahan becomes an increasingly powerful influence on administration and court politics.

events.title: Embassy of Sir Thomas Roe
events.desc: The English ambassador's mission to Jahangir's court marks a key moment in early Anglo-Mughal relations.

events.title: Death of Jahangir
events.desc: Jahangir dies at Lahore; succeeded by Shah Jahan.

people.name: Jahangir
people.note: r. 1605–1627; author of the Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri.

people.name: Nur Jahan
people.note: Wielded major administrative and political influence.

people.name: Sir Thomas Roe
people.note: Represented King James I at Jahangir's court, 1615–1619.

prelims: Jahangir installed the "Zanjir-i-Adl" (Chain of Justice) with 60 bells at Agra Fort to provide direct access to royal justice.
The fifth Sikh Guru, Guru Arjan Dev, was executed in 1606 CE during the reign of Jahangir for blessing the rebellious Prince Khusrau.
Sir Thomas Roe visited the court of Jahangir as an official ambassador of King James I of England in 1615 CE, securing trading concessions for the British East India Company.
The court painter Ustad Mansur was conferred the title "Nadir-ul-Asr" by Jahangir for his peerless scientific paintings of rare birds, animals, and flora.
The tomb of Itmad-ud-Daula in Agra, built by Nur Jahan, was the first Mughal structure made entirely of white marble adorned with extensive Pietra Dura inlay work.
Jahangir recorded his memoirs in Persian in his autobiography, the Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri.
In 1615 CE, Jahangir successfully concluded a historic peace treaty with Rana Amar Singh of Mewar, ending decades of hostilities without humiliating the Rajput house.
mains: Evaluate the political and administrative influence of Nur Jahan and the "Nur Jahan Junta" on the imperial court and foreign policy during Jahangir's reign.
Analyze the development of Mughal miniature painting under Jahangir's patronage, highlighting the naturalist works of Ustad Mansur and Abul Hasan.
Assess the commercial and geopolitical implications of the diplomatic missions of Captain William Hawkins and Sir Thomas Roe to the court of Jahangir.

quickFacts: 28 October 1627, Lahore; tomb at Shahdara, Lahore

periods.title: Shah Jahan
periods.tagline: The Patron of Architecture & Culture — Great Builder, Strong Administrator, Cultural Zenith of the Mughals
periods.overview: Shah Jahan's thirty-year reign represents the Mughal Empire at its most materially and artistically confident — the treasury full, the frontiers largely secure, and an emperor with both the resources and the personal inclination to spend them on architecture at a scale no predecessor had attempted. The result is the period's defining legacy: the Taj Mahal, built as a mausoleum for his wife Mumtaz Mahal and universally regarded as the pinnacle of Mughal architectural achievement, alongside the Red Fort, the Jama Masjid, and the new planned city of Shahjahanabad (Old Delhi) — an extraordinary concentration of white-marble, pietra-dura-inlaid construction that consumed enormous resources but left an unmatched physical legacy. This architectural confidence was underpinned by genuinely competent, if not especially innovative, administration: continuation of Akbar's revenue systems, expanding trade with European companies at Surat and other ports, and a religious policy more personally orthodox than Akbar's but still pragmatic enough to avoid reimposing the Jizya tax or banning temple construction outright. The reign's abrupt end, however, is a warning about the risks of dynastic succession in an empire without a fixed rule of inheritance: Shah Jahan's illness in 1657 triggered a brutal war among his own sons, and his eventual survivor and successor, Aurangzeb, had him deposed and imprisoned in Agra Fort for the rest of his life — leaving Shah Jahan to spend his final years, by tradition, gazing at the very monument he had built for his beloved wife.

phases.name: Accession & Consolidation
points: Ascends the throne on 8 February 1628 after the death of Jahangir; consolidation of power; submission of rivals; marriage with Arjumand Banu Begum (Mumtaz Mahal) had occurred in 1612, formal reign begins 1628

phases.name: Military Campaigns & Expansion
points: Campaign in Bundelkhand (1632); suppression of revolt of Hindu Rao in Mewar (1635); conquest of Qandahar (1636, lost again in 1639 to Safavids)
Conflict with the Portuguese at Surat and Daman (1644–45); revolt in Deccan by Qutb Shahi ruler (1645–46); war with the Ahoms of Assam (1652–53)

phases.name: Cultural Zenith
points: Strengthening of administration and empire; economic prosperity; art, culture & architecture patronage reaches its peak — Taj Mahal, Red Fort, Jama Masjid, Shahjahanabad, Shalimar Gardens

phases.name: War of Succession & Decline
points: Illness of Shah Jahan (1657) triggers a war of succession among his sons; defeat and imprisonment of Shah Jahan by Aurangzeb (1658); lived in Agra Fort till his death

phases.name: Death
points: Died in 1666 in Agra Fort; buried in the Taj Mahal, Agra, alongside Mumtaz Mahal

Political Administration: Absolute monarchy with divine right theory; strong central authority and efficient bureaucracy; Mansabdari System further regularised (ranks between 10 and 7,000)

Provincial administration: Subah → Sarkar → Pargana → Village; 17 (later 18) Subahs during his reign; revenue administration based on Todar Mal's system of measurement, Zabt (cash assessment) and Kankut
Economy: Agriculture the mainstay of the economy; Zabt system of Todar Mal continued; other revenues — Jizya (on non-Muslims), customs, transit duties, tribute, fines
Irrigation — construction of canals, tanks and wells; trade & commerce flourished, both internal & external; industries & crafts — textiles (cotton, silk), metalware, carpets, paper, glass, jewellery
Ports: Surat, Masulipatnam, Hugli, Thatta; English, Dutch, French, Portuguese companies active in trade; prosperity due to peace, good administration and flourishing trade
Religion: Personally a devout Sunni Muslim; patronised Islamic scholars and jurists; endowed madrasas, mosques and religious institutions

Did not reimpose Jizya (which was abolished by Akbar); no general ban on temples — many were built and numerous Hindu institutions received grants; promoted an atmosphere of tolerance and justice, though following a moderate (not fully liberal) policy compared to Akbar
Architecture & Cultural Achievements: Known as the 'Patron of Architecture'; use of white marble, pietra dura inlay, symmetry and grandeur; Taj Mahal, Red Fort (Delhi), Jama Masjid (Delhi), Shahjahanabad (Old Delhi)

Other buildings: Moti Masjid (Agra), Diwan-i-Khas (Delhi), Shalimar Gardens (Lahore), Masjid-i-Wazir Khan (Lahore); literature, music, painting and calligraphy flourished; court life reached its zenith
Golden Age of Mughal Architecture: Culmination of Imperial Building: Shahabuddin Muhammad Shah Jahan (r. 1628–1658 CE) represented the architectural zenith of the dynasty, shifting preference from red sandstone to pristine white Makrana marble, bulbous double domes, cusped multifoil arches, and delicate Pietra Dura floral inlay.

Taj Mahal (Agra): Built (1631–1648 CE) as a mausoleum for his beloved consort Arjumand Banu Begum (Mumtaz Mahal); designed by architect Ustad Ahmad Lahori; perfect bilateral symmetry, central white marble dome framed by four slender minarets, Charbagh garden setting, reflecting pools, and Quranic calligraphy by Amanat Khan Shirazi.

Shahjahanabad & Red Fort: Shifted imperial capital from Agra to Delhi, founding the walled metropolis of Shahjahanabad (1638 CE); constructed the massive Red Fort (Lal Qila) containing the Diwan-i-Aam, Diwan-i-Khas (inscribed: "If there is paradise on earth, it is here, it is here, it is here"), Rang Mahal, and the legendary Peacock Throne (Takht-i-Taus) studded with diamonds and emeralds; built the monumental Jama Masjid of Delhi; founded the Moti Masjid (Pearl Mosque) at Agra Fort.
Deccan Expeditions & Foreign Policy: Subjugation of Deccan: Annexed the Nizam Shahi kingdom of Ahmednagar (1633 CE); compelled Bijapur (Adil Shah) and Golconda (Qutb Shah) to accept Mughal suzerainty, pay tribute, and mention Shah Jahan in Friday Khutba (1636 CE); appointed Prince Aurangzeb as Viceroy of Deccan twice (1636–44 and 1653–57; where Murshid Quli Khan reformed Deccan revenue administration).

Central Asian failures: Dispatched three disastrous imperial expeditions to Balkh and Badakhshan (1646–47 CE) and three failed sieges of Kandahar (1649, 1652, 1653 CE) against Safavid Persia, draining over 120 million rupees from the imperial treasury without territorial gain.
Dara Shikoh & The War of Succession (165: Dara Shikoh's syncretism: Eldest son and chosen heir; mystical Sufi scholar of Qadiri order; translated 50 Upanishads from Sanskrit into Persian under the title Sirr-i-Akbar (The Great Secret); authored Majma-ul-Bahrain (The Mingling of Two Oceans), harmonizing Sufi Islam and Advaita Vedanta philosophy; translated the Bhagavad Gita and Yoga Vasistha into Persian.

War of Succession: Illness of Shah Jahan triggered a fratricidal war among his four sons: Dara Shikoh, Shah Shuja, Aurangzeb, and Murad Bakhsh; Aurangzeb defeated imperial armies at Battle of Dharmat (April 1658) and crushed Dara Shikoh at the decisive Battle of Samugarh (May 1658 near Agra); imprisoned father Shah Jahan in Agra Fort for his remaining 8 years (overlooking the Taj Mahal); executed Dara Shikoh and Murad, driving Shuja to perish in the Arakan jungles.

women.name: Mumtaz Mahal (Arjumand Banu Begum)
women.note: Beloved wife; her memory is celebrated through the Taj Mahal.

women.name: Jahanara Begum
women.note: Influential in administration, Sufi patronage, charity and architecture.

women.name: Roshanara Begum
women.note: Politically astute; played a role in the war of succession.

women.name: Women of the royal family
women.note: Had no formal political power but exercised considerable informal influence within the zenana and at court; played important roles in administration, culture and charity.

events.title: Shah Jahan's accession
events.desc: Ascends the throne after Jahangir's death and begins consolidating power.

events.title: Construction of the Taj Mahal
events.desc: Built as a mausoleum for Mumtaz Mahal, becoming the defining monument of Mughal architecture.

events.title: Qandahar campaign and loss
events.desc: Shah Jahan captures Qandahar in 1636 but loses it again to the Safavids in 1639.

events.title: War of Succession
events.desc: Shah Jahan's illness triggers a war among his sons; Aurangzeb emerges victorious and imprisons his father.

events.title: Death of Shah Jahan
events.desc: Dies in confinement at Agra Fort; buried beside Mumtaz Mahal in the Taj Mahal.

people.name: Shah Jahan
people.note: r. 1628–1658; full name Shahab-ud-din Muhammad Shah Jahan.

people.name: Mumtaz Mahal
people.note: Died 1631; the Taj Mahal was built in her memory.

people.name: Aurangzeb
people.note: Deposed and imprisoned Shah Jahan in 1658 after the war of succession.

prelims: Ustad Ahmad Lahori was the chief architect of the Taj Mahal and the Red Fort of Delhi under Shah Jahan.
Dara Shikoh translated 50 Upanishads into Persian under the title "Sirr-i-Akbar" (The Great Secret) and authored the comparative philosophical classic Majma-ul-Bahrain.
The legendary Peacock Throne (Takht-i-Taus), which housed the Koh-i-Noor diamond, was commissioned by Shah Jahan and crafted by Bebadal Khan.
The decisive Battle of Samugarh (May 1658) was fought between Aurangzeb and Dara Shikoh, determining the succession to the Mughal throne.
Shah Jahan shifted the Mughal capital from Agra to Delhi in 1638 CE, founding the new walled imperial city of Shahjahanabad.
Murshid Quli Khan reformed the land revenue administration of the Deccan during Aurangzeb's second viceroyalty under the reign of Shah Jahan.
Shah Jahan was imprisoned by Aurangzeb in the Musamman Burj of Agra Fort from 1658 until his death in 1666 CE.
mains: Critically evaluate the architectural achievements of Shah Jahan, analyzing the aesthetic, symmetry, and engineering features that distinguished his monuments from earlier Mughal buildings.
Examine the intellectual and religious contributions of Dara Shikoh, assessing the significance of his Persian translations of the Upanishads and Majma-ul-Bahrain.
Analyze the political, psychological, and military factors that led to Aurangzeb's victory over Dara Shikoh in the War of Succession (1657–1658).
Discuss the geopolitical and fiscal consequences of Shah Jahan's Central Asian expeditions (Balkh and Badakhshan) and the sieges of Kandahar.

quickFacts: 1666, Agra Fort; buried in the Taj Mahal

periods.title: Aurangzeb Alamgir
periods.tagline: The Last Great Mughal Emperor — Expansion, Centralisation, Religious Policy, Deccan Wars, and the Causes of Decline
periods.overview: Aurangzeb's forty-nine-year reign — the longest of any Mughal emperor — pushed the empire to its greatest territorial extent while simultaneously generating nearly every structural strain that would unravel it within a generation of his death, a paradox that makes him one of the most debated rulers in Indian history. Having secured the throne through a genuinely brutal war of succession, including his brother Dara Shikoh's execution, Aurangzeb spent decades in costly, ultimately indecisive campaigns against the rising Maratha power under Shivaji and his successors, eventually annexing the last independent Deccan sultanates of Bijapur and Golconda but never actually pacifying the region — a war of attrition that drained the treasury and exhausted the army even as it added territory to the map. His reimposition of the Jizya tax on non-Muslims in 1679, after Akbar had abolished it roughly a century earlier, remains the reign's most contested policy: it clearly marked a shift toward personal religious orthodoxy, but historians increasingly caution against reading it, or his uneven and regionally inconsistent treatment of temples, as evidence of a uniformly anti-Hindu state policy rather than a mix of personal conviction, political calculation, and local circumstance. Underneath these headline controversies ran a quieter but arguably more consequential problem: the jagirdari crisis, in which the number of nobles requiring land-revenue assignments as salary steadily outstripped the empire's available resources, a structural imbalance that Aurangzeb's successors inherited and never solved. By the time of his death at Ahmadnagar in 1707, the empire he left behind was larger than the one he had inherited and, in every practical sense, far more fragile.

phases.name: War of Succession & Accession
points: War of succession among Shah Jahan's sons; Battle of Dharmat (April 1658), Battle of Samugarh (29 May 1658); defeat and imprisonment of Shah Jahan in Agra Fort
Battle of Khajwa (Jan 1659) against Shah Shuja; execution of Dara Shikoh (Aug 1659); Aurangzeb assumes undisputed control (1659)

phases.name: Consolidation & Deccan Campaigns
points: Deccan and frontier campaigns; 1663 – attack by Shivaji on Shaista Khan at Pune; 1665 – Treaty of Purandar with Shivaji; 1666 – Shivaji's visit to Agra and daring escape
1670s – rise of Maratha resistance in Western Deccan; 1675 – execution of Guru Tegh Bahadur; 1679 – reimposition of Jizya on non-Muslims

phases.name: Rajput & Sikh Conflicts, Rise of the Marathas
points: Rajput conflicts (especially Mewar and Marwar); 1681 – Aurangzeb moves to the Deccan permanently; 1686 – conquest of Bijapur; 1687 – conquest of Golconda
1689 – capture and execution of Sambhaji; prolonged Deccan wars against the Marathas continue through the 1690s

phases.name: Decline & Death
points: Expansion to its greatest territorial extent but resources exhausted; Marathas became stronger; regional resistance and fragmentation of Mughal power
Death of Aurangzeb at Ahmadnagar (3 March 1707), buried at Khuldabad, Maharashtra in a simple grave as per his wishes

Political & Administrative System: Centralised monarchy — absolute authority of the emperor; Mansabdari system (ranks of 10 to 70,000) combining military & administrative responsibilities
Jagirdari system (land grants as salary to mansabdars); provincial administration: Subah → Sarkar → Pargana → Village; increasing jagirdari pressure led to a jagirdari crisis
Administrative overstretch due to long Deccan wars; intelligence system of Barid (spies) and news-writers
Economy: Agriculture the backbone of the economy; land revenue the main source of state income; Zabt system (Dahsala system of Akbar continued with modifications)
Heavy expenditure on continuous wars and military campaigns; economic consequences — decline in agrarian conditions in some regions, jagirdari crisis, peasant burdens increased
Religious Policy: Personal Sunni orthodoxy; observed Islamic practices strictly; patronage to Islamic scholars, ulema and madrasas

Fatawa-i-Alamgiri — compilation of Islamic law; reimposition of Jizya in 1679 on non-Muslims; restrictions on some religious practices, festivals, and building of new temples in specific contexts (not a uniform empire-wide policy)

UPSC caution: avoid the simplistic statement that Aurangzeb completely removed all Hindu officials or destroyed all temples — his policies varied by region, political context and period; historians debate whether his actions were political/situational or uniformly anti-Hindu
Military & Deccan Policy: Large standing army with huge numbers of cavalry; strong artillery & use of firearms; fort warfare — Mughals strong in capturing and maintaining forts
Strengths: resources, artillery, organised administration, large manpower; weaknesses: heavy expenditure, slow movement in Deccan, rigid system against fast, local-support Maratha guerrilla warfare
Relation with the Marathas: Rise of Shivaji and consolidation of Maratha power (1645–1680); Treaty of Purandar (1665); Shivaji's coronation at Raigad (1674)

Maratha resistance expands under Shivaji's successors; Aurangzeb personally leads Deccan campaigns from 1681 onward; long-term impact — Marathas emerge as a major power, Mughal control weakens in the Deccan and beyond
Orthodoxy & Administrative Measures: Ascension & Regnal Title: Muhi-ud-Din Muhammad Aurangzeb assumed title "Alamgir" (Conqueror of the World; r. 1658–1707 CE); discontinued court practices deemed un-Islamic: banned Nauroz celebration, Jharokha Darshan (balcony royal viewing), Tula Dan (weighing the Emperor against gold/silver), music at court, and drinking of alcohol; appointed Muhtasibs (censors of public morals) to enforce Sharia.

Taxation and religious measures: Re-imposed Jizya tax on non-Muslim subjects in 1679 CE; abolished nearly 80 transit tolls (Abwabs); commissioned the monumental encyclopaedic compendium of Hanafi Islamic jurisprudence, Fatawa-i-Alamgiri; executed the ninth Sikh Guru, Guru Tegh Bahadur, at Chandni Chowk Delhi (1675 CE) for defending Kashmiri Pandits.
Agrarian Crises & Popular Rebellions: Agrarian resistance: Irfan Habib's "Agrarian Crisis" thesis: hyper-exploitation by short-term Jagirdars caused flight of peasants and widespread armed revolts.

Major rebellions: 1. Jat Rebellion in Mathura/Agra led by Gokula (1669), Rajaram (1685, who plundered Akbar's tomb at Sikandra), and Churaman (founded Bharatpur kingdom); 2. Satnami Revolt (1672 near Narnaul, Haryana; armed peasant-religious revolt); 3. Bundela Rebellion under Raja Chhatrasal (establishing an autonomous Bundelkhand state); 4. Sikh resistance under Guru Gobind Singh (created Khalsa Panth in 1699 CE at Anandpur Sahib; fought battles of Chamkaur and Muktsar; sent Persian letter of moral admonition Zafarnama to Aurangzeb).
Deccan Campaigns: \"The Deccan Ulcer\": Prolonged southern quagmire: Annexed the Sultanate of Bijapur (1686 CE) and the Sultanate of Golconda (1687 CE); executed Maratha king Chhatrapati Sambhaji (1689 CE) and imprisoned infant Shahu.

The Deccan Ulcer: Spent the last 25 uninterrupted years of his reign (1681–1707 CE) living in military tents in the Deccan fighting intractable Maratha guerrilla warfare (led by Rajaram, Santaji Ghorpade, Dhanaji Jadhav, and Queen Tarabai); drained imperial finances, neglected North Indian administration, and ruined the grand army; historian V.A. Smith remarked: "The Deccan was the grave of his reputation as well as of his body."

women.name: Zeb-un-Nissa
women.note: Daughter of Aurangzeb (1639–1702); scholar, poet (pen name 'Makfi'); well-educated in Persian, Arabic and literature.

women.name: Zinat-un-Nissa Begum
women.note: Known for charity, held political influence and supported religious institutions.

women.name: Women of the Royal Household
women.note: Patronage of mosques, sarais, gardens and charitable works; influence in politics and court life during early Aurangzeb period.

events.title: War of Succession
events.desc: Aurangzeb defeats his brothers in a bitter succession struggle and imprisons Shah Jahan.

events.title: Reimposition of Jizya
events.desc: Aurangzeb reimposes the tax on non-Muslims, abolished decades earlier by Akbar, a defining and controversial policy shift.

events.title: Conquest of Bijapur and Golconda
events.desc: Aurangzeb annexes the last major Deccan sultanates, extending the empire to its greatest territorial extent.

events.title: Execution of Sambhaji
events.desc: The Maratha leader Sambhaji is captured and executed, but Maratha resistance continues under his successors.

events.title: Death of Aurangzeb
events.desc: Dies at Ahmadnagar after prolonged Deccan wars; his death marks the beginning of rapid Mughal decline.

people.name: Aurangzeb (Alamgir)
people.note: r. 1658–1707; 'Conqueror of the World'.

people.name: Dara Shikoh
people.note: Executed by Aurangzeb in 1659.

people.name: Shivaji
people.note: Chief Deccan adversary; challenged Mughal authority.

people.name: Sambhaji
people.note: Son of Shivaji; captured and executed by Aurangzeb in 1689.

prelims: Aurangzeb re-imposed the Jizya tax on non-Muslim subjects in 1679 CE, 115 years after its repeal by Akbar.
Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Sikh Guru, was executed at Chandni Chowk in Delhi in 1675 CE on the orders of Aurangzeb; Gurdwara Sis Ganj marks the site.
Aurangzeb annexed the Sultanate of Bijapur in 1686 CE and the Sultanate of Golconda in 1687 CE into the Mughal Empire.
Fatawa-i-Alamgiri, the comprehensive encyclopaedia of Islamic law (Hanafi jurisprudence), was compiled by a board of scholars under Aurangzeb's patronage.
Aurangzeb built the Bibi ka Maqbara at Aurangabad in 1679 CE as a memorial to his wife Dilras Banu Begum (Rabia-ud-Daurani), known as the "Poor Man's Taj".
Aurangzeb appointed moral officers called "Muhtasibs" to inspect markets, regulate weights, and enforce Islamic ethical codes in public life.
The Zafarnama (Epistle of Victory) was a famous Persian letter of moral defiance written by the tenth Sikh Guru, Guru Gobind Singh, addressed to Aurangzeb in 1705 CE.
mains: Critically evaluate the religious policies of Aurangzeb, analyzing whether his measures (re-imposition of Jizya, demolition of temples, banning of court music) were religiously dogmatic or politically motivated.

Examine the "Deccan Ulcer" thesis with reference to Aurangzeb's 25-year campaigns in South India, explaining how the annexation of Bijapur and Golconda contributed to the financial and military collapse of the Mughal Empire.
Analyze the socio-economic causes of agrarian rebellions during Aurangzeb's reign, specifically the uprisings of the Jats, Satnamis, and Bundelas.
Discuss the Jagirdari Crisis of the late 17th century as articulated by Satish Chandra, examining the imbalance between Paibaqi land and Mansabdar expectations (Be-Jagiri).

quickFacts: 3 March 1707, Ahmadnagar; buried at Khuldabad, Maharashtra

periods.title: The Maratha Empire & Confederacy
periods.tagline: Hindavi Swarajya under Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj, the Ashtapradhan, Peshwa Ascendancy, Panipat III & Resistance to British Colonialism
periods.overview: Founded by Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj in 1674 amidst the rugged Sahyadri terrain of the Western Ghats, the Maratha state transformed from a regional kingdom into the supreme military power of 18th-century India. Resisting Mughal onslaughts under Aurangzeb through prolonged guerrilla resistance (under Sambhaji, Rajaram, and Maharani Tarabai), the Marathas rose to pan-Indian hegemony under the hereditary Peshwas (Balaji Vishwanath, Baji Rao I, and Balaji Baji Rao). Operating as a vast confederacy (Scindias, Holkars, Gaekwads, Bhonsles), the Marathas collected Chauth and Sardeshmukhi across the subcontinent until the catastrophic Third Battle of Panipat (1761) and eventual defeat in the three Anglo-Maratha Wars (1775–1818).

phases.name: Chhatrapati Shivaji & The Founding of Hindavi Swarajya
points: Shivaji captured Torna Fort (1646), killed Afzal Khan at Pratapgad (1659), and raided Shaista Khan's camp in Pune (1663).
Treaty of Purandar (1665) signed with Jai Singh; Shivaji's daring escape from Aurangzeb's captivity in Agra (1666).
Coronation (Rajyabhisheka) at Raigad Fort in 1674; assumed title of Chhatrapati and established sovereign coinage (Shivrai and Hon).

phases.name: The War of 27 Years & Regency of Maharani Tarabai
points: Aurangzeb personally moved his imperial court to the Deccan to crush the Marathas.
Execution of Chhatrapati Sambhaji (1689); Rajaram established capital at Jinji (Tamil Nadu) during an 8-year siege.
Maharani Tarabai took leadership in 1700, rallying Maratha sardars and launching counter-invasions into Mughal Malwa and Gujarat, wearing down Aurangzeb until his death in 1707.

phases.name: Peshwa Ascendancy & Pan-Indian Expansion
points: Chhatrapati Shahu appointed Balaji Vishwanath as Peshwa (1713), establishing hereditary ministerial power centered at Shaniwar Wada, Pune.
Peshwa Baji Rao I (1720–1740) led 41 victorious military campaigns ('Strike at the trunk of the withering Mughal tree'), defeating the Nizam at Palkhed (1728) and Bhopal (1737).
Balaji Baji Rao (Nana Saheb) expanded the empire to its territorial zenith, planting the saffron flag (Bhagwa Dhwaj) on the banks of the Indus at Attock (1758).

phases.name: Panipat III, The Confederacy & Anglo-Maratha Wars
points: Third Battle of Panipat (14 January 1761): Ahmad Shah Abdali crushed the Maratha army under Sadashivrao Bhau and Vishwasrao.
Maratha Resurrection under Peshwa Madhavrao I and Mahadji Scindia, restoring Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II to the Delhi throne.
Internal factionalism after Nana Fadnavis led to the Maratha Confederacy (Peshwa, Scindia of Gwalior, Holkar of Indore, Gaekwad of Baroda, Bhonsle of Nagpur).
Three Anglo-Maratha Wars (1775–1818) ended in the dissolution of the Peshwaship and British annexation of Maharashtra.

Revenue System: Chauth & Sardeshmukhi: Chauth: 1/4th (25%) of land revenue levied on non-Maratha territories as protection money against Maratha raids.
Sardeshmukhi: An additional 1/10th (10%) levy claimed by the Maratha ruler as hereditary supreme head (Sardeshmukh) of the land.
Kathi system: Shivaji measured agricultural land using a standardized rod (Kathi) and eliminated oppressive Zamindari intermediaries (Deshmukhs and Kulkarnis).
Military System & Fort Architecture: Ganimi Kava: Masterful guerrilla warfare utilizing hill forts, rapid light cavalry, and deep knowledge of Sahyadri geography.
Extensive network of over 300 hill and coastal forts (Raigad, Rajgad, Pratapgad, Sinhagad, Sindhudurg sea fort, Vijaydurg).
Pioneering Maratha Navy (Armada) organized under Admiral Kanhoji Angre, dominating the western coastline against Portuguese, Dutch, and English fleets.
Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj & Hindavi Sw: Early career and fort conquests: Born at Shivneri Fort (1630 CE); inspired by mother Jijabai and mentor Dadoji Kondadev; conquered strategic hill-forts: Torna (1646, first conquest), Kondana (renamed Sinhagad), and Raigad; slayed Bijapur general Afzal Khan with tiger claws (Bagh Nakh) at Pratapgad (1659); wounded Mughal viceroy Shaista Khan in a night raid on his palace at Lal Mahal, Pune (1663); sacked the premier Mughal commercial port of Surat twice (1664 and 1670).

Treaty of Purandar (1665 CE): Concluded with Rajput general Raja Jai Singh I; Shivaji surrendered 23 of his 35 hill forts to the Mughals, retaining 12 forts; agreed to send son Sambhaji as a 5,000 Mansabdar; escaped from house arrest in Agra in a sweetmeat basket (1666 CE).

Coronation & Royal Titles (1674 CE): Solemnly crowned as sovereign monarch (Chhatrapati) at Raigad Fort on 6 June 1674 by Pandit Gaga Bhatt of Varanasi; assumed titles "Haidava Dharmoddharak" (Protector of the Hindu Faith) and "Kshatriya Kulavantas".
Ashtapradhan Council & Fiscal Structure: Ashtapradhan (Council of Eight Ministers): Advisory cabinet directly responsible to the King: 1. Peshwa / Mukhya Pradhan (Prime Minister / general administration), 2. Amatya / Majumdar (Finance and revenue minister), 3. Senapati / Sari-Naubat (Commander-in-Chief of army), 4. Waqia-Navis / Mantri (Intelligence and home records), 5. Sachiv / Shuru-Navis (Royal correspondence and edicts), 6. Sumant / Dabir (Foreign minister), 7. Nyayadhish (Chief Justice), 8. Panditrao (Charity, religious endowments, and rituals).

Revenue system (Chauth & Sardeshmukhi): Assessment based on Kathi measuring rod (Malik Ambar system); state share fixed at 40% of produce; extracted two famous levies from neighboring Mughal and foreign territories: 1. Chauth (one-fourth / 25% of gross revenue collected in exchange for protection against Maratha raids), 2. Sardeshmukhi (additional 10% levy claimed by Shivaji as the hereditary supreme lord / Sardeshmukh of Maharashtra).

Military organization: Disciplined cavalry divided into Bargirs (state-mounted troopers provided with state horses and weapons) and Silahdars (cavalrymen bringing their own horses and arms); naval fleet (pioneered by Kanhoji Angre, "Father of the Indian Navy").
Peshwa Hegemony & The Panipat Catastroph: Rise of the Peshwas: Balaji Vishwanath (First hereditary Peshwa, 1713–1720; secured imperial Farman from Farrukhsiyar in 1719 recognizing Chauth/Sardeshmukhi rights across the 6 Deccan Subahs); Baji Rao I (1720–1740; brilliant cavalry commander, champion of "Hindu Pad-Padshahi", conquered Malwa, Gujarat, Bundelkhand, defeated Nizam at Palkhed 1728, dashed to Delhi gates 1737: "Strike at the trunk of the withered tree, and the branches will fall of themselves").

Balaji Baji Rao (Nana Saheb, 1740–1761): Sangola Agreement (1750) transferring de facto imperial sovereignty from the Chhatrapati to the Peshwa at Pune; Maratha power expanded from Cuttack to Attock (hoisting flag on Indus under Raghunath Rao 1758).

Third Battle of Panipat (14 January 1761): Maratha confederacy army led by Sadashivrao Bhau and Vishwasrao, with artillery under Ibrahim Khan Gardi, confronted Afghan invader Ahmad Shah Abdali; alienated potential allies (Rajputs, Jats, Awadh Nawab Shuja-ud-Daula backed Abdali); Marathas were annihilated, losing 100,000 soldiers and top leadership; shattered dream of pan-Indian Maratha empire and cleared the way for the British East India Company.

women.name: Jijabai (Rajmata)
women.role: Mother, Mentor & Political Guide of Shivaji
women.note: Instilled principles of swarajya, dharma, and righteous governance in Shivaji; managed the Pune Jagir with exceptional judicial acumen.

women.name: Maharani Tarabai
women.note: Led the Maratha resistance (1700–1707) after husband Rajaram's death; personally planned offensive campaigns against Aurangzeb's grand army.

women.name: Ahilyabai Holkar
women.note: Revered administrator who transformed Indore, defended her state against invaders, and rebuilt major Hindu temples across India (Kashi Vishwanath, Somnath, Gaya).

events.title: Coronation of Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj
events.desc: Shivaji is crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad Fort by Pandit Gaga Bhatt, establishing sovereign Hindavi Swarajya.

events.title: Battle of Palkhed
events.desc: Peshwa Baji Rao I defeats Nizam-ul-Mulk of Hyderabad using brilliant mobile cavalry maneuvers.

events.title: Maratha Conquest of Attock
events.desc: Raghunathrao and Malhar Rao Holkar capture Attock, expanding Maratha boundaries to the Khyber Pass.

events.title: Third Battle of Panipat
events.desc: Ahmad Shah Durrani defeats the Marathas in one of the bloodiest single-day battles of the 18th century.

events.title: End of Maratha Power (Third Anglo-Maratha War)
events.desc: Battle of Koregaon and defeat of Peshwa Baji Rao II; British abolish the Peshwaship.

people.name: Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj
people.note: Strategic genius who established Hindavi Swarajya, built a powerful navy and fort system, and formulated the Ashtapradhan administration.

people.name: Peshwa Baji Rao I
people.note: Undefeated general in 41 battles; transformed the Maratha state into a pan-Indian empire through blitzkrieg cavalry maneuvers.

people.name: Mahadji Scindia
people.role: Ruler of Gwalior & Regent of Delhi
people.note: Modernized the Maratha army with European discipline (under Benoit de Boigne) and dominated North Indian politics.

people.name: Nana Fadnavis
people.role: Statesman & Chief Minister of the Confederacy
people.note: Known as the 'Maratha Machiavelli' for holding together the Maratha Confederacy against internal intrigues and British diplomacy.

prelims: Shivaji was formally crowned as "Chhatrapati" at Raigad Fort in 1674 CE by Pandit Gaga Bhatt of Varanasi.
The Treaty of Purandar was signed in 1665 CE between Chhatrapati Shivaji and Raja Jai Singh I representing Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb.
Shivaji's council of eight ministers was known as the "Ashtapradhan", with the Peshwa serving as the prime minister.
In the Maratha fiscal system, "Chauth" was 25% of land revenue collected from neighboring regions for protection, while "Sardeshmukhi" was an additional 10% levy claimed as hereditary chief.
In the Maratha cavalry, "Bargirs" were soldiers supplied with horses and equipment by the state, whereas "Silahdars" provided their own horses and arms.
Peshwa Baji Rao I defeated the Nizam of Hyderabad at the Battle of Palkhed in 1728 CE through brilliant cavalry mobility.
The Third Battle of Panipat took place on 14 January 1761, where Ahmad Shah Abdali crushed the Maratha army led by Sadashivrao Bhau.
mains: Evaluate the military strategy and administrative institutions of Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj, analyzing how the Ashtapradhan and hill-fort defense system helped establish "Swarajya".
Examine the nature and economic impact of Chauth and Sardeshmukhi in the expansion of the Maratha Empire across the Deccan and Northern India.
Critically analyze the causes and long-term historical consequences of the Maratha defeat at the Third Battle of Panipat (1761), assessing its impact on British colonial ascendancy.
Trace the transformation of the Maratha state from Shivaji's centralized monarchy to the decentralized Peshwa-led Maratha Confederacy (Scindia, Holkar, Gaekwad, Bhonsle).

periods.title: Later Mughal Empire
periods.tagline: From Aurangzeb's Death to the End of Mughal Rule in India — Decline of Central Authority, Regionalisation, Economic Strain, European Intervention
periods.overview: The century and a half between Aurangzeb's death and the formal end of Mughal rule amid the 1857 Revolt is less a single coherent period than a long, accelerating collapse, punctuated by a rapid and often violent succession of largely powerless emperors while real authority drained away to nobles, regional governors, and eventually foreign powers. The pattern is set almost immediately: no fewer than a dozen emperors occupy the throne in this period, most controlled by court factions, and the damage inflicted by external invasions — Nadir Shah's catastrophic 1739 sack of Delhi, which carried off the Peacock Throne and the Koh-i-Noor diamond, followed by Ahmad Shah Abdali's five separate invasions between 1748 and 1761 — repeatedly shattered whatever fragile authority remained at the centre. Into the resulting vacuum stepped a new generation of genuinely independent regional powers: the Marathas, expanding rapidly out of the Deccan; the Sikh Misls consolidating in Punjab; the Jats under Suraj Mal in Bharatpur; the Rohillas in western Uttar Pradesh; and increasingly autonomous Nawabs in Bengal and Awadh, until the Mughal Empire existed in name more than in fact, a loose confederation of effectively sovereign states that merely continued to seek symbolic legitimacy from Delhi. It was the East India Company, however, that ultimately profited most from this fragmentation, using victories at Plassey (1757) and Buxar (1764) and the resulting grant of Diwani revenue rights over Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa in 1765 to convert commercial privilege into genuine territorial and fiscal power — setting the stage for a century of British expansion that would end, in 1857, with the last Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah II deposed and exiled, and Mughal rule formally extinguished.

phases.name: Aurangzeb's Death & War of Succession
points: Death of Aurangzeb at Ahmadnagar (3 March 1707); war of succession among his sons; Bahadur Shah I (Shah Alam) becomes emperor — an able soldier but faces the Marathas & Sikhs

phases.name: Rapid Succession of Weak Emperors
points: Jahandar Shah (1712–13) – indulgent, short reign; Farrukhsiyar (1713–19) – increased influence of the Sayyid Brothers; Rafi-ud-Darajat & Rafi-ud-Daula (1719–1727) – weak, figurehead rulers
Muhammad Shah 'Rangeela' (1727–1748) – cultural patronage but weak politically; Nadir Shah invades India and sacks Delhi (March 1739)

phases.name: Rise of Regional Powers
points: Ahmad Shah Abdali's invasions (5 major invasions, 1740–1754); Battle of Plassey (1757) and Battle of Buxar (1764) establish British political power
Diwani rights granted to the English East India Company (Bengal, Bihar, Orissa) in 1765

phases.name: Mughal Emperor as a Puppet
points: Shah Alam II under nominal, then British, control (1772–1806); Delhi occupied by Lord Lake (1803); Akbar Shah II under British control (1806–1837)

phases.name: Revolt of 1857 & End of Mughal Rule
points: Bahadur Shah II (Zafar), the last Mughal, becomes a symbol of the Revolt of 1857 (the First War of Independence)
Deposition of Bahadur Shah II (Sept 1857); end of Mughal rule and beginning of British Crown rule (1858)

Political & Administrative System: Central authority declined sharply; emperors became figureheads; real power passed to nobles, court factions and provincial governors
Mansabdari & Jagirdari systems collapsed gradually; increase in jagirdari crisis — jagirs became insufficient and unpaid
Provincial governors became independent — Nizam (Hyderabad), Nawabs (Bengal, Awadh), Marathas, Sikhs, Jats, Rohillas; factions at court — Irani, Turani, Hindustani, Deccani, Sayyid Brothers
Economy: Agriculture remained the mainstay; land revenue system in decline; heavy exactions by jagirdars, zamindars and intermediaries

Jagirdari crisis led to revenue farming and corruption; trade and commerce declined in inland regions; crafts and industries suffered due to instability, invasions and competition with Europeans; Company gained Diwani (1765) — financial control over rich provinces
External Invasions: 1739: Nadir Shah invaded, defeated the Mughals at Karnal, sacked Delhi, took the Koh-i-Noor and Peacock Throne
1748–1757: Ahmad Shah Abdali's repeated invasions (five in total); caused immense destruction, loss of prestige, wealth and control; encouraged regional powers to assert independence
Rise of Regional Powers: Marathas emerged as the strongest power; controlled Malwa, Gujarat, Bundelkhand, Delhi at times; Sikhs formed Misls; challenged Mughal power in Punjab
