Jats — Suraj Mal established strong rule in Bharatpur; Rohillas powerful in Rohilkhand region; Awadh, Bengal and Hyderabad Nawabs/Nizams became independent; the Mughal Empire became a loose confederation of independent states
Succession Anarchy & Kingmakers: Bahadur Shah I (Shah Alam I, r. 1707–1712): Son of Aurangzeb; assumed title "Shah-i-Bekhabar" (The Careless King); pacified Marathas by releasing Shahu; concluded peace with Guru Gobind Singh and Chhatrasal Bundela.

Jahandar Shah & Farrukhsiyar: Jahandar Shah (r. 1712–1713, puppet of Zulfiqar Khan; abolished Jizya; introduced Ijarah tax-farming); Farrukhsiyar (r. 1713–1719; raised to throne by the Sayyid Brothers - Abdullah Khan and Husain Ali Khan, known as the "Kingmakers"); granted the fateful 1717 Royal Farman to the British East India Company (termed "Magna Carta of the Company" by John Surman, granting duty-free trade in Bengal in exchange for Rs. 3,000 annually and right to mint coins).

Muhammad Shah "Rangeela" (r. 1719–1748): Overthrew the Sayyid Brothers with help of Nizam-ul-Mulk; reign witnessed complete disintegration of the empire as provincial governors declared de facto independence: Murshid Quli Khan in Bengal (1717), Saadat Khan Burhan-ul-Mulk in Awadh (1722), Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah in Hyderabad (1724).
Foreign Cataclysms: Nadir Shah & Abdali: Nadir Shah's Sack of Delhi (1739): Persian conqueror routed imperial Mughal army at Battle of Karnal (February 1739); occupied Delhi; ordered the general massacre (Qatl-e-Aam) of 30,000 citizens in Chandni Chowk; plundered the imperial treasury, carrying away the Peacock Throne (Takht-i-Taus) and the priceless Koh-i-Noor diamond.

Ahmad Shah Abdali (Durrani): Afghan ruler invaded India 8 times between 1748 and 1767; annexed Punjab; crushed the Marathas at the Third Battle of Panipat (1761); left Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II as a blind, helpless puppet ("The Empire of Shah Alam extends from Delhi to Palam").

events.title: Death of Aurangzeb
events.desc: Aurangzeb's death at Ahmadnagar triggers a war of succession and the beginning of rapid Mughal decline.

events.title: Nadir Shah invades and sacks Delhi
events.desc: Nadir Shah defeats the Mughals at Karnal, plunders Delhi, and carries off the Peacock Throne and the Koh-i-Noor diamond.

events.title: Battle of Plassey
events.desc: The English East India Company defeats the Nawab of Bengal, marking the beginning of British political control in India.

events.title: Battle of Buxar
events.desc: A decisive Company victory establishes British supremacy in North India.

events.title: Diwani rights granted
events.desc: The Mughal emperor grants the East India Company revenue-collection rights over Bengal, Bihar and Orissa.

events.title: Revolt of 1857 and end of Mughal rule
events.desc: Bahadur Shah II becomes a symbol of the Revolt; his deposition in 1857 and the start of British Crown rule in 1858 formally end the Mughal Empire.

people.name: Bahadur Shah I (Shah Alam)
people.note: r. 1707–1712; able soldier but faced the Marathas & Sikhs.

people.name: Muhammad Shah 'Rangeela'
people.note: r. 1727–1748; cultural patronage but politically weak; reign saw Nadir Shah's invasion.

people.name: Shah Alam II
people.note: r. 1759–1806; real power lay with the Marathas, then the British.

people.name: Bahadur Shah II (Zafar)
people.note: r. 1837–1857; poet and symbol of the 1857 Revolt; deposed and exiled by the British.

prelims: The Sayyid Brothers (Abdullah Khan and Husain Ali Khan) were known as the "Kingmakers" of the Later Mughal era, making and unmaking four emperors.
Mughal Emperor Farrukhsiyar granted the historic Farman of 1717 (the "Magna Carta of the Company") to the British East India Company delegation led by John Surman.
Nadir Shah of Persia invaded India in 1739 during the reign of Muhammad Shah Rangeela, defeating the Mughals at the Battle of Karnal and looting the Peacock Throne.
The regional state of Hyderabad was founded in 1724 by Chin Qilich Khan (Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah) following his victory at the Battle of Shakar Kheda.
Saadat Khan Burhan-ul-Mulk founded the autonomous principality of Awadh in 1722.
Murshid Quli Khan was appointed Governor of Bengal in 1717 and transferred the capital from Dacca to Murshidabad.
Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II granted the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa to the British East India Company following the Battle of Buxar in 1765.
mains: Analyze the internal political, agrarian, and structural factors that caused the rapid disintegration of the Mughal Empire in the first half of the 18th century.
Examine the invasion of Nadir Shah in 1739 and evaluate its psychological, military, and financial impact on the prestige and authority of the Mughal Emperor.
Discuss the emergence of regional successor states (Bengal, Awadh, Hyderabad) in 18th-century India, assessing whether this period was one of "anarchy and decline" or regional economic restructuring.

quickFacts: Nadir Shah (1739), Ahmad Shah Abdali (5 invasions, 1740–1754)

periods.title: Establishment of British Power in India
periods.tagline: From Merchants to Masters — The Journey from Trade to Territorial Power
periods.overview: This page tells the story of the East India Company's slow, almost accidental transformation from a licensed trading corporation into the dominant political power in Bengal and, eventually, North India — a transformation that took roughly a century and a half and that, at nearly every step, looked to contemporaries less like conquest than like the ordinary business of protecting trade. The Company arrived in 1600 seeking only commercial privileges, and for its first hundred years in India that is essentially all it sought: fortified trading posts at Surat, Madras, Bombay, and Calcutta, favourable farmans (trading permits) from Mughal authorities, and the ordinary competitive rivalry with Dutch, Portuguese, and especially French trading companies. What changed the calculation was the same broader Mughal decline covered on other pages of this site: as central authority weakened after Aurangzeb's death, the Company found that its private armies, originally intended purely for defending warehouses, could be used to intervene in regional politics — supporting one claimant against another, extracting ever-larger trading privileges, and eventually simply seizing territory outright. The decisive turn came in Bengal, the empire's wealthiest province: Robert Clive's victory at Plassey in 1757, engineered as much through bribery and conspiracy against the Nawab Siraj-ud-Daulah as through battlefield skill, gave the Company effective control of Bengal's government; the subsequent victory at Buxar in 1764 secured that control against a coalition of Indian rulers; and the 1765 grant of Diwani rights — the authority to collect Bengal's land revenue directly — converted the Company from a trading concern with political influence into something closer to a genuine, revenue-extracting territorial state, the foundation on which the entire subsequent British Empire in India would be built.

phases.name: Arrival as Traders
points: East India Company established (31 December 1600); Captain William Hawkins reaches Surat (1608); English factory (trading post) at Surat (1612)

phases.name: Trading Factories & Privileges
points: Sir Thomas Roe's embassy to Jahangir's court (1615–17); Madras (Fort St. George) obtained (1639); Bombay given to the EIC by Charles II (1661, dowry of Catherine of Braganza); Calcutta (Fort William) established (1690)

phases.name: Expansion of Trade & Rivalry with Europeans
points: Farman from Mughal Emperor Farrukhsiyar (1717) grants major trading privileges; War of Austrian Succession — EIC vs. French begins in India (1740–48)
Rivalry with French and Dutch in Pondicherry, Chandernagore; Carnatic Wars (1746–63)

phases.name: Territorial Conquests
points: Capture of Madras by the French (1746); returned by Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (1748); Robert Clive becomes Military Governor of Fort St. George (1751)
Siraj-ud-Daulah captures Calcutta (Black Hole incident, 1756); Battle of Plassey (23 June 1757); Battle of Buxar (22 October 1764); Allahabad Treaty — Diwani rights of Bengal, Bihar & Odisha (1765)

Key Features of Early British Expansion: Began as a trading company, not a territorial power; sought trade privileges, not immediate conquest
Took advantage of the weakness of the Mughal Empire; used diplomacy, bribery, deceit and military force

Established forts to protect trade and later as bases of power; created private armies and gradually interfered in politics; followed a policy of 'Divide and Rule'; control over the revenue system gave financial strength; defeated the French to become the chief European power
Strategies Used by the British: Diplomacy & Treaties — farmans, agreements, alliances; Divide and Rule — used internal disputes; Support to Claimants — supported one ruler against another

Bribery & Corruption — bought officials and nobles; Military Strength — well trained army, modern weapons; Economic Control — control of trade & revenue; Building Forts — bases for defence & future expansion; Intelligence Network — use of spies and information
Administrative Steps After Gaining Power: Dual System in Bengal (1765–72): Diwani (Revenue) — EIC; Nizamat (Administration) — Nawab

Appointment of Company officials as Collectors; gradual control over civil, criminal & military administration; establishment of Courts; reorganisation of revenue collection; the British became the real rulers behind the name of the Nawab
Stages of Colonial Penetration & Diploma: Mercantile Conquest & Elimination of Rivals: The British East India Company methodically eliminated European competitors — defeating the Portuguese (Battle of Swally 1612), the Dutch (Battle of Bedara/Chinsurah 1759), and the French in three Carnatic Wars (culminating in the Battle of Wandiwash 1760 and Treaty of Paris 1763).

The Bengal Lever & Treaty of Allahabad (1765): Following Plassey (1757) and Buxar (1764), Robert Clive secured the Diwani (civil and revenue administration) of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa from Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II for an annual tribute of 26 lakh rupees, introducing the predatory Dual System of Government (1765-1772) where the Company wielded power without responsibility.

The Ring Fence Policy (Warren Hastings, 1772-1785): Created buffer zones around Company territories to defend frontiers against Marathas and Afghans, famously turning Awadh into a dependent buffer state whose defense costs were borne by the Nawab.

Subsidiary Alliance Framework (Lord Wellesley, 1798-1805): Codified Dupleix's pioneer mercenary mechanism into a four-stage imperial subjugation tool: Company promised troops -> Stationed permanent subsidiary force inside native territory -> Demanded territorial cessions or cash subsidies -> Controlled external relations and stationed a British Resident, stripping native rulers of external sovereignty (Hyderabad 1798, Mysore 1799, Tanjore 1799, Awadh 1801, Peshwa Baji Rao II Treaty of Bassein 1802).
Anglo-French Carnatic Rivalry: Commercial duel in South India: Austrian War of Succession and Seven Years' War triggered three Carnatic Wars (1746–1763) between the British (Robert Clive, Stringer Lawrence) and French (Dupleix, Bussy, Lally).

Decisive Battles: Battle of St. Thome (1746; tiny disciplined French force routed the large army of Nawab Anwaruddin, proving the superiority of European military drill); Clive's daring siege and defense of Arcot (1751); Battle of Wandiwash (22 January 1760; British General Sir Eyre Coote crushed French General Count de Lally, ending French imperial ambitions in India).
Conquest of Bengal: Plassey to Buxar: Battle of Plassey (23 June 1757): Siraj-ud-Daulah clashed with Clive over fortification of Calcutta (Fort William) and alleged Black Hole tragedy; Mir Jafar (Commander-in-Chief), Rai Durlabh, Yar Lutuf Khan, and banker Jagat Seth betrayed Siraj; Clive achieved victory with minimal fighting, installing Mir Jafar as puppet Nawab; East India Company received 24 Parganas zamindari.

Battle of Buxar (22 October 1764): Most decisive battle in modern Indian history; Major Hector Munro defeated the combined confederate army of Mir Qasim (deposed Nawab of Bengal), Shuja-ud-Daula (Nawab of Awadh), and Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II; demonstrated outright battlefield superiority of the Company army over Indian imperial powers.

Treaty of Allahabad (August 1765) & Dual Government: Robert Clive secured the Diwani (right to collect revenue) of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa from Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II in exchange for an annual tribute of 26 lakh rupees and the districts of Kora and Allahabad; instituted the "Dual System of Government" in Bengal (1765–1772): Company controlled Diwani (revenue and military defence) without administrative responsibility, while puppet Nawab held Nizamat (criminal justice and civil administration) without financial resources, causing the devastating Great Bengal Famine of 1770 (killing one-third of the population).

women.name: Rani Lakshmibai
women.note: Fought bravely in 1857 against British rule (referenced here as symbol of resistance and courage; her main role belongs to the later 1857 Revolt).

women.name: Begum Hazrat Mahal
women.note: Led revolt in Awadh in 1857; administered Lucknow in the name of young prince Birjis Qadr.

women.name: Rani Chennamma
women.note: One of the earliest queens against British annexation (Karnataka, 1824).

women.name: Velu Nachiyar
women.note: First queen to revolt against the British in South India (Sivagangai, 1780).

events.title: East India Company established
events.desc: Chartered as an English trading company on 31 December 1600.

events.title: English factory at Surat
events.desc: The first English trading post is established in India.

events.title: Farrukhsiyar's farman
events.desc: The Mughal emperor grants sweeping trading privileges, later misused by the Company as a base for expanding power.

events.title: Battle of Plassey
events.desc: Robert Clive's victory over Siraj-ud-Daulah gives the Company political control over Bengal — the real beginning of British rule.

events.title: Battle of Buxar
events.desc: A decisive Company victory establishes supremacy in North India.

events.title: Grant of Diwani rights
events.desc: The Allahabad Treaty grants the Company revenue rights over Bengal, Bihar and Odisha — the economic foundation of British rule.

people.name: Robert Clive
people.note: Key architect of British victory at Plassey (1757) and the acquisition of Diwani rights (1765).

people.name: Siraj-ud-Daulah
people.note: Defeated by the British at the Battle of Plassey, 1757.

people.name: Sir Thomas Roe
people.note: Obtained important trading farmans from Jahangir's court, 1615–17.

prelims: The Battle of Wandiwash (1760) ended French imperial ambitions in India, in which British General Eyre Coote decisively defeated Count de Lally.
The Battle of Plassey was fought on 23 June 1757 on the banks of the Bhagirathi river, where Robert Clive defeated Siraj-ud-Daulah through the betrayal of Mir Jafar and Jagat Seth.
Major Hector Munro commanded the victorious British East India Company forces at the decisive Battle of Buxar on 22 October 1764.
Under the Treaty of Allahabad (1765), Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II granted the Diwani rights of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa to the British East India Company.
Robert Clive introduced the Dual System of Government in Bengal in 1765, which was abolished by Warren Hastings in 1772.
The disastrous Great Bengal Famine of 1770 occurred under the Dual Government, resulting in the death of an estimated 10 million people (one-third of Bengal's population).
mains: Compare and contrast the political, military, and historical significance of the Battle of Plassey (1757) and the Battle of Buxar (1764). Why is Buxar considered far more decisive than Plassey?
Critically examine the working and economic consequences of Robert Clive's Dual System of Government in Bengal (1765–1772).
Analyze the causes of the failure of the French East India Company under Dupleix against the British in the Carnatic Wars.

periods.title: The Sikh Empire
periods.tagline: Rise of a Powerful Indian Empire — Unity, Military Excellence & Good Governance
periods.overview: The Sikh Empire is the story of how a religious community founded on egalitarian and devotional principles by Guru Nanak in the late 15th century evolved, through repeated persecution and a deliberate turn toward militarisation under later Gurus, into a genuinely formidable regional power under Maharaja Ranjit Singh — one of the very few Indian states of the period able to negotiate with the expanding British on roughly equal terms rather than simply being absorbed by them. Ranjit Singh's achievement was not merely military, though his modernised army, trained partly by European officers and equipped with advanced artillery, was formidable enough to check Afghan incursions and hold its own against neighbouring powers; it was also a genuine, and by the standards of the era unusually deliberate, policy of religious pluralism, employing Muslim, Hindu, and Sikh officials in senior positions and funding mosques and temples alongside Sikh institutions like his rebuilt Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple) — a record that later commentary is careful not to flatten into simple communal narratives in either direction. The Treaty of Amritsar in 1809 fixed the Sutlej River as a stable boundary with British territory for three decades, a rare example of sustained peaceful coexistence between an independent Indian power and the Company. That stability, however, depended heavily on Ranjit Singh's personal authority: his death in 1839 triggered exactly the kind of court factionalism and succession chaos that had undone other Indian states before it, and within a decade two costly Anglo-Sikh Wars had ended in British victory and the outright annexation of Punjab in 1849 — the last major independent Indian kingdom to fall before the 1857 Revolt.

phases.name: Rise of Sikh Power (Background)
points: 1469: Guru Nanak Dev Ji — founder of Sikhism; 1606: Guru Hargobind Ji — militarisation begins; 1699: Khalsa Panth founded by Guru Gobind Singh Ji
1716: death of Banda Singh Bahadur; 1748: rise of the Sikh Confederacy (Misls); 1780s: rise of Sardar Ranjit Singh

phases.name: Sardar Ranjit Singh's Rise
points: 1799: Ranjit Singh captures Lahore (7 July); 1801: coronation of Ranjit Singh as Maharaja

phases.name: Capture of Lahore & Coronation
points: Conquests in Punjab & Cis-Sutlej states; 1809: Treaty of Amritsar with the British (Sutlej as boundary)

phases.name: Expansion & Conquests
points: 1813: conquest of Kangra; 1818: control over Multan; 1819: control over Kashmir; 1834: suppression of Peshawar & Hazara

phases.name: Peace & Stability, then Decline
points: 1839: death of Ranjit Singh (27 June, Lahore); decline after Ranjit Singh due to weak successors, court factions and British interference
1845–46: First Anglo-Sikh War; 1848–49: Second Anglo-Sikh War; 29 March 1849: annexation of Punjab by the British

Political Administration: Absolute monarchy under Maharaja Ranjit Singh; centralised administration with efficient officials
Divided into 3 main areas: Lahore, Multan, Peshawar (with several districts); local administration through Amils (revenue officers); village system largely unchanged — Panchayats existed
Strong intelligence network; merit-based appointments; provincial tolerance and equal treatment to all faiths
Economy: Agriculture the mainstay; canals, wells & new lands; land revenue moderate and just — no harsh exactions

Encouraged peasants and protected them from oppression; trade & commerce flourished; main exports — shawls, textiles, horses, dry fruits; major trade routes to Kabul, Central Asia, Multan, Kashmir, Sindh, etc.
Coins — Rupee (Nanakshahi) introduced; state monopolies on some goods (salt, opium etc.) to increase revenue
Military Strength: One of the most disciplined armies of India; strong cavalry, infantry and artillery; modern weapons & European training

French and Italian officers — Allard, Ventura, Court, Avitabile; famous artillery — 'Zamzama' (giant cannon); well-equipped with muskets, cannons, rockets; forts strengthened — Lahore, Attock, Multan, Peshawar, Kashmir, etc.
Religious Policy: Deeply religious but broad-minded ruler; great respect for all religions; patronised Sikhism, Hinduism, Islam, Jainism, Buddhism and Christianity

Rebuilt Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple); donated to temples, mosques, gurdwaras; employed Muslim, Hindu, Sikh officials in high positions; coined in the name of Guru Nanak Dev Ji; never forced conversion — ensured religious harmony
Caution: do not portray Ranjit Singh as a communal ruler — he was known for his religious tolerance, justice and secular administration
Ten Gurus & Evolution of the Khalsa: Spiritual foundations: Guru Nanak (1469–1539, founded Sikhism, Langar institution); Guru Angad (standardized Gurmukhi script); Guru Amar Das (Manji system, opposed Sati and Purdah); Guru Ram Das (founded Amritsar / Ramdaspur); Guru Arjan Dev (compiled the Adi Granth in 1604 CE, built Harmandir Sahib / Golden Temple, executed by Jahangir in 1606 CE).

Militarization: Guru Hargobind (introduced concept of Miri / temporal authority and Piri / spiritual authority, constructed the Akal Takht opposite Golden Temple); Guru Har Rai and Guru Har Krishan; Guru Tegh Bahadur (martyred by Aurangzeb in 1675 at Chandni Chowk); Guru Gobind Singh (created the Khalsa Panth on Baisakhi 1699 at Anandpur Sahib, instituting the Five Ks: Kesh, Kangha, Kara, Kachhera, Kirpan; ended personal Guruship, vesting eternal spiritual authority in Guru Granth Sahib).

Banda Singh Bahadur & 12 Misls: Banda Singh Bahadur abolished the Zamindari system in Punjab and struck coins in the names of Guru Nanak and Guru Gobind Singh; martyred in Delhi (1716 CE); rise of Dal Khalsa and 12 autonomous military confederacies (Misls: Sukerchakia, Bhangi, Ahluwalia, Phulkian, Ramgarhia, etc.).
Maharaja Ranjit Singh & The Sikh Empire: Unification of Punjab: Born into the Sukerchakia Misl; captured Lahore (1799 CE, made his capital) and Amritsar (1802 CE); unified Punjab from the Satluj to Khyber Pass, including Kashmir (1819), Multan (1818), and Peshawar (1834); styled "Sher-e-Punjab" (Lion of Punjab); gilded the sanctum of Harmandir Sahib with gold leaf; recovered the Koh-i-Noor diamond from Afghan ruler Shah Shuja.

Military Modernization (Fauj-i-Khas): Created the second most formidable standing army in Asia after the British; recruited European generals (General Jean-Baptiste Ventura, Jean-Francois Allard, Paolo Avitabile, Claude Court) to drill infantry and artillery along modern Napoleonic lines; established royal foundries producing horse-artillery cannons in Lahore.

Anglo-Sikh Wars & Annexation: Treaty of Amritsar (1809) with Lord Minto fixed the Satluj river as the eastern boundary; death of Ranjit Singh (1839) led to court anarchy; First Anglo-Sikh War (1845–46: battles of Mudki, Ferozeshah, Aliwal, Sobraon; concluded by Treaty of Lahore 1846); Second Anglo-Sikh War (1848–49: battles of Ramnagar, Chillianwala, Gujarat; Punjab annexed on 29 March 1849 by Lord Dalhousie; young Maharaja Duleep Singh pensioned off to England and Koh-i-Noor surrendered to Queen Victoria).

people.name: Maharaja Ranjit Singh

prelims: Guru Gobind Singh established the Khalsa Panth at Anandpur Sahib on Baisakhi day in 1699 CE, introducing the "Five Ks" and the baptismal ceremony of Khande di Pahul.
The Akal Takht (Throne of the Timeless One) facing the Harmandir Sahib was established in 1606 CE by the sixth Sikh Guru, Guru Hargobind.

Critically evaluate the administrative, military, and secular statecraft of Maharaja Ranjit Singh, highlighting the modern organization of the Fauj-i-Khas.
Analyze the causes, military campaigns, and geopolitical consequences of the two Anglo-Sikh Wars (1845–1849), leading to the annexation of Punjab by the British East India Company.

periods.title: British Colonial Rule in India
periods.tagline: From Traders to Rulers: Conquest, Control, Exploitation & Resistance
periods.overview: This overview page traces the full 190-year arc of British rule in India, from the political foundations laid at Plassey and Buxar through Company administration, the seismic rupture of the 1857 Revolt, direct Crown rule, and the long buildup of organised nationalist resistance to the final transfer of power in 1947 — a story this site explores in far more depth across its dedicated pages on British administration, the freedom struggle's individual phases, and independence itself. The essential pattern, visible across the whole period, is a system organised for extraction dressed in the language of order and improvement: railways, telegraphs, and a uniform legal code were genuinely built, but primarily to move raw materials to ports and administer colonial control efficiently, while traditional industries like handloom textiles were deliberately or incidentally destroyed by competition from machine-made British goods, land revenue demands regularly pushed peasants into indebtedness, and recurring famines under colonial administration killed millions. Against this system, Indian resistance evolved through recognisable stages: early, localised revolts through the 18th and early 19th centuries; the 1857 Revolt's brief but genuinely broad-based challenge to Company rule; the Indian National Congress's initial decades of moderate constitutional petitioning after 1885; the more assertive Swadeshi and Extremist politics that followed the 1905 Partition of Bengal; and finally the sustained, genuinely mass-participation Gandhian movements — Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience, and Quit India — that, combined with the economic and political exhaustion Britain suffered through two World Wars, made continued colonial rule untenable by 1947.

phases.name: Political Control & Territorial Expansion
points: Arrival of British traders (1600) leading to trading privileges & factories; political interference and military victories lead to territorial expansion

1757: Battle of Plassey — Bengal under British control; 1764: Battle of Buxar; 1773: Regulating Act — first step towards British control; 1793: Permanent Settlement; 1798–1818: Subsidiary Alliance & Expansion

phases.name: Economic Consolidation & Administrative Change
points: 1813: Charter Act — end of Company's trade monopoly; 1833: Charter Act — end of Company's commercial activities; 1835: Macaulay's Minute on Education
1857: Revolt of 1857 — First War of Independence; 1858: Government of India Act — Crown rule begins; 1861: Indian Councils Act

phases.name: Social & Cultural Changes, Rise of Nationalism
points: 1876–78: Great Famine; 1885: Formation of Indian National Congress; 1905: Partition of Bengal; 1911: capital shifted to Delhi; Bengal Partition annulled
1914–18: India's role in World War I; 1919: Rowlatt Act & Jallianwala Bagh Massacre

phases.name: Mass Movements & Transfer of Power
points: 1930: Civil Disobedience Movement; 1935: Government of India Act; 1942: Quit India Movement
1947: India gains Independence on 15 August

Economy — Exploitation & Drain of Wealth: India turned into a source of raw materials and a market for British goods; traditional industries (handloom, handicrafts) destroyed by machine-made British goods
Heavy land revenue demands extracted maximum surplus from peasants; 'Drain of Wealth' — Dadabhai Naoroji exposed economic exploitation; destruction of indigenous banking, trade and shipping
Frequent famines due to colonial policies (major famines 1770, 1876–78, 1896–97, 1899–1900); development of railways, telegraph, post, irrigation — but for imperial interests
Land Revenue Systems: Permanent Settlement (1793): Bengal, Bihar, Odisha; Zamindars as landowners
Ryotwari System — Madras, Bombay Presidency; revenue collected from cultivators
Mahalwari System — North-Western Provinces, Punjab; revenue collected from village communities
Result: exploitation of peasants, indebtedness, land alienation and rural distress
Political & Administrative System: From Company Rule to Crown Rule (1858); Governor-General → Viceroy system; centralised administration; Indian Civil Service (ICS) — steel frame of empire

District administration — Collector as key official; police, judiciary & legal system; legislative councils with limited representation; 1835 onwards — law codification (Indian Penal Code 1860, Civil Procedure Code 1859, Evidence Act 1872, etc.); Divide and Rule policy — communal & regional divisions; Princely States — indirect control through Paramountcy
Social & Cultural Impact: Introduction of Western education system (Macaulay's Minute, 1835); spread of Christianity through missionaries; social evils — sati, female infanticide, child marriage continued in many areas

Social reform movements emerged; new social classes — educated middle class, professionals, clerks; printing press & newspapers created new public opinion; Western ideas — liberty, equality, nationalism inspired leaders
Resistance & Rise of Nationalism: Early resistance: Sannyasi & Fakir Rebellion (18th c.), Poligar Rebellions (South India), Vellore Mutiny (1806), Paika Rebellion (1817), tribal revolts (Kittur, Kol, Bhil, Santhal, Munda revolts)
1857 Revolt — First War of Independence (soldiers, peasants, zamindars, rulers united); tribal revolts continued (Santhal 1855, Munda 1899, Bhil, Rampa, etc.)

Rise of nationalism in three phases: Moderate (1885–1905), Extremist (1905–1919), Gandhian Mass Phase (1919–1947); formation of the Indian National Congress (1885); ideologies of Swadeshi, Boycott, National Education, Swaraj
Marxist Paradigm: 3 Stages of Colonialis: Stage I: Mercantile Capitalist Phase (1757–1813): Direct plunder and monopolistic trade. The Company used territorial land revenues of Bengal to buy Indian textiles and spices ('investment') for export to Europe without any inflow of bullion into India, draining raw wealth at the point of origin.

Stage II: Industrial Capitalist Phase (1813–1858): Post-Charter Act of 1813, the Company's trade monopoly was abolished. India was systematically converted into an agrarian appendage of the British metropolis — an exporter of raw materials (cotton, jute, indigo, opium, tea) and an open market for Manchester machine-made cotton goods, precipitating catastrophic deindustrialization and the collapse of urban artisan guild centers (Dhaka, Murshidabad, Surat).

Stage III: Financial Capitalist Phase (Post-1858): Export of British surplus capital into India under state-guaranteed returns. British capitalists invested in Indian railways (with a guaranteed 5% return paid from Indian tax revenues, termed 'private enterprise at public risk'), public debt, tea plantations, mining, and managing agency houses.
The Drain of Wealth & Famine Policy Matr: Mechanisms of Economic Drain: Conceptualized by Dadabhai Naoroji ('Poverty and Un-British Rule in India'), Romesh Chunder Dutt ('Economic History of India'), and M.G. Ranade. The drain comprised Home Charges (pensions and salaries of India Office officials, interest on Indian public debt, guaranteed railway interest, military procurement abroad) and unrequited commodity exports.

Commercialization of Agriculture: Forced shift from subsistence foodgrains to cash crops (indigo, cotton, opium, sugarcane) driven by rigid, monetized land revenue demands. This severed the traditional village famine cushion, rendering the peasantry defenseless during monsoonal droughts.

Evolution of Famine Policy & Commissions: Campbell Commission (1866 Orissa Famine - recommended government responsibility for famine relief); Strachey Commission (1880 - formulated the Provisional Famine Code, creation of Famine Insurance Fund); Lyall Commission (1897); MacDonnell Commission (1901 - recommended 'moral strategy' of advance loans, agricultural banks, and irrigation development).
Lord Wellesley & The Subsidiary Alliance: Imperial annexation strategy: Designed to subjugate Indian princely states without British financial expenditure; princely state compelled to accept a permanent British subsidiary army stationed in its territory, pay a heavy annual subsidy (or cede fertile territory in perpetuity), expel all European advisors of non-British nationality, conduct external diplomacy only through the British Resident, and surrender sovereign foreign policy.

Chronological accession of states: 1. Nizam of Hyderabad (1798 and 1800 - first state to enter alliance), 2. Mysore (1799, after Fourth Anglo-Mysore War and death of Tipu Sultan), 3. Tanjore (1799), 4. Awadh (1801, ceding Rohilkhand and the fertile Doab), 5. Peshwa Baji Rao II (Treaty of Bassein, 1802), 6. Bhonsle of Nagpur (1803), 7. Scindia of Gwalior (1804).
Lord Dalhousie & The Doctrine of Lapse (: Annexation of childless principalities: Stated that if a dependent Indian princely state had no natural male biological heir, the adopted son could inherit the ruler's private personal property, but the state sovereignty lapsed automatically to the paramount British Crown.

Annexed states in order: 1. Satara (1848 - first state annexed), 2. Jaitpur and Sambalpur (1849), 3. Baghat (1850), 4. Udaipur (1852), 5. Jhansi (1853 - Gangadhar Rao died, rejecting adopted son Damodar Rao, provoking Rani Lakshmibai's 1857 defiance), 6. Nagpur (1854 - royal jewels auctioned off in Calcutta bazaar).

Annexation of Awadh (1856): Nawab Wajid Ali Shah had natural heirs; Dalhousie annexed Awadh on the pretext of "persistent gross misgovernance and maladministration" based on the exaggerated report of Resident Outram; deeply outraged the Bengal Army sepoys (75,000 of whom were recruited from peasant families of Awadh, "the nursery of the Bengal Army").

prelims: Lord Wellesley introduced the Subsidiary Alliance system in 1798; the Nizam of Hyderabad was the first Indian ruler to accept it.
Under the Doctrine of Lapse introduced by Lord Dalhousie, Satara (1848) was the first princely state to be annexed, followed by Sambalpur, Jhansi (1853), and Nagpur (1854).
Awadh was annexed by Lord Dalhousie in February 1856 on the grounds of "misgovernance" based on the report of British Resident James Outram.
The Treaty of Bassein was signed on 31 December 1802 between Peshwa Baji Rao II and the British East India Company, triggering the Second Anglo-Maratha War.
Tipu Sultan died defending his capital Srirangapatna on 4 May 1799 during the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War against Lord Wellesley.
The Charter Act of 1833 ended all commercial trading monopolies of the East India Company (including tea and trade with China), transforming it purely into an administrative body.
Lord Dalhousie introduced the first electric telegraph line in India in 1853 between Calcutta and Agra.
mains: Compare and contrast Lord Wellesley's Subsidiary Alliance System and Lord Dalhousie's Doctrine of Lapse as instruments of British colonial territorial expansion in India.
Critically examine the annexation of Awadh by Lord Dalhousie in 1856 and analyze its direct role in triggering the Revolt of 1857 among the Bengal Army sepoys.
Discuss the four Anglo-Mysore Wars (1767–1799) and evaluate the military, technological, and diplomatic strategies of Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan against the British.

periods.title: British Administration in India
periods.tagline: From Company Rule to Crown Rule — Structure, Policies & Impact
periods.overview: Where the broader colonial-rule story covers politics and resistance, this page looks specifically at the machinery British India actually ran on — a system that began with the fairly limited Regulating Act of 1773 and grew, over nearly two centuries, into one of the most extensive bureaucratic structures ever built, anchored by what its own officials proudly called the 'steel frame': the Indian Civil Service. What is genuinely striking about this administrative architecture, viewed as a whole, is how deliberately centralised and hierarchical it became — a chain running from the Secretary of State for India in London, through the Viceroy and provincial Governors, down to the District Collector, who combined revenue, magisterial, and general executive authority in a single office and stood, in practice, as the most powerful figure most ordinary Indians would ever directly encounter. The same period saw genuine institutional innovations that would outlast British rule entirely — codified law through the Indian Penal Code and Evidence Act, a professionalised (if racially exclusionary) police and judicial system, the Allahabad and other High Courts, and, from 1882 onward, tentative experiments in local self-government through municipalities and district boards. But the system's stated purpose and its practical function were never quite the same thing, and even sympathetic later assessments generally conclude what the source material for this page states directly: that British administration in India was efficient in organisation but unjust in purpose, serving imperial interests first and Indian aspirations, at best, a distant second.

phases.name: Foundations of Control
points: 1773: Regulating Act — first step towards control of the EIC; Governor-General of Bengal (Warren Hastings), Executive Council, Supreme Court at Calcutta
1784: Pitt's India Act — dual control via the Board of Control; 1793: Cornwallis Code — major administrative reforms, separation of judicial & revenue functions

phases.name: Centralisation & Company Rule
points: 1813 & 1833: Charter Acts end the Company's trade monopoly and commercial activities; 1833: Governor-General of Bengal becomes Governor-General of India (centralisation)
1835: Macaulay's Minute — English education policy; 1853: Charter Act opens Civil Services to open competitive examination (theory of merit)

phases.name: Transition to Crown Rule
points: 1857: Revolt — end of Company rule; 1858: Government of India Act — start of Crown rule, Secretary of State for India, India Council

1861: Indian Councils Act — reorganisation, Indians nominated to councils, portfolio system in provinces; 1872: financial decentralisation — provincial finance; 1882: Lord Ripon's Local Self-Government Resolution — the 'Magna Carta of Local Self-Government in India'; 1892: Indian Councils Act — indirect election, limited discussion of budget

phases.name: Limited Reform & Dyarchy
points: 1909: Morley-Minto Reforms — separate electorates for Muslims, increase in councils; 1919: Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms — dyarchy in provinces, bicameral legislature at the Centre
1935: Government of India Act — provincial autonomy, federal structure proposed (not fully implemented); 1947: end of British rule in India

Structure of British Administration: British Crown (after 1858) → Secretary of State for India (in Britain) → India Council (advisory body) → Viceroy & Governor-General of India (representative of the Crown in India)
Executive: Governor (Provinces) → Lt. Governor/Chief Commissioner → Division → District → Sub-Division/Taluka → Village
Legislature: Imperial Legislative Council → Provincial Legislative Councils; Judiciary: Federal Court (from 1937) → High Courts → District & Subordinate Courts
ICS — The Steel Frame: Indian Civil Service (ICS) — highest administrative service; ensured unity, stability and efficiency in administration; selected through a tough competitive exam (in London till 1922, in India also after 1922 but still difficult)
High salaries, security of tenure, retirement benefits; racial bias — Indians few in number; instrument of British policy and control
Provincial Administration: Provinces governed by a Governor (later Lieutenant Governor); divided into Divisions headed by Commissioners; District headed by Collector & District Magistrate (DM) — key official for revenue, executive, judicial & police powers

Below the DM: Sub-Division (SDO)/Taluka headed by Tehsildar/Naib Tehsildar; Village — Patwari/Lambardar/Village headman; objective was efficient revenue collection, law & order and maintenance of peace
Revenue, Police & Judicial Administratio: Land revenue was the main source of government income, through Permanent Settlement (Bengal, Bihar, Orissa — Zamindars as owners), Ryotwari System (Madras, Bombay, Assam — settlement with cultivators/ryots) and Mahalwari System (North-Western Provinces, Punjab — settlement with village community)

Police Act (1861) established a modern, highly centralised police system — Superintendent of Police (SP) at district level, Thana (police station) as basic unit; Supreme Court at Calcutta (1774), Bombay (1823), Madras (1801); High Courts established in 1862; codification of laws — Indian Penal Code (1860), Code of Civil Procedure (1859), Code of Criminal Procedure (1861), Indian Evidence Act (1872)
Local Self-Government & Reforms: Lord Ripon's Resolution (1882) — the 'Magna Carta of Local Self-Government in India'; municipalities in towns, District Boards in rural areas; elected bodies with limited powers and financial dependence on government

Key reforms: Cornwallis Code (1793) — civil service reforms; Macaulay's Minute (1835) — promoted English education; Wood's Despatch (1854) — blueprint of English education in India; Hunter Commission (1882) — expansion of primary education; Montagu Declaration (1917) — pledged gradual self-government in India

Constitutional Acts at a Glance.intro: Each of these Acts is discussed elsewhere on this site within its broader historical narrative; this table exists purely as a compressed, Act-by-Act quick reference, including how contemporaries themselves judged each one's significance.
points: Regulating Act, 1773: began parliamentary oversight of the Company; made the Governor of Bengal the Governor-General over Bombay and Madras; established a Supreme Court at Fort William. Lord North described it as aimed at putting the Company's affairs on “a solid, clear and decisive establishment”, while Edmund Burke condemned it in Parliament as “an infringement of national right, national faith and national justice”

Pitt's India Act, 1784: reasserted Parliament's supremacy over the Company's administration; reduced the Governor-General's Council from four members to three; formally termed Company territories “the British possessions in India”; the jurist Sir C. Ilbert later judged that its system of checks and counter-checks remained substantially in force all the way up to 1858

Charter Act, 1813: ended the Company's monopoly over Indian trade, opening it to all British subjects, and permitted Christian missionaries to operate in India for the first time under Company sanction

Charter Act, 1833: redesignated the Governor-General of Bengal as Governor-General of India; created the first faint beginnings of a central legislature; formally promised fair and impartial treatment of Indians in selection for state service — an act the later Liberal statesman Lord Morley judged the most significant piece of Parliamentary legislation on India up to 1909

Charter Act, 1853: the last of the Charter Acts; opened the Indian Civil Service to competitive entry in principle; gave the legislature the right to frame its own rules of procedure for the first time

Government of India Act, 1858: transferred Indian administration directly from the Company to the Crown; created the office of Secretary of State for India and an advisory Council of India; the Governor-General now also carried the title of Viceroy
Indian Councils Act, 1861: established Legislative Councils at the centre and in the presidencies and provinces, for the first time including non-official members

Indian Councils Act, 1892: enlarged the size and functions of the central and provincial councils; allowed councils to discuss the budget under certain conditions and granted members the right to ask questions

Indian Councils Act, 1909 (Morley-Minto Reforms): the first genuine attempt at introducing a representative, popular element into the councils; introduced separate electorates for Muslims; allowed the beginning of non-official resolutions

Government of India Act, 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms): introduced dyarchy in the provinces, relaxing central control; made the legislature more representative and bicameral, with a Legislative Assembly and a Council of State

Government of India Act, 1935: the most elaborate constitutional document of the colonial period, providing for provincial autonomy and proposing an All-India Federation that was never actually implemented — covered in more depth on this site's Independence of India and United Provinces During Modern India pages

Land Revenue Systems Matrix (Pratik Naya: Permanent Settlement / Zamindari System (1793): Introduced by Lord Cornwallis and John Shore across Bengal, Bihar, Orissa, Northern Carnatic (covering ~19% of British India). Zamindars recognized as absolute proprietors of land with hereditary rights. State demand fixed permanently at 10/11th for the Company and 1/11th for the Zamindar. Sunset Law dictated auction of estates if revenue was not deposited by sunset of the specified day. Resulted in rampant absentee landlordism, sub-infeudation, and pauperization of the ryots.

Ryotwari System (1820): Devised by Thomas Munro and Alexander Read across Madras, Bombay Presidency, parts of Assam and Coorg (~51% of British India). Direct settlement with the individual peasant (ryot). Land surveyed and classified; revenue demand revised periodically (every 20–30 years), often reaching 45%–55% of gross produce. Led to direct state extortion and widespread indebtedness to moneylenders.

Mahalwari System (1822/1833): Formulated by Holt Mackenzie (Regulation VII of 1822) and reformed by Merttins Bird and James Thomason (1833) across North-Western Provinces, Central Provinces, and Punjab (~30% of British India). Revenue settled with the village community or estate (Mahal) collectively through the village headman (Lambardar). Revenue demand initially set at 66% (later reduced to 50% under William Bentinck).
Civil Services, Police & Judiciary Evolu: Civil Services: Lord Cornwallis ('Father of Civil Services in India') separated revenue collection from commercial functions, established high European salaries to combat corruption, and instituted the Cornwallis Code (1793). Charter Act of 1853 introduced open competitive exams. Satyendranath Tagore became the first Indian to qualify for the ICS (1863). Aitchison Commission (1886) classified services into Imperial, Provincial, and Subordinate. Lee Commission (1924) recommended establishing a Public Service Commission (created 1926).

Press Policy Chronology: Censorship of Press Act 1799 (Wellesley); Licensing Regulations 1823 (John Adams, forced closure of Raja Rammohan Roy's Mirat-ul-Akhbar); Press Act of 1835 (Charles Metcalfe - 'Liberator of the Indian Press', repealed 1823 regulations); Vernacular Press Act 1878 (Lord Lytton - 'The Gagging Act', discriminated against vernacular papers, repealed by Lord Ripon in 1882); Newspaper (Incitement to Offences) Act 1908 and Indian Press Act 1910.

Educational Commissions Pipeline: Charter Act 1813 (1 lakh education grant); Orientalist-Anglicist Controversy (H.T. Prinsep vs Macaulay); Macaulay's Minute 1835 (Infiltration Theory - creating 'a class of persons Indian in blood and colour, but English in taste, in opinions, in morals and in intellect'); Wood's Despatch 1854 ('Magna Carta of English Education in India', recommended female education, vernacular primary schools, Anglo-vernacular high schools, and affiliating universities in Calcutta, Bombay, Madras 1857); Hunter Commission 1882 (primary & secondary education); Raleigh Commission & Indian Universities Act 1904 (Curzon); Sadler Commission 1917 (Calcutta University, secondary board reforms); Hartog Committee 1929 (consolidation against hasty expansion); Wardha Scheme of Basic Education 1937 (Zakir Husain Committee, learning through craft); Sargent Plan of Education 1944.
Constitutional Acts: 1773 to 1853: Regulating Act of 1773: First step of British parliamentary control over East India Company; transformed Governor of Bengal into Governor-General of Bengal (Warren Hastings); established a 4-member Executive Council; created the Supreme Court of Judicature at Fort William, Calcutta (1774, Sir Elijah Impey as first Chief Justice); prohibited servants of the Company from engaging in private trade.

Pitt's India Act of 1784: Instituted a "System of Double Government": Board of Control (6 commissioners appointed by Crown to supervise civil, military, and revenue affairs) and Court of Directors (managing commercial affairs); styled Company possessions for the first time as "British possessions in India".

Charter Act of 1813: Abolished Company's commercial trade monopoly in India, opening Indian trade to all British subjects (except monopoly over tea trade and trade with China); allocated an annual sum of one lakh rupees for the promotion of literature and science in India; permitted Christian missionaries to enter India.

Charter Act of 1833: Centralization climax: Governor-General of Bengal redesignated as the Governor-General of India (Lord William Bentinck); deprived Bombay and Madras governors of legislative powers; ended all remaining commercial activities of the Company; added a fourth member (Law Member, Lord Macaulay) to Governor-General's Executive Council, establishing the First Law Commission (which drafted the Indian Penal Code).

Charter Act of 1853: Separated executive and legislative functions of the Council; introduced open competitive examinations for recruitment to the covenanted Indian Civil Service (ending patronage of Court of Directors); Macaulay Committee on Civil Services appointed in 1854.
Administrative Pillars: Civil Service, P: Civil Service: Lord Cornwallis regarded as the "Father of Civil Services in India"; separated commercial and administrative branches; banned private trade; Lord Wellesley established Fort William College at Calcutta (1800) to train young civil servants (later shifted to Haileybury College in England).

Police Organization: Cornwallis relieved Zamindars of police duties, establishing a regular police force; divided districts into Thanas (circles of approx 20 miles) under a Daroga (police inspector); appointed District Superintendent of Police (SP); Police Act of 1861 created modern police organizational hierarchy.

Judiciary: Cornwallis Code of 1793 separated revenue collection from judicial administration (depriving Collector of judicial powers); established a hierarchy of courts: Munsif Courts, District/Zilla Courts (headed by District Judge), Provincial Courts of Appeal, and Sadar Diwani Adalat (civil) / Sadar Nizamat Adalat (criminal); replaced Islamic criminal law with codified secular law.

periods.title: Governors-General and Viceroys of India
periods.tagline: The Complete Ruler-by-Ruler Administrative Spine of British India
periods.overview: Almost every major event covered across this site's British-era pages — the Regulating Act, the Permanent Settlement, the Doctrine of Lapse, the 1857 Revolt, the Partition of Bengal, the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms, the transfer of power itself — happened under the watch of one of only twenty men who held the top office of British India across 175 years, first as Governor-General (1773–1858) and then, after the Crown took over direct rule from the East India Company, as Viceroy (1858–1947). This page exists purely as a dense, ruler-by-ruler reference spine: rather than repeating the fuller narrative accounts of the Establishment of British Power, British Administration, and Later Mughal Empire pages elsewhere on this site, it lets you look up which specific administrator was in office when any particular act, war, or reform actually happened — the kind of precise who-was-in-charge-when detail that recurs constantly in UPSC's Prelims-style factual questions and that a purely thematic or narrative account rarely makes easy to check at a glance.

phases.name: Governors-General of Bengal / India (Company Rule)
points: Warren Hastings, Lord Cornwallis, Sir John Shore, Lord Wellesley, Sir George Barlow, Lord Minto, Lord Hastings, Lord Amherst, and Lord William Bentinck each held the title 'Governor-General of Bengal' with varying degrees of authority over the other Presidencies
The Charter Act of 1833 formally redesignated the office as 'Governor-General of India', reflecting the office's growing authority over the whole of British India rather than Bengal alone

phases.name: Governors-General of India
points: Lord William Bentinck (continuing under the new title), Lord Metcalfe, Lord Auckland, Lord Ellenborough, Lord Hardinge, and Lord Dalhousie preside over the era of maximum territorial annexation, including the Doctrine of Lapse
Lord Canning, the final Governor-General, is in office when the 1857 Revolt breaks out and remains in post through the transition to Crown rule the following year

phases.name: Viceroys of India (Crown Rule)
points: The Government of India Act, 1858 transferred administration from the East India Company directly to the British Crown, and the same officeholder (initially Lord Canning) now carried the additional, better-known title of Viceroy alongside Governor-General

The following nineteen Viceroys governed through the growth of organised nationalism, the two World Wars, and finally the negotiations that produced Independence and Partition, ending with Lord Mountbatten in 1947–48

Governors-General of Bengal / India (177.intro: Use this table to anchor any early-colonial event to the specific administrator in charge — several of the site's most-cited acts and wars (the Regulating Act, the Permanent Settlement, the Doctrine of Lapse) are named after or closely associated with the Governor-General who enacted them.
points: Warren Hastings (1773–1785): Regulating Act (1773); Pitt's India Act (1784, passed near the end of his term); the Rohilla War (1774); First Maratha War (1775–82) and Treaty of Salbai (1782); Second Mysore War (1780–84); founded the Asiatic Society of Bengal (1784); later impeached in England over his conduct toward the Raja of Benaras

Lord Cornwallis (1786–1793): Third Mysore War (1790–92) and Treaty of Seringapatam; the Cornwallis Code (1793) separating revenue administration from civil jurisdiction; the Permanent Settlement of Bengal (1793); Europeanisation of the administrative machinery and introduction of the civil services
Sir John Shore (1793–1798): Charter Act of 1793; Battle of Kharda between the Nizam and the Marathas (1795)

Lord Wellesley (1798–1805): introduced the Subsidiary Alliance System (1798), starting with the Nizam of Hyderabad; Fourth Mysore War (1799); Second Maratha War (1803–05); annexed Tanjore, Surat, and the Carnatic; Treaty of Bassein (1802)
Sir George Barlow (1805–1807): the Vellore Mutiny (1806)
Lord Minto (1807–1813): Treaty of Amritsar with Maharaja Ranjit Singh (1809)

Lord Hastings (1813–1823): Anglo-Nepal War (1814–16) and Treaty of Sugauli; Third Maratha War (1817–19) and the dissolution of the Maratha Confederacy; creation of the Bombay Presidency (1818); conflict with the Pindaris; the Ryotwari System introduced by Thomas Munro in Madras (1820)
Lord Amherst (1823–1828): First Burmese War (1824–26); capture of Bharatpur (1826)

Lord William Bentinck (1828–1835): abolition of sati (1829); suppression of thagi; Charter Act of 1833; the 1835 Resolution introducing English as the medium of higher education; annexation of Mysore, Coorg, and Central Cachar
Lord Metcalfe (1835–1836): repealed restrictions on the press
Lord Auckland (1836–1842): First Afghan War (1838–42); death of Ranjit Singh (1839)
Lord Ellenborough (1842–1844): annexation of Sindh (1843); war with Gwalior (1843)
Lord Hardinge (1844–1848): First Anglo-Sikh War (1845–46) and Treaty of Lahore; social reforms including the abolition of female infanticide and human sacrifice in some regions

Lord Dalhousie (1848–1856): Second Anglo-Sikh War (1848–49) and annexation of Punjab; annexation of Lower Burma (Pegu, 1852); the Doctrine of Lapse, applied to Satara, Jaitpur, Sambalpur, Udaipur, Jhansi, Nagpur, and Awadh; Wood's Educational Despatch (1854); the first railway line (Bombay–Thane, 1853) and major telegraph and postal reforms; the Widow Remarriage Act (1856)
Lord Canning (1856–1858 as Governor-General): founding of the universities of Calcutta, Madras, and Bombay (1857); in office during the Revolt of 1857

Viceroys of India (1858–1947).intro: The same office continues here under the additional title of Viceroy after the 1858 transfer of power to the Crown — this table is the direct administrative counterpart to the freedom-struggle narrative told in more depth on this site's Indian Freedom Struggle, Mahatma Gandhi, and Independence of India pages.
points: Lord Canning (1858–1862): formal transfer of control from the East India Company to the Crown under the Government of India Act, 1858; the 'White Mutiny' by European troops (1859)
Lord Lawrence, Lord Mayo, Lord Northbrook, and Lord Lytton govern through the 1860s and 1870s, a period covered in more administrative depth on this site's British Administration page
Lord Ripon (1880–1884): Local Self-Government Resolution (1882), often called the 'Magna Carta of Local Self-Government in India'; repeal of the Vernacular Press Act; the controversial Ilbert Bill

Lord Dufferin (1884–1888): in office when the Indian National Congress was founded (December 1885) — the same period this site's dedicated Foundation of the Indian National Congress page examines in detail, including the 'Safety Valve' theory of Congress's origins that names Dufferin specifically

Lord Lansdowne, Lord Elgin II, and Lord Curzon (1899–1905) follow, with Curzon's tenure most remembered for the deeply controversial Partition of Bengal (1905), which directly triggered the Swadeshi Movement covered on the Indian Freedom Struggle page

Lord Minto II (1905–1910): continued Swadeshi and Extremist agitation following the Bengal partition; the Morley-Minto Reforms (Indian Councils Act, 1909), introducing separate electorates for Muslims

Lord Hardinge II (1910–1916): annulment of the Partition of Bengal (1911); transfer of the capital from Calcutta to Delhi (1911); a bomb attack on Hardinge himself during the Delhi Durbar procession (1912)

Lord Chelmsford (1916–1921): the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms and Government of India Act, 1919 introducing dyarchy in the provinces; the Rowlatt Act and the Jallianwala Bagh Massacre (1919); the launch of the Non-Cooperation Movement (1920)
Lord Reading (1921–1926): the Chauri Chaura incident and withdrawal of Non-Cooperation (1922); the Kakori Conspiracy (1925)
Lord Irwin (1926–1931): the Simon Commission's arrival and boycott (1928); the Purna Swaraj resolution and Dandi Salt March launching Civil Disobedience (1930); the Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931)
Lord Willingdon (1931–1936): continuation and eventual suppression of Civil Disobedience; the Government of India Act, 1935 introducing provincial autonomy

Lord Linlithgow (1936–1944): 1937 provincial elections and formation of Congress ministries; India's entry into the Second World War without Indian consultation (1939) and the resulting resignation of Congress ministries; the Cripps Mission (1942) and its failure; the Quit India Movement (1942) and the mass arrest of the Congress leadership

Lord Wavell (1944–1947): the Wavell Plan and Simla Conference; the end of the Second World War (1945); the Cabinet Mission's proposals (1946) and their acceptance by Congress; the Muslim League's 'Direct Action Day' (16 August 1946); elections to the Constituent Assembly and formation of the Interim Government; Clement Attlee's announcement of the end of British rule (20 February 1947)

Lord Mountbatten (1947–1948): the June Third Plan (1947) announcing Partition; introduction of the Indian Independence Bill in the House of Commons; appointment of the Radcliffe boundary commissions for Bengal and Punjab; served briefly as independent India's first Governor-General after 15 August 1947

Key Governors-General (1773–1858): Warren Hastings (1772–1785): Abolished Dual Government in Bengal (1772); Asiatic Society of Bengal founded by Sir William Jones (1784); First Anglo-Maratha War (Treaty of Salbai 1782); Second Anglo-Mysore War; impeached in British Parliament on return to England (defended by Edmund Burke).
Lord Cornwallis (1786–1793): Permanent Settlement of Bengal (1793); Cornwallis Code; Third Anglo-Mysore War (Treaty of Srirangapatna 1792); father of Indian Civil Service.
Lord Wellesley (1798–1805): Subsidiary Alliance system; Fourth Anglo-Mysore War (1799); Treaty of Bassein (1802) and Second Anglo-Maratha War; styled himself "A Bengal Tiger".

Lord William Bentinck (1828–1835): Abolition of Sati (1829); suppression of Thuggee by Colonel William Sleeman; English Education Act of 1835 based on Macaulay's Minute; first Governor-General of India.

Lord Dalhousie (1848–1856): Doctrine of Lapse; Second Anglo-Sikh War and annexation of Punjab (1849); Annexation of Awadh (1856); First railway line (Bombay to Thane, 1853); First electric telegraph line (Calcutta to Agra, 1853); Post Office Act 1854; Wood's Despatch on Education (1854 - "Magna Carta of English Education in India"); Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act (1856).
Key Viceroys (1858–1947): Lord Canning (1856–1862): Last Governor-General of Company and First Viceroy of Crown (Government of India Act 1858); Queen Victoria's Proclamation; Indian Councils Act 1861; Indian Penal Code (1860); Universities of Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras established (1857).

Lord Lytton (1876–1880): Reactionary imperialist; Vernacular Press Act (1878 - "Gagging Act" targeting Amrita Bazar Patrika); Arms Act (1878); Delhi Durbar of 1877 amidst catastrophic famine (Queen Victoria proclaimed Kaiser-i-Hind); Second Anglo-Afghan War (1878–80); lowered maximum age for ICS exam from 21 to 19.

Lord Ripon (1880–1884): Most popular and liberal Viceroy; repealed Vernacular Press Act (1882); First Factory Act of 1881 (child labour reform); Local Self-Government Resolution (1882 - "Father of Local Self-Government in India"); Hunter Commission on Education (1882); Ilbert Bill Controversy (1883 - proposed allowing Indian judges to try Europeans, provoking racist white mutiny).
Lord Curzon (1899–1905): Indian Universities Act (1904); Ancient Monuments Preservation Act (1904); Partition of Bengal (1905); Younghusband Expedition to Tibet (1904).
Lord Chelmsford (1916–1921): Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms / Government of India Act 1919 (introduced Dyarchy in provinces); Jallianwala Bagh Massacre (1919); Non-Cooperation and Khilafat Movements.
Lord Irwin (1926–1931): Simon Commission boycott (1928); Nehru Report; Lahore Session (Purna Swaraj 1929); Civil Disobedience Movement and Dandi March (1930); Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931).
Lord Mountbatten (March–August 1947): Last Viceroy and first Governor-General of independent India; June 3rd Plan; oversaw partition and transfer of power.

periods.title: Tribal Revolts and Movements in Colonial India
periods.tagline: A Long, Continuous Current of Resistance the Mainstream Freedom-Struggle Narrative Often Under-Represents
periods.overview: Long before the Indian National Congress held its first session, and continuing well after Gandhi's mass movements had come to dominate the national narrative, India's tribal communities were engaged in a nearly continuous series of armed uprisings against the disruption colonial rule brought to their forests, land rights, and ways of life. These revolts are frequently under-represented in a freedom-struggle narrative built primarily around the Congress, the Muslim League, and elite urban politics — yet the grievances driving them were genuinely distinct and, in their own regions, no less significant: colonial forest laws that criminalised traditional shifting cultivation and access to forest produce, the intrusion of outside moneylenders and landlords (often enabled by new colonial land-revenue and property-rights systems that tribal communities had no prior experience of), missionary activity that some communities experienced as a further threat to their autonomy, and forced labour and taxation imposed by an administration with little understanding of or interest in existing tribal social structures. What emerges across nearly two centuries of these revolts — from the Pahariyas and Chuars in the 1770s, through the Kol, Ho, Munda, and Santhal uprisings of the early-to-mid 19th century, to the Bhil, Naikada, Koya, and Rampa movements of the later colonial period, and finally to explicitly religious-political movements like the Tana Bhagat movement and the North-East's tribal resistance — is a pattern of resistance rooted in the specific material and cultural disruption of colonial rule, sometimes running in parallel with, and sometimes almost entirely separate from, the mainstream nationalist movement covered in more depth elsewhere on this site.

phases.name: Early Revolts
points: Pahariyas' Rebellion (from 1778) and the Chuar Uprisings (from 1776) in the Bengal-Bihar region are among the earliest recorded organised resistance to the East India Company's expanding land-revenue demands
Kol Uprising (1831–32), led by figures including Buddho Bhagat, resisted the growing presence of outside (mostly Bengali and Sikh) moneylenders and landlords in the Chota Nagpur region

phases.name: The Great Mid-Century Uprisings
points: Ho and Munda Uprisings, including Raja Parahat's revolt (1827) in Singhbhum against the extension of the colonial revenue system into tribal areas

The Santhal Rebellion (Santhal Hul, 1855–56), led by the brothers Sido and Kanhu, was one of the largest tribal uprisings in colonial history, directed against moneylenders, landlords, and the colonial state simultaneously, and led directly to the creation of a separate Santhal Pargana administrative area

phases.name: Later 19th-Century Movements
points: The Kandh uprisings under Chakra Bisoi and the Naikada Movement in Gujarat resisted, respectively, colonial interference in traditional practices and outside economic penetration of tribal land

The Ulgulan ('Great Tumult'), led by Birsa Munda (1899–1900), combined agrarian grievance with an explicitly religious-reform movement and remains one of the most celebrated tribal uprisings in Indian nationalist memory

phases.name: Early 20th-Century Movements
points: Bhil Revolts (1913 and after), Koya Revolts, and the Bastar Revolt (1910) in central India continued the pattern of resistance to forest-law restrictions and outside economic intrusion
The Rampa Revolts in the Andhra region and a wave of Forest Satyagrahas across central India specifically targeted colonial restrictions on traditional forest use and access

phases.name: Movements Merging with the National Struggle
points: The Tana Bhagat Movement combined religious reform with direct participation in Gandhian civil disobedience, showing tribal resistance increasingly intersecting with mainstream nationalist politics by this period

In the North-East, a distinct and long-running current of tribal resistance — among the Ahoms, Khasis, Singphos, Kukis, and in Tripura, later including the Naga movement and the Heraka/Zeliangrong cultural-religious movement — continued largely on its own terms into the 1940s and beyond, only partially overlapping with the pan-Indian Congress-led movement

Common Causes Across Movements.intro: Despite spanning nearly two centuries and every region of the subcontinent, these revolts show a remarkably consistent underlying grievance structure worth recognising as a pattern rather than treating each uprising as an isolated local event.
points: Colonial forest laws restricting or criminalising traditional shifting cultivation, grazing, and the collection of forest produce that tribal economies had always depended on

The introduction of outside moneylenders and landlords into regions where land had previously been held under customary, often communal, tribal systems rather than the individual private property the colonial revenue system assumed and enforced
Forced labour (begar) and new forms of taxation imposed with little regard for existing tribal social and economic structures
In some regions, resentment of missionary activity and outside cultural or religious interference compounded the economic and land-related grievances

North-East Frontier Tribal Movements.intro: The North-East's tribal resistance forms a genuinely distinct sub-current within this broader story, shaped by the region's particular colonial administrative history and its comparative geographic and political separation from the Congress-dominated politics of the Gangetic plains.
points: Resistance among the Ahoms in Assam, the Khasis in the Khasi Hills, the Singphos, and the Kukis each responded to the specific pattern of British annexation and administrative control in their own territories
Tripura saw its own distinct tradition of resistance to colonial and outside encroachment on tribal land and autonomy

The later Naga movement and the Zeliangrong cultural-religious revival (including the Heraka faith movement) show tribal resistance in this region evolving into more explicitly political and cultural self-determination movements as the colonial period drew to a close, with consequences that would extend well beyond 1947

Why This Topic Matters for a Complete Pi.intro: Reading this page alongside the site's Indian Freedom Struggle and Revolt of 1857 pages is useful precisely because it complicates the picture those pages present on their own.
points: Tribal resistance was neither uniformly separate from nor uniformly part of the Congress-led national movement; some currents (like the Tana Bhagat movement) merged directly into Gandhian civil disobedience, while others (much of the North-East's resistance) remained largely independent throughout the colonial period

The specific grievances driving tribal revolts — forest law, land alienation to outside moneylenders, forced labour — were often only loosely connected to the constitutional and political demands (self-government, dominion status, complete independence) that dominated Congress politics, a reminder that 'the freedom struggle' was never a single, uniform movement with one shared grievance or one shared theory of what freedom should mean

Several of the specific administrative responses these revolts provoked — including the creation of separate tribal administrative areas like the Santhal Parganas — shaped the institutional and legal framework for tribal areas that independent India inherited and continues to build on

Causes of Tribal & Peasant Resentment: Colonial forest encroachments: Forest Acts of 1865 and 1878 transformed traditional tribal communal forests into state-reserved property, criminalizing shifting cultivation (Jhum), grazing, and collection of minor forest produce.

Infiltration of Dikus (Outsiders): Money-lenders (Mahajans), zamindars, traders, and European contractors supported by British police seized ancestral tribal land through fraudulent debt mortgages, turning free adivasis into bonded agricultural laborers (Kamia / Beth-begari).
Major Tribal Uprisings: Santhal Hool (1855–1856): Led by four brothers (Sidho, Kanhu, Chand, and Bhairav) in the Damin-i-Koh region (Rajmahal Hills, Bihar/Jharkhand) against British revenue officers, Bengali Mahajans, and railway contractors; mobilized 60,000 Santhals; brutally suppressed with martial law; led to creation of the separate non-regulation Santhal Parganas district.

Munda Ulgulan / The Great Tumult (1899–1900): Led by charismatic religious leader Birsa Munda ("Dharti Aaba" / Father of the Earth) in the Chotanagpur plateau; fought against the destruction of the ancestral Khuntkatti joint-landholding system by Thikadars and Christian missionaries; Birsa declared an independent Munda Raj; captured and died in Ranchi jail (1900); prompted enactment of the Chotanagpur Tenancy Act (1908) banning transfer of tribal land to non-tribals.

Other key uprisings: Kol Mutiny (1831–32 under Buddho Bhagat in Chotanagpur); Khasi Uprising (1829–33 led by U Tirot Sing in Meghalaya against road construction); Rampa Rebellion (1922–24 in Andhra Pradesh led by Alluri Sitarama Raju using guerrilla warfare against Madras Forest Act); Chenchu tribal revolt.
Major Peasant Movements: Indigo Revolt / Nil Bidroho (1859–1860): Led by Digambar Biswas and Bishnu Biswas in Nadia (Bengal); peasants took solemn oath refusing to cultivate indigo; popularized by Dinabandhu Mitra's Bengali play Nil Darpan (translated into English by Michael Madhusudan Dutta); led to appointment of Indigo Commission (1860) declaring indigo cultivation cannot be forced.

Pabna Agrarian League (1873 in East Bengal, resisting rent hikes via legal litigation) and Deccan Riots (1875 in Pune/Ahmednagar, burning debt bonds of Gujarati/Marwari moneylenders; led to Deccan Agriculturists' Relief Act 1879).

periods.title: Socio-Religious Reforms During British Rule
periods.tagline: Awakening of India — Reform in Society, Renaissance of Minds
periods.overview: The nineteenth century's wave of socio-religious reform movements is where colonial-era India's intellectual and moral energy is arguably most visible — a genuinely creative response to the collision between traditional religious and social practice, on one side, and Western education, Christian missionary criticism, and Enlightenment-derived ideas of reason and individual rights, on the other, that produced not imitation but a series of deliberate, often quite different syntheses. Raja Ram Mohan Roy's Brahmo Samaj, founded in 1828, set the template: a rationalist, monotheistic reinterpretation of Hindu scripture that campaigned successfully against sati and for women's education and widow remarriage, working through both public argument and direct legislative pressure. Later movements took the same basic impulse in genuinely divergent directions — Swami Dayanand Saraswati's Arya Samaj looked backward to Vedic authority rather than forward to Western rationalism, framing reform as a 'return' rather than an innovation; the Aligarh Movement under Sir Syed Ahmad Khan pursued a parallel project of modern education specifically for Muslims; and the Ramakrishna Mission, building on Swami Vivekananda's synthesis of Vedanta philosophy and practical social service, turned reform toward hospitals, schools, and disaster relief rather than doctrinal argument. What unites this genuinely varied landscape of movements is a shared, largely successful legislative legacy — the Sati Regulation of 1829, the Widow Remarriage Act of 1856, the Age of Consent Act of 1891, and eventually the Child Marriage Restraint Act of 1929 — and a less obvious but equally important effect: these movements built the institutions, the vocabulary of rights and equality, and in some cases the individual leaders who would go on to power the nationalist movement that followed. Historians studying this period generally caution against two opposite oversimplifications: treating the reform movements as either a simple, grateful import of Western ideas, or as a wholly independent revival that owed nothing to the colonial encounter. The more accurate picture is that colonial rule and Western education acted as a catalyst and a point of comparison — occasioning a searching, often uncomfortable re-examination of long-standing social and religious practice — while the intellectual resources reformers actually drew on, and the specific practices they chose to attack or defend, came overwhelmingly from within India's own religious and philosophical traditions. Reformers also differed sharply on method: some, like Ram Mohan Roy on the question of sati, argued that a targeted practice was not sanctioned by scripture at all and could therefore be reformed from within religious orthodoxy; others were willing to argue that where scripture and ethics conflicted, ethics should prevail regardless of textual sanction. This same period also saw an important and sometimes overlooked current of reform focused specifically on caste rather than religion as such — most notably Jyotirao Phule's sustained campaign against Brahmanical social dominance in western India, and Narayana Guru's parallel movement for the dignity and temple-entry rights of lower castes in Kerala — a reminder that 'social reform' in this era was never a single, uniform programme but a genuinely contested set of debates about what Indian society should become.

phases.name: Aligarh, Deoband & Singh Sabha Movements
points: Aligarh Movement (1875) — founder Sir Syed Ahmed Khan; modern education for Muslims, scientific temper; established the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College, Aligarh (later Aligarh Muslim University)
Deoband Movement (1866) — founders Maulana Muhammad Qasim Nanautavi; preservation of Islamic faith and values; established Darul Uloom, Deoband
