Shravasti — Lord Buddha's stay; Kaushambi — Buddhist site; Mathura — Lord Krishna's birthplace; Agra — Taj Mahal, Fatehpur Sikri; Jhansi — Rani Lakshmibai; Lucknow — Nawabi culture & capital

Important Personalities.intro: This is a preview list only; the fuller Important Cities & Personalities page later in this track, and the individual period pages for each name, go into far more depth on every figure named here.
points: Gautam Buddha, Mahavira, Chandragupta Maurya, Ashoka, Harshavardhana, Raja Suheldev, Alauddin Khalji, Akbar, Begum Hazrat Mahal, Nana Saheb, Govind Ballabh Pant

Chronological Horizons of Uttar Pradesh: Deep Time & Prehistoric Archaeology: Belan Valley (Prayagraj) yielding Lower Palaeolithic to Neolithic stratigraphic sequences; Lahuradewa (Sant Kabir Nagar) yielding the earliest domesticated rice in South Asia (c. 7000–6000 BCE); Chopani Mando wild-to-settled transition; Sarai Nahar Rai, Damdama, and Mahadaha (Pratapgarh) showing Mesolithic microlithic cemeteries and bone ornaments.
Vedic & Mahajanapada Era: Heartland of Later Vedic Kuru-Panchala culture; 8 of the 16 Mahajanapadas flourished in UP: Kuru, Panchala, Shurasena, Vatsa, Kosala, Malla, Chedi, and Kashi.

Classical to Medieval Empires: Sarnath (Ashoka's Lion Capital, First Sermon); Mathura (Kushana second capital, Mathura school of red sandstone sculpture); Gupta masterpieces at Deogarh (Dashavatara temple) and Bhitargaon (brick temple); Kannauj under Harshavardhana, Pratiharas, and Gahadavalas; Jaunpur Sharqi Sultanate ("Shiraz of the East"); Mughal Agra and Fatehpur Sikri; Awadh Nawabi culture in Lucknow.

Colonial Resistance & Modern Formation: Epicenter of the Revolt of 1857 (Mangal Pandey, Meerut, Lucknow, Kanpur, Jhansi, Bareilly, Allahabad); cradle of the mass freedom struggle (Chauri Chaura, Swaraj Party, Kakori Action, Azad martyrdom, Ballia parallel government); official evolution from North-Western Provinces (1836) to United Provinces of Agra & Oudh (1902) to Uttar Pradesh (24 January 1950).

events.title: 16 Mahajanapadas in the Ganga-Yamuna Doab
events.desc: Kashi, Kosala, Vatsa, Kuru, Panchala and Surasena — six of the sixteen Mahajanapadas — are centred in present-day Uttar Pradesh.

events.title: Uttar Pradesh comes into existence
events.desc: The United Provinces are renamed Uttar Pradesh under the U.P. Act, 1950, with Lucknow as its capital.

events.title: Uttarakhand carved out
events.desc: The hill districts of Uttar Pradesh are separated to form the new state of Uttarakhand (initially Uttaranchal).

prelims: Uttar Pradesh officially received its current name on 24 January 1950; 24 January is celebrated annually as "UP Diwas" (Uttar Pradesh Day).
Eight of the sixteen ancient Mahajanapadas were located entirely or predominantly within the modern boundaries of Uttar Pradesh.
Lahuradewa in Sant Kabir Nagar district of UP has yielded the oldest archaeological evidence of domesticated rice in South Asia, dating to c. 7000–6000 BCE.
The National Emblem of India is adopted from the Lion Capital of Ashoka excavated at Sarnath near Varanasi.
The Dashavatara Temple at Deogarh (Lalitpur district, UP) is the earliest surviving structural temple in India built on a complete Panchayatana layout.
The First Spark of the 1857 Revolt erupted on 10 May 1857 at Meerut, initiated by sepoys of the 3rd Native Cavalry.
Ballia was the first district in India to establish a parallel government (Prati Sarkar) during the Quit India Movement in August 1942 under Chittu Pandey.
mains: Trace the historical evolution of Uttar Pradesh from the prehistoric settlements of the Belan Valley to the formation of the modern state in 1950.
Evaluate the role of the Ganga-Yamuna Doab in shaping the political, agrarian, and urban history of Northern India from the ancient Mahajanapadas to the Mughal era.
Discuss the contributions of Uttar Pradesh to India's national freedom struggle, highlighting the key revolutionary actions, mass movements, and peasant uprisings.

quickFacts: Birthplace of Lord Ram (Ayodhya), Lord Krishna (Mathura), and home to Buddhism's and Jainism's earliest sites

periods.title: Prehistoric & Early Settlements of Uttar Pradesh
periods.tagline: From Earliest Times to 1500 BCE (Before the Vedic Period) — U.P. in the Cradle of Indian Civilization
periods.overview: Uttar Pradesh's prehistoric record deserves its own page rather than a footnote on the national Prehistoric Age entry because it happens to preserve one of the longest and most complete cultural sequences anywhere in India — sites like Belan Valley, Sarai Nahar Rai, Chopani-Mando, and above all Lahuradewa, among the earliest known rice-cultivation sites in South Asia, let archaeologists trace the same broad Palaeolithic-to-Chalcolithic transition described in the national overview, but with an unusually dense and well-excavated local evidence base. What the U.P.-specific record adds to the wider national picture is texture: rock paintings at Chopani-Mando showing early artistic and ritual life, house remains and agricultural evidence at Mahagara and Lahuradewa documenting the actual mechanics of the shift from foraging to farming, and Painted Grey Ware traditions at Narhan and Atranjikhera that carry directly forward into the Vedic-age settlements the next page in this track covers. Read alongside the national Prehistoric Age page's broader four-stage framework, this page functions as the detailed regional case study — the specific sites and dates that make U.P. 'the ancient land of human civilization and culture', as the source material puts it, rather than merely one region among many where that broader prehistoric story happened to play out.

phases.name: Old Stone Age (Palaeolithic)
points: Early humans, hunting and food gathering; use of crude stone tools; nomadic life

phases.name: Mesolithic Age
points: Microlithic tools; hunting, fishing, food gathering; rock shelters & cave habitations

phases.name: Neolithic Age
points: Neolithic (polished) tools; agriculture begins; domestication of animals; semi-settled life

phases.name: Early Settlements / Chalcolithic
points: Copper tools and pottery; permanent settlements; trade & exchange; early social & cultural development

phases.name: Transition to Vedic Period
points: Aryan settlements begin in Western U.P.; transition from the prehistoric to the historical age

Life & Culture by Phase.intro: This table exists to show the same four-stage transition the national Prehistoric Age page describes in outline — nomadic to settled, foraging to farming — but tracked in parallel columns across society, technology, shelter, and religion specifically as the U.P. archaeological record documents it.
points: Old Stone Age: nomadic life, hunting/fishing/food gathering, hand axes/cleavers/choppers, caves & rock shelters, small bands based on family groups, animism

Mesolithic Age: semi-nomadic, microlithic tools (blades, points, scrapers), bow & arrow, rock shelters/seasonal camps, clan-based groups, spirit worship & early Mother Goddess worship, rock paintings (Chopani-Mando)

Neolithic Age: settled life begins, agriculture (rice, wheat, barley), domestication of cattle/buffalo/goat/dog, mud huts, polished stone tools (axes, adzes), headman as early form of leader, worship of Mother Goddess & fertility cult

Chalcolithic/Early Settlements: permanent villages, planned rectangular houses, copper tools alongside stone tools, surplus production & barter trade, growth of villages and division of labour, mother goddess idols and terracotta figurines

Important Archaeological Sites.intro: Each of these sites is a physical, excavated anchor for the more abstract stages described above; Lahuradewa in particular deserves special attention since its early rice-cultivation evidence is one of the most UPPSC-relevant single facts in this entire period.
points: Belan Valley (Mirzapur, Sonbhadra) — one of the earliest human habitations in India, Acheulian tools found
Chopani-Mando (Pratapgarh) — Mesolithic rock shelter, microlithic tools, animal drawings
Mahagara (Rae Bareli) — Neolithic-Chalcolithic site, pottery, stone tools, house remains, agriculture evidence
Sarai Nahar Rai (Baghpat) — Chalcolithic settlement (2600–1900 BCE), copper objects, pottery, beads, remains of huts
Lahuradewa (Sant Kabir Nagar) — one of the earliest known agricultural sites in India (7000–2000 BCE), rice cultivation evidence
Narhan (Ballia) — Chalcolithic culture, Painted Grey Ware (later stage), early farming community
Atranjikhera (Etah) — early urban settlement (2nd millennium BCE), beads, seals, terracotta figurines

Contribution of Men & Women.intro: The source material is explicit that both sexes contributed materially to early society's development, a point worth remembering precisely because it becomes harder to trace with the same clarity once the more hierarchical Vedic-age social structures covered on the next page take hold.
points: Men: hunting & protection of the group, making tools & weapons, clearing land for agriculture, construction of huts, trade & exchange, leadership roles

Women: collection of fruits/roots/seeds, early agriculture (sowing, weeding, harvesting), pottery making, care of children & elderly, domestication of animals, making ornaments & handicrafts; both men and women contributed equally to the development of society and culture

Belan Valley & Gangetic Mesolithic Sites: Belan Valley Stratigraphy: Located in Prayagraj and Mirzapur districts; excavated by Prof. G.R. Sharma (University of Allahabad); rare site in South Asia revealing continuous stratigraphic sequence from Lower Palaeolithic through Middle and Upper Palaeolithic to Mesolithic and Neolithic; Lopamudra / Belan gravel beds yielded Acheulian handaxes, cleavers, and a famous Upper Palaeolithic carved bone female figurine (Mother Goddess) from Lohanda Nala.

Sarai Nahar Rai (Pratapgarh): Earliest Mesolithic settlement in the Ganga plains (c. 8400 BCE); revealed 14 human burials (extended inhumation oriented west-east) with microlith grave goods and bone ornaments; earliest evidence of violent human conflict (skeleton with a stone microlith embedded in a lumbar vertebra).

Mahadaha & Damdama (Pratapgarh): Damdama revealed 41 human burials, including double burials (joint male-female burials) and a unique triple burial; circular and oblong pit hearths; abundant animal bones (wild cattle, deer, pig, turtle, birds); bone arrowheads, points, and rings.
Chopani Mando & Lahuradewa: Chopani Mando (Belan Valley): Shows transition from wild hunter-gatherer existence to semi-sedentary life; beehive-shaped huts with reed-plastered floors; earliest crude handmade cord-impressed pottery in North India.

Lahuradewa (Sant Kabir Nagar): Breakthrough excavation by UP State Archaeology Department (Rakesh Tewari); yielded carbonized domesticated rice (Oryza sativa) grains and ceramic sherds dating back to c. 7000–6000 BCE, pushing back the origin of Asian rice farming by millennia.

events.title: Rice cultivation at Lahuradewa
events.desc: One of the earliest known agricultural sites in South Asia, providing key evidence for the origins of settled farming in the region.

events.title: Transition to the Vedic Age begins
events.desc: Aryan settlements appear in Western U.P., marking the transition from prehistory to the historical Vedic period.

prelims: The bone figurine of a Mother Goddess dating to the Upper Palaeolithic period was excavated from Lohanda Nala in the Belan Valley (Prayagraj).
The earliest human skeletal remains and extended burials in the Gangetic plain were excavated at Sarai Nahar Rai, Mahadaha, and Damdama in Pratapgarh district, UP.
Damdama (Pratapgarh) has yielded evidence of 41 human burials, including joint burials and a rare triple burial, alongside bone ornaments and microliths.
Lahuradewa in Sant Kabir Nagar (UP) has yielded radiocarbon dates of c. 7000–6000 BCE for domesticated rice, revolutionizing ancient agricultural chronologies.
Chopani Mando in the Belan Valley exhibits a continuous three-phase transition from food gathering to early pottery and circular hut settlements.
The prehistoric rock art sites of Uttar Pradesh are concentrated in the Vindhyan sandstone caves of Mirzapur, Sonbhadra, and Prayagraj districts.
Robert Bruce Foote and subsequent archaeologists confirmed that the Belan Valley holds a continuous stratified record from the Lower Palaeolithic to the Neolithic.
mains: Critically examine the archaeological significance of the Belan Valley excavations in establishing the prehistoric cultural sequence of Northern India.
Analyze the Mesolithic burial practices, skeletal morphology, and tool industries of Sarai Nahar Rai, Mahadaha, and Damdama in Uttar Pradesh.
Evaluate the impact of the Lahuradewa excavations on the global understanding of the origin and antiquity of rice domestication in South Asia.

quickFacts: Belan Valley (Mirzapur, Sonbhadra) — earliest human habitation
Vedic Age begins in Western U.P., c. 1500 BCE

periods.title: Vedic Age in Uttar Pradesh
periods.tagline: The Evolution of Vedic Culture in the Land of Ganga-Yamuna Doab
periods.overview: As Vedic tribes moved east out of the Sapta-Sindhu region, the Ganga-Yamuna Doab became not just one Vedic settlement area among several but the specific geographic stage on which most of the process described more broadly on this site's national Vedic Age page actually happened: the Janapadas of Kuru (capital Hastinapur), Panchala (Ahichchhatra), Kashi (Varanasi), Kosala (Ayodhya), and Surasena (Mathura) that emerge by the end of this period are, between them, a majority of the political geography the age produced, and every one of them sits inside present-day U.P. This regional lens also makes visible something easy to lose in the pan-Indian account: the same women recorded nationally as hymn-composers and philosophers — Gargi Vachaknavi, Maitreyi, Lopamudra, Apala, Ghosha — were operating specifically within this Doab-centred world, debating and composing at the same learning centres (Ahichchhatra, Hastinapur, Kashi) that were simultaneously becoming the region's first real seats of political power. By the time this period closes, in other words, the national story of 'tribes becoming Mahajanapadas' and the U.P.-specific story of 'the Doab becoming the political heart of North India' are describing, quite literally, the same process from two different distances.

phases.name: Early Vedic
points: Aryans enter the Sapta-Sindhu region and gradually move east; in U.P., they settle along the Ganga-Yamuna Doab; cattle rearing, simple agriculture, clan-based life

phases.name: Later Vedic
points: Expansion across U.P. plains; permanent settlements established; rise of Janas and early states; development of agriculture, irrigation and trade

phases.name: Late Vedic / Upanishadic
points: Rise of Kuru-Panchala culture in western U.P.; growth of learning and philosophy (Upanishads); social & political systems become more complex

phases.name: Transition to Mahajanapadas
points: Janapadas emerge: Kuru, Panchala, Kashi, Kosala, Surasena; urbanization, trade & crafts grow; society moves towards the Mahajanapada era

Society, Polity & Economy by Phase.intro: Reading this table left to right traces the same narrowing of social flexibility that the overview above describes in prose — note in particular how the 'Position of women' and 'Family & Social Life' rows shift across the four columns, since that trajectory doesn't reverse for the rest of this track.
points: Early Vedic: tribal (Jana) based society, no rigid hierarchy; Gana (clan) based polity, King (Rajan) elected; cattle rearing main occupation; nature worship (Indra, Agni, Varuna)

Later Vedic: Varna system develops, families become patriarchal; monarchy becomes hereditary; agriculture (plough used), surplus production, trade & craft development; more rituals and Yajnas, gods like Prajapati/Vishnu/Rudra

Late Vedic/Upanishadic: caste system becomes stronger, joint family system; Janapadas more organized, kings powerful, taxation begins; iron tools used, trade routes active; rise of philosophy & Upanishads

Transition: society complex, emergence of urban class; formation of Janapadas — Kuru, Panchala, Kosala, Kashi; trade & commerce grow, coinage (punch-marked) begins; rise of Shramana traditions (Buddhism, Jainism later)

Important Janas / States in Vedic Age U..intro: These five Janas are the direct institutional ancestors of the Mahajanapadas covered on the very next page — every capital named here (Hastinapur, Ahichchhatra, Varanasi, Ayodhya, Mathura) remains a major U.P. city today, worth memorising as a set.
points: Kuru (1500–600 BCE): capital Hastinapur; powerful tribe, Rigvedic & later Vedic importance
Panchala (1500–600 BCE): capital Ahichchhatra, North & South Panchala; centre of learning & culture
Kashi (1500–600 BCE): capital Varanasi; ancient settlement on Ganga, trade & culture centre
Kosala (1000–600 BCE): capital Ayodhya; powerful kingdom on Sarayu, important in the Later Vedic age
Surasena (800–600 BCE): capital Mathura; Yadu tribe, trade & cultural importance

Important Vedic Literature Composed.intro: This chronological list of texts is best read as a dating tool: knowing that the Rigveda belongs to the Early Vedic phase while the Upanishads belong to the Late Vedic/Upanishadic phase lets you place any Vedic-era fact correctly on a timeline even without memorising exact years.
points: Rigveda — early Vedic hymns (1500–1200 BCE); Samaveda, Yajurveda, Atharvaveda — later Vedic composition; Brahmanas, Aranyakas, Upanishads (700–500 BCE); Vedangas — phonetics, grammar, astronomy

Kuru-Panchala Cultural Heartland: Geographical epicentre: Western and Central Uttar Pradesh formed the core heartland of the Later Vedic civilization; Kuru realm spanned Meerut, Delhi, and Thaneshwar (capital: Asandivat, later Hastinapur); Panchala realm encompassed Bareilly, Badaun, and Farrukhabad (capitals: Ahichchhatra in Bareilly and Kampilya in Farrukhabad).

Painted Grey Ware (PGW) Horizon: Archaeological excavations by B.B. Lal at Hastinapur, Atranjikhera (Etah), Alamgirpur (Meerut), and Jakhera (Kasganj) confirmed that PGW culture corresponds directly to the Later Vedic horizon; Jakhera yielded iron plowshares and early urban fortifications; flood layer at Hastinapur confirmed Puranic tradition of shifting the capital to Kaushambi.

Philosophical debates in UP: King Pravahana Jaivali of Panchala hosted assemblies of Vedic scholars; royal court of King Janaka of Videha attracted scholars like sage Yajnavalkya, Gargi Vachaknavi, and Maitreyi.

women.name: Gargi Vachaknavi
women.note: Debated in Brahmavadini gatherings; associated with the region's philosophical tradition.

women.name: Maitreyi
women.note: Seeker of knowledge; wife of Yajnavalkya.

women.name: Lopamudra
women.note: Composer of Rigvedic hymns.

women.name: Apala
women.note: Rigvedic seer.

women.name: Ghosha
women.note: Vedic hymn composer.

events.title: Rigveda composed
events.desc: As Aryan tribes settle in the Sapta-Sindhu region and begin moving toward the Ganga-Yamuna Doab, the earliest Vedic hymns are composed.

events.title: Settlement of the Ganga-Yamuna Doab
events.desc: Later Vedic tribes establish permanent settlements across the plains of Uttar Pradesh, laying the ground for the Janapadas.

events.title: Formation of Janapadas
events.desc: Kuru, Panchala, Kashi, Kosala and Surasena emerge as organized Janapadas, setting the stage for the Mahajanapada age.

people.name: Maharishi Vashishtha
people.note: Mentor of kings.

people.name: Yajnavalkya
people.note: Associated with the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad.

people.name: Bharata (of Kurus)
people.note: After whom 'Bharatvarsha' is named, per tradition.

prelims: The Painted Grey Ware (PGW) culture, associated with the Later Vedic period, was prominently excavated at Hastinapur and Atranjikhera in Uttar Pradesh.
Atranjikhera in Etah district (UP) has provided the earliest extensive evidence of regular iron tool usage (Krishna Ayas) in agriculture dating to c. 1000 BCE.
The capital of the northern Panchala kingdom was Ahichchhatra (Ramnagar, Bareilly), while the southern capital was Kampilya (Farrukhabad).
Excavations at Hastinapur conducted by Prof. B.B. Lal confirmed a massive flood layer in the Ganga, supporting Puranic records of capital relocation to Kaushambi.
King Pravahana Jaivali, a prominent philosopher-king celebrated in the Chandogya Upanishad, ruled over the Panchala realm in Uttar Pradesh.
Jakhera in Kasganj district (UP) yielded early iron sickles, hoes, and agricultural implements reflecting the transition to settled agrarian life.
The sacred confluence (Sangam) of Ganga, Yamuna, and mythical Saraswati at Prayagraj was already venerated in Later Vedic literature.
mains: Discuss the archaeological and literary evidence correlating the Painted Grey Ware (PGW) culture with the Later Vedic settlements in the Ganga-Yamuna Doab of Uttar Pradesh.
Examine the political and cultural pre-eminence of the Kuru and Panchala kingdoms during the Later Vedic transformation.
Analyze the role of iron technology (excavations at Atranjikhera and Jakhera) in facilitating agricultural clearing and urbanization in ancient Uttar Pradesh.

periods.title: Mahajanapadas of Uttar Pradesh
periods.tagline: Complete Flow, Map & Timeline — U.P. at the Heart of the Mahajanapada Age
periods.overview: Where the national Age of Mahajanapadas page surveys all sixteen states across the whole of North India, this page makes explicit just how disproportionately concentrated in present-day U.P. that political geography actually was: Kashi, Kosala, Vatsa, Kuru, Panchala, and Surasena — six of the sixteen, and among the most consequential — were all centred here, with the partly U.P.-associated republic of Malla (Kushinagara, Pava) adding a seventh. That concentration matters for more than trivia: it means the region was simultaneously home to both major political models the age produced, hereditary monarchies like Kosala and Kashi alongside the oligarchic Gana-Sangha tradition the Malla republic represented, giving U.P. an unusually complete cross-section of Mahajanapada-era statecraft in one place. It is also, not coincidentally, the setting for most of the religious ferment the national page describes only in outline: the Buddha and Mahavira both taught extensively across these same U.P.-based Janapadas, meaning the region that hosted the political transition from tribe to territorial state was, at the very same moment, hosting the intellectual movements that would challenge the Brahmanical order those states had been built on.

phases.name: Later Vedic Transformation
points: From tribal life to settled agriculture; iron use; surplus production

phases.name: Rise of Janapadas
points: Political-territorial units emerge

phases.name: Rise of Mahajanapadas
points: 16 Mahajanapadas emerge across North India

phases.name: Urbanization & Religious Movements
points: Growth of towns and trade; Buddhism, Jainism and Shramana traditions spread

phases.name: Increasing Magadhan Power
points: Bimbisara and Ajatashatru expand Magadha

phases.name: Nanda Expansion & Mauryan Empire
points: Nanda expansion (large empire, centralized rule); Mauryan Empire founded (322 BCE) by Chandragupta Maurya

The 16 Mahajanapadas and Their Link to U.intro: This is arguably the single most exam-relevant fact in this entire track — six of the sixteen Mahajanapadas sat inside present-day U.P. — so the specific list of which six, and which capital belonged to which, is worth committing to memory before moving further into this period.
points: Directly associated with present-day U.P.: Kashi (capital Varanasi), Kosala (capital Shravasti), Vatsa (capital Kaushambi), Kuru (capital Hastinapura), Panchala (capital Ahichchhatra/Kampilya), Surasena (capital Mathura)

Malla (capital Kushinagara/Pava) is partly associated with U.P./Bihar; the remaining Mahajanapadas (Anga, Magadha, Avanti, Chedi, Matsya, Vajji, Gandhara, Kamboja, Assaka) lay outside present-day U.P.

Polity & Governance.intro: The two-column structure here (Monarchical vs. Gana-Sangha) matters because U.P. is one of the few regions where both political models existed simultaneously and in close proximity, giving this page an unusually complete picture of Mahajanapada-era statecraft.
points: Evolution of political form: Tribe/Jana → Janapada → Territorial State → Mahajanapada
Monarchical states: hereditary kingship, king as political & military authority, ministers & officials, tax collection, army, fortified cities (examples: Kosala, Kashi, Vatsa, Surasena)
Gana-Sangha/Republican traditions: collective leadership, assemblies (Sabha, Sanstha), clan-based participation, oligarchic system (important in wider U.P. region, e.g. Malla of Kushinagara, Pava)

Society & Economy.intro: Note how tightly linked these two categories are in the source material: the same iron tools and agricultural surplus that reshaped society also financed the armies and urban infrastructure the next page's Mauryan conquest would later inherit and formalise.
points: Evolution of society: Clan-based → Territorial → Urban society; Varna system becomes more structured; emergence of occupational specialization (farmers, artisans, merchants, traders, officials, rulers)

Economic features: agriculture as the main occupation, iron tools increase productivity, surplus production; craft production (pottery, metalwork, textiles, bead making); trade & commerce (local and long distance); use of punch-marked coins; growth of towns and urban centres; banking and credit in early forms

Role & Contribution of Men and Women.intro: This table's honest caveat about limited and regionally uneven sources is worth taking seriously — it is a reminder that the relatively good visibility of women in Vedic-age debate, described on the previous page, does not automatically carry forward at the same level of detail into every subsequent period.
points: Men: political & military roles (kings, warriors, ministers, administrators, fortification builders); economic roles (farmers, artisans, merchants, caravan traders, metalworkers, potters); intellectual & religious roles (Brahmins, teachers/acharyas, philosophers, monks)

Women: participated in household and economic production; elite women could influence political & dynastic relationships; participated in religious & intellectual traditions; Buddhist and Jain traditions welcomed women (Bhikkhuni Sangha, Jain Sadhvis); some women known for learning, wisdom & philosophical dialogues (Gargi, Maitreyi in tradition); property rights were limited but not entirely absent

Eight Mahajanapadas of Uttar Pradesh: 1. Kuru: Western UP (Meerut, Hastinapur, Ghaziabad; capitals: Indraprastha / Hastinapur; later adopted republican constitution).
2. Panchala: Rohilkhand and Central UP (Bareilly, Badaun, Farrukhabad; northern capital Ahichchhatra, southern capital Kampilya; famed for textile production).
3. Shurasena: Braj region (Mathura on the Yamuna; capital Mathura; ruled by Yadava dynasty; Krishna associated with Shurasena; centre of Krishna / Bhagavata cult).
4. Vatsa: Central Doab (Prayagraj, Kaushambi; capital Kaushambi on Yamuna; King Udayana was a contemporary of Buddha; central junction of Uttarapatha and Dakshinapatha trade routes).

5. Kosala: Awadh region (Faizabad, Ayodhya, Shravasti; capital Shravasti / Sahet-Mahet on Rapti river; King Prasenjit was contemporary of Buddha; Buddha spent 25 rainy seasons / Vassa at Jetavana monastery in Shravasti).
6. Malla: Eastern UP (Deoria, Gorakhpur, Kushinagar; republican Gana-Sangha; two branches: Kusinara / Kasia where Buddha attained Mahaparinirvana, and Pava where Mahavira attained Nirvana).
7. Chedi: Bundelkhand region (Banda, Lalitpur, Ken river; capital Shuktimati / Sotthivati; King Shishupala).
8. Kashi: Eastern UP (Varanasi; capital Varanasi between Varuna and Assi rivers; famed for cotton textiles, ivory crafts, and religious learning; annexed by Kosala and later Magadha).

women.name: Women in the Mahajanapada Age
women.note: Participated in household & economic production; some elite women influenced political and dynastic relationships and engaged in religious and philosophical traditions, though sources are limited and regional variations existed.

events.title: Formation of the 16 Mahajanapadas
events.desc: Territorial states with defined capitals emerge across North India, six of them centred in present-day U.P.

events.title: Rise of Magadhan power
events.desc: Bimbisara and Ajatashatru expand Magadha's influence, eventually eclipsing many U.P.-based Mahajanapadas.

events.title: Foundation of the Mauryan Empire
events.desc: Chandragupta Maurya establishes the Mauryan Empire, absorbing the Mahajanapadas of the Gangetic plains including those in present-day U.P.

people.name: Prasenajit
people.note: A prominent Mahajanapada ruler based at Shravasti.

people.name: Udayana
people.note: Based at Kaushambi.

people.name: Gautama Buddha
people.note: Active across the Mahajanapadas of the region.

people.name: Mahavira

prelims: Eight of the 16 ancient Mahajanapadas were situated in Uttar Pradesh: Kuru, Panchala, Shurasena, Vatsa, Kosala, Malla, Chedi, and Kashi.
The capital of the Vatsa Mahajanapada was Kaushambi, situated on the Yamuna river near modern Prayagraj, ruled by King Udayana.
Gautama Buddha spent the maximum number of rainy seasons (25 Varshavasas) at the Jetavana monastery in Shravasti (capital of Kosala).
The capital of Shurasena was Mathura, located at the junction of Uttarapatha and Dakshinapatha, associated with the Yadava clan and Lord Krishna.
Gautama Buddha attained Mahaparinirvana at Kusinara (Kushinagar), which was the capital of the Malla republican Mahajanapada in Eastern UP.
Vardhamana Mahavira attained Nirvana at Pava, which was the second major centre of the Malla Mahajanapada in UP.
The ancient city of Kaushambi features a massive fortified mud-brick rampart with burnt-brick revetment and the celebrated Ghoshitarama monastery.
mains: Examine the geographical distribution and political characteristics of the eight Mahajanapadas located within Uttar Pradesh.
Analyze the religious and historical significance of Uttar Pradesh in early Buddhism and Jainism with special reference to Sarnath, Shravasti, Kushinagar, and Pava.
Discuss the urban and commercial prominence of Kaushambi and Mathura as nodal centres on the trans-subcontinental trade routes (Uttarapatha and Dakshinapatha).

quickFacts: Kashi, Kosala, Vatsa, Kuru, Panchala, Surasena
Varanasi, Shravasti, Kaushambi, Hastinapura, Ahichchhatra/Kampilya, Mathura
Absorption into the Mauryan Empire, 322 BCE

periods.title: Maurya Period in Uttar Pradesh
periods.tagline: Complete Study Chart — U.P. as a Core Part of the Mauryan Empire
periods.overview: The national Mauryan Empire and Ashoka the Great pages describe an empire and an emperor; this page describes what that empire actually looked like on the ground in one of its most thoroughly integrated core provinces — Kosala, Kashi, Panchala, Vatsa, and Surasena, administered through the same Pradesha-and-Ahara provincial system the Arthashastra prescribes, with named officials (Samaharta for revenue, Nagarak for city administration) whose functions the national account only summarises. Nowhere is this regional specificity more vivid than at Sarnath, where Ashoka's edicts and the Sarnath Lion Capital mark the actual site of the Buddha's first sermon — the same Ashoka whose empire-wide Dhamma policy the national page explores in depth is here visible in a single, concrete place, inscribing his moral philosophy onto the exact landscape where Buddhism itself had begun roughly two and a half centuries earlier. Kaushambi's urban and administrative remains, Mathura's Mauryan-era sculpture, and Prayagraj's role as a religious and strategic confluence together let this page show something the national account, working at empire-wide scale, cannot: how deeply and specifically Mauryan administration, religion, and infrastructure were woven into this one region's existing sacred geography.

phases.name: Chandragupta Maurya
points: Establishes the Mauryan Empire; Pataliputra (Magadha) capital; Uttar Pradesh integrated into a unified empire

phases.name: Bindusara
points: Extends the empire further south and west

phases.name: Ashoka the Great
points: Kalinga War (c. 261 BCE); embraces Dhamma; intensive administrative, economic and religious developments in U.P.

phases.name: Post-Ashoka
points: Gradual decline, rise of provincial governors' autonomy

phases.name: End of the Mauryas
points: Last Maurya ruler Brihadratha killed by his general Pushyamitra Shunga

Maurya Administration & Important Centre.intro: Each city listed here corresponds to one of the five Mahajanapada-era regions carried straight over from the previous page — Kosala's Shravasti, Kashi's Varanasi, Panchala's Ahichchhatra and Kampilya, Vatsa's Kaushambi, and Surasena's Mathura — showing administrative continuity rather than a clean break at the moment of Mauryan conquest.
points: Ahichchhatra (Panchala region) — important Mauryan administrative & military centre; Shravasti (Kosala) — provincial capital during Mauryan rule; Hastinapura (Kuru region) — Mauryan presence, part of the northern provincial system

Kampilya (Panchala) — Mauryan control over Panchala territory; Sarnath (near Varanasi) — where the Buddha delivered the Dhammachakra Pravartana, major Buddhist centre especially under Ashoka; Varanasi (Kashi) — important city, trade & craft centre under the Mauryas; Kaushambi (Vatsa region) — important urban & administrative centre on the Yamuna; Prayagraj (ancient Prayaga) — confluence (Triveni), important religious/economic/strategic centre; Mathura (Surasena region) — major urban centre, trade & religion (Mauryan sculptures, Yakshi, inscriptions)

Maurya Administrative System (Arthashast.intro: This official-by-official breakdown is the regional, on-the-ground version of the same Arthashastra-based administrative theory the national Mauryan Empire page discusses at empire-wide scale; knowing these specific titles (Samaharta, Sannidhata, Nagarak) is a common Prelims trap since they sound similar but cover distinct functions.
points: King (Chakravartin) at the apex; Mantri Parishad (council of ministers), Yuvaraja, Mahamatras (high officials), Kumara/Aryaputra (provincial governors)

Important officials: Samaharta (revenue collection), Sannidhata (treasury officer), Dandanayaka (military chief), Nagarak (city superintendent), Pautavadhyaksha (weights & measures), Dharma Mahamatras (moral welfare)
U.P. was divided into Pradeshas (provinces) and Ahara/Vishayas (districts); strong central administration with a network of officers; use of spies/secret agents (gudhapurusha)

Maurya Economy in U.P..intro: State control over key sectors here — mines, trade, coinage — is the same policy the Arthashastra prescribes nationally, but this table shows it concretely applied to the Ganga-Yamuna trade routes running directly through this region.
points: Agriculture: well-developed irrigation, use of plough and seeds; trade & commerce: active trade on Ganga-Yamuna routes; industry & crafts: textiles, pottery, metalwork, ivory, beads, stone craft; state control over mines, forests, salt, liquor; punch-marked coins in circulation

Public Works & Ashoka's Dhamma.intro: This is where the national Ashoka the Great page's account of Dhamma-based governance becomes locally specific: Sarnath, listed here, is not merely one Buddhist site among many but the exact location of the Buddha's first sermon, which is precisely why Ashoka chose it for some of his most significant inscriptions.
points: Construction of roads, bridges, rest houses; tree plantation, wells, tanks; ferries and boating facilities; fortified towns

After the Kalinga War, Ashoka adopted Dhamma — promoting non-violence, compassion, respect for all sects; inscriptions and edicts spread across U.P.; support to Buddhism while respecting other religions; establishment of stupas, viharas, pillars; Dhamma-Mahamatras appointed for moral upliftment

Art & Architecture in U.P..intro: The polished pillars and Sarnath Lion Capital described here are the physical evidence for the administrative and religious claims made in the two categories above — inscribed stone that has survived over two millennia to confirm what the textual sources report.
points: Polished Mauryan pillars; Sarnath Lion Capital; Yakshi sculptures (Mathura); Barabar-style influence on cave architecture; stupas & monasteries at Sarnath, Kaushambi

Ashokan Epigraphy & Architecture in UP: Lion Capital of Sarnath: Carved from polished Chunar sandstone; features four Asiatic lions back-to-back, an abacus with high-relief sculptures of an elephant, horse, bull, and lion separated by Dharmachakra wheels, resting on an inverted bell lotus; adopted as the National Emblem of India on 26 January 1950; Wheel of Law adopted on the National Flag.

Ashokan Pillar Edicts in UP: 1. Prayagraj / Allahabad Pillar (inscribed with 6 Major Pillar Edicts of Ashoka, Queen's Edict regarding Karuvaki, and the Schism Edict warning monks; later inscribed with Samudragupta's Prayag Prashasti and Jahangir's genealogy), 2. Meerut Pillar (transported by Firuz Shah Tughlaq to Delhi Ridge in the 14th century), 3. Topra Pillar (transported from Haryana to Feroz Shah Kotla, Delhi), 4. Kaushambi Pillar.

Buddhist Monasteries & Stupas: Dharmarajika Stupa and Dhamek Stupa at Sarnath commissioned by Ashoka; ancient brick monastic complexes at Shravasti (Jetavana) and Sankissa (Farrukhabad, where Buddha legendarily descended from heaven on a jeweled ladder; Ashokan elephant capital).

events.title: U.P. integrated into the Mauryan Empire
events.desc: Chandragupta Maurya's establishment of the empire brings the region's former Mahajanapadas under unified Mauryan rule.

events.title: Ashoka's edicts appear across U.P.
events.desc: Following the Kalinga War, Ashoka's Dhamma-based inscriptions and edicts spread across Mauryan U.P., especially at Kaushambi and Sarnath.

events.title: End of Mauryan rule
events.desc: Pushyamitra Shunga assassinates the last Mauryan ruler, ending Mauryan control over the region.

people.name: Chandragupta Maurya
people.note: Integrated U.P. into a unified empire.

people.name: Ashoka the Great
people.note: Left the deepest imprint on U.P. through Dhamma and inscriptions.

people.name: Kumara Mahendra
people.note: Sent to Sri Lanka for Buddhism, per tradition.

people.name: Chanakya
people.note: All-India Mauryan figure.

prelims: The Sarnath Lion Capital, sculpted from Chunar sandstone under Ashoka, was officially adopted as the National Emblem of India on 26 January 1950.
The Allahabad / Prayagraj Pillar bears inscriptions of three distinct emperors: Ashoka (Pillar Edicts, Queen's Edict), Samudragupta (Prayag Prashasti), and Jahangir.
The Queen's Edict on the Allahabad Pillar is the only Ashokan inscription that names a queen (Karuvaki, mother of Prince Tivara).
Ashoka built the Dharmarajika Stupa at Sarnath to enshrine the sacred relics of Gautama Buddha.
Sankissa in Farrukhabad district (UP) is celebrated in Buddhist tradition as the site of Buddha's descent from Trayastrimsa Heaven, marked by an Ashokan elephant capital.
The Meerut Ashokan Pillar was transported and re-erected on the Delhi Ridge by Sultan Firuz Shah Tughlaq in the 14th century.
The Schism Edict warning Buddhist monks against causing divisions in the Sangha is found on pillars at Sarnath and Kaushambi.
mains: Critically evaluate the artistic, technological, and ideological features of the Mauryan sculptures and pillars in Uttar Pradesh, with specific reference to the Sarnath Lion Capital.
Analyze the epigraphical significance of the Allahabad / Prayagraj Pillar Inscription as a multi-layered historical record spanning Ashoka, the Guptas, and the Mughals.
Examine the spread of Buddhist monastic architecture under Mauryan patronage at Sarnath, Shravasti, and Sankissa.

quickFacts: Regions of Maurya Administration in U.P.
Administrative practices, urban centres and spread of Buddhism continued after Mauryan decline

periods.title: Post-Maurya Period in Uttar Pradesh
periods.tagline: From the Decline of the Mauryas to the Rise of the Gupta Empire in North India
periods.overview: The national Post-Mauryan Period page describes a genuinely fragmented political map — Shungas, Kanvas, Indo-Greeks, Sakas, Parthians, and Kushans ruling simultaneously across different parts of the subcontinent; this page narrows that same 185 BCE–320 CE span specifically to what happened in U.P., where Mathura in particular becomes something close to the era's defining case study in cultural synthesis. Under Kushana rule especially, Mathura functioned as a genuine second capital alongside the dynasty's Central Asian territories, producing the distinctive red-sandstone Mathura School of Art — Yaksha-Yakshi figures, Buddha images, Jain Tirthankaras — that developed in active dialogue with the more Hellenistic-influenced Gandhara school the national page discusses at empire-wide scale. What this regional focus reveals that the broader account cannot is just how much political fragmentation and cultural vibrancy coexisted at the level of a single province: Shunga, Kanva, Indo-Greek, Saka, Parthian, and Kushana authority each held sway over parts of U.P. in fairly rapid succession, yet Buddhism, Jainism, and a reviving Brahmanism all continued to flourish together at the same sites — Sarnath, Kaushambi, Sankisa — regardless of who currently held nominal political control.

phases.name: Shunga & Kanva Influence
points: Decline of the Mauryas; Pushyamitra Shunga establishes the Shunga Dynasty (185–73 BCE), influence extended in eastern U.P. including Prayagraj; Kanva Dynasty (73–28 BCE) ruled from Pataliputra, controlled parts of eastern U.P.

phases.name: Indo-Greek & Indo-Scythian Influence
points: Rise of local powers, Indo-Greek, Indo-Scythian (Shaka), Indo-Parthian and early Kushanas; western U.P. (Mathura, Saketa, Panchala region) under their influence

phases.name: Kushana Power
points: Kushanas become a major power in U.P. (1st–3rd century CE); important centres: Mathura (capital of Kushana Satraps), Saketa, Kaushambi, Varanasi; growth of urban centres, trade, Buddhism, Jainism, Brahmanism

phases.name: Rise of Gupta Power
points: From c. 320 CE, Gupta power expands from Magadha into the U.P. region, ending the Post-Mauryan phase

Major Dynasties / Powers (185 BCE – 320.intro: The sheer number of overlapping dynasties in this single table is the point: no other period in this track shows quite this level of simultaneous political fragmentation, which makes the cultural continuity described in the categories below all the more notable by contrast.
points: Shunga (185–73 BCE): capital Pataliputra; rise of Brahmanical traditions, Buddhist patronage continued
Kanva (73–28 BCE): capital Pataliputra; continuation of Shunga policies, gradual decline
Indo-Greek (c. 2nd–1st century BCE): capital Saketa/Mathura; Greek rulers, bilingual coins, trade & culture exchange
Indo-Scythian/Shaka (1st century BCE–1st century CE): Mathura region; Kshatrapas ruled, silver coins, rise of trade
Indo-Parthian (1st–2nd century CE): Mathura region; bridged Greeks and Kushanas, issued coins
Kushana (1st–3rd century CE): capital Mathura; major power, great patronage to Buddhism, art & trade
Early Local Dynasties (Nagas, Yaudheyas, Kunindas etc., 1st–3rd century CE): various parts of western U.P.; republican traditions, issue of coins

Polity & Governance.intro: Pay attention to the coexistence of monarchical and republican traditions in the same broad era and region that the up-mahajanapadas page already introduced — that older Gana-Sangha model, per the note here, persisted at the edges of U.P. even as larger monarchies like the Kushanas dominated the centre.
points: Monarchies: hereditary kingship, king as supreme authority, council of ministers (Mantriparishad), officials (Mahamatras, Amatyas, Senapati), tax collection, maintenance of army & forts, law and order through local officials

Republican traditions: clan-based oligarchic republics, decisions taken in assemblies (Sabhas/Sanghas), headed by chiefs or elected representatives (examples in the wider region: Yaudheyas, Malavas, Arjunayanas, Kunindas, Nagas) — note: republican systems were oligarchic, not democratic in the modern sense

Society & Economy.intro: Guild-based craft production and standardised coinage in this table are the direct economic legacy of the Mauryan administrative systems covered two pages earlier — the state control has loosened, but the underlying commercial infrastructure it built kept functioning regardless of who held political power.
points: Varna system continued and became more rigid; Brahmins gained importance; Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, Shudras had traditional roles; growth of new social groups — artisans, traders, guilds (Shrenis); urbanisation increased

Agriculture, crafts & industries (pottery, metal, beads, textiles); trade & commerce (caravan, river routes, ports); use of coins (punch-marked, die-struck, gold, silver, copper); guilds (Shrenis) & occupational specialisation; important trade centres — Mathura (international trade hub), Saketa (Ayodhya), Kaushambi, Prayaga, Varanasi

Religious & Cultural Developments.intro: Notice that all three traditions — Buddhism, Jainism, and a reviving Brahmanism — are described as flourishing at the very same sites in the very same decades; this genuine, sustained religious pluralism is one of this period's most distinctive and frequently tested features.
points: Buddhism: continued patronage under Shungas and Kushanas; monasteries & stupas developed (Sarnath, Kaushambi, Sankisa)
Jainism: flourished; spread of Digambara and Svetambara traditions; Jain monks travelled widely, supported by merchants & urban groups
Brahmanism & Hinduism: revival of Brahmanical traditions under Shungas; construction of temples began; worship of Vishnu, Shiva, Skanda, Devi; development of Puranic traditions

Art & Architecture.intro: The Mathura School of Art introduced in this table is the direct forerunner of the sculptural tradition the next page's Gupta Period will bring to full maturity, so it is worth reading this category alongside the up-gupta-period page's own art section.
points: Mathura School of Art — red sandstone sculptures, Yaksha-yakshi and Buddha images, Jain Tirthankaras, realistic human figures
Stupas & Monuments — Sarnath, Kaushambi, Sankisa important Buddhist sites; early temple architecture developed; brick & stone structures; Brahmi and Kharoshthi scripts used in inscriptions

Kushanas at Mathura & Shunga Ayodhya: Mathura as Kushana Southern Capital: Mathura functioned as the premier political, administrative, and artistic metropolis of the Kushana Empire in India under Kanishka I, Huvishka, and Vasudeva; imperial portrait shrine (Devakula) excavated at Mat near Mathura, yielding the colossal headless standing statue of Kanishka I wearing a heavy nomadic coat and boots, holding a mace and sword, with the inscription "Maharaja Rajadhiraja Devaputra Kanishka".

Mathura School of Sculpture: Flourished from 1st century BCE to 4th century CE; material: distinctive local mottled / spotted red sandstone from Karri/Sikri quarries; sculpted the earliest indigenous anthropomorphic images of Gautama Buddha (seated Katra Buddha under Bodhi tree with snail-shell curls, smiling countenance, and Abhayaprada gesture), 24 Jain Tirthankaras (Kankali Tila stupa and Ayagapattas votive slabs), and Hindu deities (four-armed Vishnu, Shiva-lingams, Kartikeya, Mahishasuramardini).

Ayodhya Inscription of Dhanadeva: Inscribed stone slab found at Ayodhya recording that King Dhanadeva, the 6th descendant of Senapati Pushyamitra Shunga, performed two Ashvamedha sacrifices, establishing Shunga royal lineage and revival of Vedic rituals in UP.

events.title: Decline of Mauryas, rise of the Shungas
events.desc: Pusyamitra Shunga establishes the Shunga Dynasty following the fall of the Mauryas.

events.title: Kushana rule centred at Mathura
events.desc: The Kushanas make Mathura a key centre of Buddhist art, trade and patronage.

events.title: Rise of Gupta power
events.desc: Gupta power begins expanding from Magadha into the U.P. region, ending the Post-Mauryan phase.

people.name: Kanishka
people.note: Centred power at Mathura.

prelims: Mathura served as the second imperial capital and primary commercial hub of the Kushana Empire in Northern India.
The famous headless statue of Emperor Kanishka I wearing Central Asian boots and tunic was excavated from the royal portrait shrine (Devakula) at Mat near Mathura.
The Mathura School of Art exclusively used mottled / spotted red sandstone quarried from nearby Sikri and Fatehpur.
The earliest indigenous anthropomorphic images of the Buddha and Jain Tirthankaras in Indian art were crafted by the Mathura School of Sculpture.
The Ayodhya Stone Inscription of King Dhanadeva confirms that Pushyamitra Shunga performed two Ashvamedha sacrifices.
Kankali Tila in Mathura is a world-famous archaeological site renowned for the excavation of an ancient Jain stupa and beautifully carved Ayagapattas (votive tablets).
The Greek ambassador Heliodorus visited Vidisha from Taxila, but Indo-Greek coins of Menander have been found in extensive hoards at Mathura and Rohilkhand.
mains: Analyze the stylistic, iconographical, and material characteristics of the Mathura School of Art during the Kushana period, comparing it with the Gandhara School.
Examine the political and commercial importance of Mathura as the Kushana imperial capital and meeting point of major trans-Indian trade routes.
Discuss the significance of the Ayodhya Inscription of Dhanadeva in reconstructing the post-Mauryan Shunga history and religious revival in Uttar Pradesh.

quickFacts: Shunga, Kanva, Indo-Greek, Indo-Scythian, Indo-Parthian, Kushana
Mathura, Saketa, Kaushambi, Prayaga, Varanasi, Sravasti, Ahichchhatra
Brahmi, Kharoshthi / Punch-marked, Silver, Copper, Gold (die-struck)

periods.title: Gupta Period in Uttar Pradesh
periods.tagline: Golden Age of India — U.P. as a Core Region of the Gupta Empire
periods.overview: If the national Gupta Age page explains why the period earns the label 'Golden Age of India', this page shows precisely where that gold was minted, in the most literal sense the region's history allows: Samudragupta's Allahabad Pillar Inscription — composed by the court poet Harisena and physically standing in present-day Prayagraj — remains the single most important primary source for the entire Gupta dynasty's political history, describing conquests across a region that heavily overlaps with modern U.P. Beyond that one inscription's outsized importance, the region hosted the empire's genuine cultural infrastructure: Kashi, Mathura, and Sarnath as major religious and educational centres patronised directly by Chandragupta II and his successors, and the Mathura School of sculpture carrying forward the artistic tradition already established in the Post-Mauryan period into its classical Gupta-era maturity. Reading this page alongside the national Gupta Age account makes clear that U.P. was not simply one province among several benefiting from Gupta stability, but the specific administrative and cultural spine — running from Prayaga through Kashi to Mathura — along which the empire's much-discussed prosperity, religious tolerance, and artistic achievement were most concretely produced and displayed.

phases.name: Chandragupta I
points: Rise of Gupta power; consolidates power in Magadha, influence extends to the Prayag region

phases.name: Samudragupta
points: Conquests across North India including U.P. regions (Prayag, Kosala, Panchala etc.); gains titles like 'Prayagaprasasti' (Allahabad Pillar Inscription)

phases.name: Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya)
points: Expansion, prosperity, cultural efflorescence; Ujjain and Pataliputra important centres

phases.name: Kumaragupta I
points: Stability, continuation of administration and cultural progress

phases.name: Skandagupta
points: Defeated the Huns (Pushyamitras) in the North-West, protected the empire including the U.P. region

phases.name: Later Guptas
points: Gradual decline due to succession disputes, Huna pressure and regional assertion

Gupta Rulers and Their Connection with U.intro: This ruler-by-ruler table is the regional companion to the national Gupta Age page's dynastic narrative — use the 'Connection with U.P.' column specifically to see which emperor is responsible for which local development, since the national page does not break this down by region.
points: Chandragupta I (c. 320–335 CE): Pataliputra; consolidated power in Magadha, influence extended to Prayag region
Samudragupta (c. 335–375 CE): Pataliputra; covered Aryavarta including U.P. regions (Prayag, Kosala, Panchala etc.); described as the 'Napoleon of India'
Chandragupta II Vikramaditya (c. 375–415 CE): Ujjain, Pataliputra; patronized Kashi, Mathura, Sarnath and other centres, strengthened administration; cultural boom, expansion of trade and gold coins
Kumaragupta I (c. 415–455 CE): Pataliputra; continued prosperity in U.P., Mathura art and temples flourished; stable administration, economic growth
Skandagupta (c. 455–467 CE): Pataliputra; defended the empire from Huns (Pushyamitras) in the North-West, protected the U.P. region; military victories, continuity maintained

Administration & Governance.intro: The Bhukti-Vishaya-Vithi-Grama hierarchy described here is the Gupta era's specific refinement of the same basic provincial structure the Mauryas used centuries earlier, adapted for a more decentralised, feudatory-inclusive style of rule.
points: Well-organised centralised administration with provincial and local divisions; King (Maharajadhiraja) at the apex, assisted by Mantri Parishad (council of ministers), Amatyas (high officials), Uparika (provincial governor)

Administrative divisions: Bhukti (province) → Vishaya (district) → Vithi (sub-district) → Grama (village); officials — Uparika, Vishayapati, Dandapashika, Mahadandanayaka, Ayuktas; record keeping, revenue collection and judicial system well developed

Society & Economy.intro: The note on women's status here — respected in family and society, some acting as scholars — is worth cross-referencing against the more mixed picture given on the up-vedic-age page, since Gupta-era U.P. represents something of a high point before later medieval restrictions tighten again.
points: Varna system continued with greater rigidity; Brahmins enjoyed high status and received land grants; growth of towns and urban life; artisans, merchants and traders formed important groups; women enjoyed respect in family & society, some were scholars

Agriculture remained the backbone; use of iron plough, better irrigation, multiple cropping; growth of trade & commerce (internal & external); guilds (shrenis) of traders and artisans flourished; use of gold coins (Dinars) extensively

Religion & Culture.intro: This category's core claim — that Hinduism, Buddhism, and Jainism all received patronage simultaneously — is exactly the same religious pluralism the up-post-maurya-period page already documented two pages earlier, showing it as a persistent regional pattern rather than a one-off.
points: Hinduism (Vaishnavism & Shaivism) was the dominant religion; Buddhism continued with royal patronage (Sarnath, Kushinagar, Kaushambi, Sravasti); Jainism also existed in urban centres; Sanskrit language flourished, classical literature, drama, poetry and epics developed; education centres flourished (Kashi, Mathura, Sarnath); science, mathematics, astronomy, Ayurveda and metallurgy progressed

Land Grants (A Key Feature).intro: Land grants are singled out here because this is the specific administrative mechanism, well documented through surviving copper-plate inscriptions at Sarnath, Damodarpur, and Mathura, by which the Gupta state actually extended its authority and its favoured religious institutions into the countryside.
points: Gupta rulers granted land to Brahmins, religious institutions and officials; land grants promoted agriculture, settlement and Sanskritisation; done through copper plate inscriptions (important sites: Sarnath, Damodarpur near Varanasi, Prayag, Rohilkhand region, Mathura region)

Gupta Architectural Zenith in UP: Dashavatara Temple at Deogarh (Lalitpur district): Consecrated c. 500 CE; earliest surviving Hindu temple built on a complete Panchayatana layout (central sanctum surrounded by four subsidiary corner shrines); soaring pyramidal shikhara (early Nagara style); monumental sculpted relief panels: Sheshashayi Vishnu (Vishnu reclining on cosmic serpent Ananta, surrounded by Lakshmi, Garuda, and the Pandavas), Gajendramoksha, and Nara-Narayana meditation; river goddesses Ganga (on Makara) and Yamuna (on Kurma tortoise) adorning sanctum doorjambs.

Bhitargaon Brick Temple (Kanpur district): Earliest and largest surviving classical Hindu temple built entirely of terracotta and kiln-fired bricks; dating to the 5th century CE; prominent curvilinear shikhara rising over 70 feet; historic use of the "true arch" (semi-circular voussoir arch) centuries before Islamic architecture in India; adorned with terracotta panels of Shiva, Parvati, Ganesha, and Ramayana episodes.

Sarnath Seated Buddha & Prayag Prashasti: Sarnath School achieved the classical apex of Buddhist art: the world-famous Sarnath Seated Buddha in Dharmachakrapravartana Mudra (carved in Chunar sandstone with transparent drapery, serene downcast eyes, and a lavishly carved halo featuring celestial gandharvas); Allahabad Pillar preserved Harishena's Prayag Prashasti detailing Samudragupta's conquests.

events.title: Samudragupta's conquests and the Prayagaprasasti
events.desc: The Allahabad Pillar Inscription, composed by Harisena, records Samudragupta's extensive conquests including regions in present-day U.P.

events.title: Chandragupta II's cultural patronage
events.desc: Kashi, Mathura, and Sarnath flourish culturally under Chandragupta II Vikramaditya's patronage.

events.title: Skandagupta repels the Huns
events.desc: Skandagupta successfully defends the empire, including the U.P. region, against Huna incursions from the North-West.

people.name: Samudragupta
people.note: Called the 'Napoleon of India'; Allahabad Pillar Inscription records his conquests.

people.name: Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya)
people.note: Patron of Kashi, Mathura, Sarnath.

people.name: Kalidasa
people.note: Gem of Sanskrit literature associated with the Gupta court.

people.name: Harisena
people.note: Composed the Prayagaprasasti (Allahabad Pillar Inscription).

prelims: The Dashavatara Temple at Deogarh (Lalitpur district, UP) is the earliest known temple featuring a complete Panchayatana plan and early Nagara shikhara.
The monumental Sheshashayi Vishnu panel, depicting Vishnu reclining on the coils of serpent Sheshanaga, is sculpted on the wall of the Deogarh Temple.
The Bhitargaon Temple in Kanpur district is the oldest surviving brick temple in India featuring a shikhara and true arch construction.
The iconic Sarnath Seated Buddha image preaching the First Sermon in Dharmachakrapravartana Mudra is a masterwork of the 5th-century Gupta classical style.
The Prayag Prashasti (composed by Harishena on the Allahabad Pillar) details Samudragupta's four-fold military strategy across Aryavarta and Dakshinapatha.
The Bhitari Pillar Inscription in Ghazipur district (UP) records the heroic defense of the Gupta Empire against the invading White Hunas by Skandagupta.
Eran inscription (MP) records the first dated evidence of Sati (510 CE), while Bhitari and Mankuwar inscriptions document Gupta royal land grants in UP.
mains: Critically evaluate the architectural evolution of North Indian temples during the Gupta period with specific reference to the Deogarh Dashavatara Temple and Bhitargaon Brick Temple in Uttar Pradesh.
Analyze the aesthetic and spiritual qualities of the Gupta sculpture school of Sarnath, contrasting it with the earlier Mathura School.
Examine the historical and geographical significance of the Bhitari Pillar Inscription of Skandagupta in Ghazipur in documenting the Huna invasion.

quickFacts: Pataliputra (outside U.P.) / Prayag, Kashi, Mathura, Kaushambi, Sravasti, Ahichchhatra
Culture, Art, Literature, Science — Golden Age of India

periods.title: The Harsha Period in Uttar Pradesh
periods.tagline: Golden Age After Gupta — Political Unity, Cultural Flowering, Religious Harmony, Patronage of Learning & Art
periods.overview: Harsha's reign gets only a brief mention on the national Post-Gupta Age page as one of several regional post-Gupta kingdoms; here, because Kanyakubja (Kannauj) was his actual capital and the seat of his empire, the reign receives the depth its regional significance deserves. What makes Harsha's U.P.-centred rule genuinely well-documented, in contrast to many contemporaneous regional kings, is the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang's unusually detailed eyewitness account of his court, administration, and the grand five-yearly religious assemblies Harsha held at Prayaga — a level of external documentation that lets historians reconstruct daily administrative and religious life in this one kingdom with a precision most 7th-century Indian states simply do not have. This page's real significance within the broader U.P. track is transitional: Harsha's death without a capable successor in 647 CE, and the resulting fragmentation of his Kannauj-centred empire, is the direct origin point for the centuries of regional-kingdom rivalry — Gurjara-Pratiharas, Palas, Rashtrakutas, and eventually the Chandellas and Gahadavalas — that the next several pages in this track trace, all of them fighting, in one way or another, over the same prize: control of the city Harsha had made the era's most prestigious capital.

phases.name: Accession
points: Harsha becomes King of Thanesar after the death of his brother Rajyavardhana

phases.name: Consolidation
points: Establishes control over Punjab, Haryana and parts of Uttar Pradesh

phases.name: Expansion
points: Consolidation of power in Uttar Pradesh and North India; defeats many rulers

phases.name: Conflict with the Chalukyas
points: Conflict with Chalukya king Pulakeshin II; the Narmada River becomes the southern boundary

phases.name: Grand Assembly at Prayaga
points: Grand religious assembly at Prayaga (Allahabad) — distribution of wealth to the people

phases.name: Death of Harsha
points: Death of Harsha at Kanyakubja (Kannauj)

Harsha — The King & His Empire.intro: This category's description of an empire 'not highly centralized like the Mauryas' is an important nuance — Harsha's Kannauj-based rule looked impressive on the map but rested on a genuinely looser, more negotiated relationship with regional governors than the tightly administered empires covered earlier in this track.
points: Belonged to the Pushyabhuti dynasty; succeeded his brother Rajyavardhana; a great conqueror, able administrator and patron of arts, literature and religion

His empire extended over Punjab, Haryana and parts of Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and Bengal; the Narmada River formed the southern boundary (following conflict with the Chalukyas); administration was efficient but not as highly centralized as the Mauryas

Administration & Governance.intro: Compare this table's Bhukti-Vishaya-Pataka structure to the very similar Gupta-era hierarchy on the previous page — the continuity in terminology shows how much Harsha's administration was consciously modelled on the Gupta system, even without the same level of central control.
points: Monarchical rule: Harsha was a benevolent king who exercised personal supervision over administration; territorial division: empire divided into Bhuktis (provinces), further divided into Vishayas (districts) and Patakas (sub-districts)

Officials: Upa-Rajukas, Vishaya-patis, Dandanayakas, Mahattaras and Sresthins were important officials; king was the supreme authority in justice, punishment for crime was moderate; land revenue was the main source, with trade, taxes, fines and tributes as other sources; large standing army with infantry, cavalry, elephants and chariots; maintained friendly relations with neighbouring states through embassies

Religion & Culture.intro: The description of Harsha as a Buddhist patron who nonetheless respected all religions is the same broad-tolerance pattern this track has already documented under the Guptas and Post-Mauryan dynasties — evidence that this was a durable regional norm rather than any single ruler's personal quirk.
points: Harsha was a great patron of Buddhism, but respected all religions; himself described as a follower of Mahayana Buddhism; supported Brahmanism, Jainism and other sects; grand religious assemblies at Prayaga (c. 643–644 CE) once every five years

Flourishing of Sanskrit literature and learning; Harsha himself was a scholar and playwright; famous works: Nagananda and Ratnavali (dramas), and Priyadarshika (these are among the known works); development of art, sculpture and architecture continued; centres of learning — Nalanda, Valabhi, Kanyakubja, Varanasi and Mathura

Chinese Traveller — Xuanzang (Hsuan Tsan.intro: Xuanzang's account is singled out in its own category because it is genuinely unusual: very few 7th-century Indian rulers have a detailed, independent, outside eyewitness record of their court, which is exactly why Harsha's reign is so much better documented than most contemporaneous regional kingdoms.
points: Xuanzang visited Harsha's court c. 630–645 CE; described Harsha as a kind, generous and religious king; provided a detailed account of cities, administration, society, religion, education and economy of the period; his travelogue 'Si-yu-ki' is a valuable historical source

Decline of Harsha's Empire.intro: This category is the direct hinge to the rest of the medieval section of this track — every dynasty covered on the following several pages (Gurjara-Pratiharas, Palas, Rashtrakutas, Chandellas, Gahadavalas) emerges specifically because Harsha left no capable successor to hold his Kannauj-centred empire together.
points: No capable successor after Harsha's death in 647 CE; the empire broke into smaller states; rise of regional powers — Gurjara-Pratiharas, Palas and Rashtrakutas in the later period; feudal tendencies and land grants led to disintegration

Kannauj as Imperial Capital & Assemblies: Rise of Kannauj (Mahodaya / Kanyakubja): Harsha shifted his capital from Thaneshwar to Kannauj in 606 CE following the death of Grahavarman Maukhari; Kannauj replaced Pataliputra as the premier political and imperial metropolis of Northern India, remaining the imperial prize for five centuries.

Kannauj Assembly (643 CE): Grand multi-faith assembly convened by Harsha to honor Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang and demonstrate the supremacy of Mahayana Buddhism; attended by 20 tributary kings (including Bhaskaravarman of Kamarupa), 3,000 Buddhist monks, 3,000 Jains and orthodox Brahmanas; orthodox conspiracy: disgruntled Brahmanas set fire to the 100-foot temporary pavilion and attempted to assassinate Harsha; conspirators banished.

Prayag Mahamokshaparishad (643 CE): Quinquennial assembly convened at the holy confluence of Ganga and Yamuna at Prayagraj; 75-day festival attended by 500,000 people; Harsha worshipped Buddha on the first day, Sun god on the second, and Shiva on the third; distributed all accumulated royal treasury riches, jewels, cloth, and even his personal royal robes in charity, begging a worn garment from his sister Rajyashri.

events.title: Harsha becomes King
events.desc: Harsha ascends the throne at Thanesar after his brother Rajyavardhana's death, beginning his reign centred on North India including U.P.

events.title: Grand assembly at Prayaga
events.desc: Harsha holds a grand religious assembly at Prayaga, distributing wealth to the people every five years.

events.title: Xuanzang visits Harsha's court
events.desc: The Chinese pilgrim's detailed travelogue, 'Si-yu-ki', becomes a key historical source on Harsha's India.

events.title: Death of Harsha
events.desc: Harsha dies at Kanyakubja (Kannauj) without a capable successor, leading to the empire's fragmentation.

people.name: Harshavardhana
people.note: r. c. 606–647 CE; made Kannauj his later capital.

people.name: Xuanzang (Hsuan Tsang)
people.note: Visited Harsha's court c. 630–645 CE; authored 'Si-yu-ki'.

people.name: Pulakeshin II
people.note: Defeated Harsha's southward ambitions at the Narmada.

prelims: Harshavardhana transferred the imperial capital of his empire from Thaneshwar (Haryana) to Kannauj (Uttar Pradesh) in 606 CE.
Harsha convened the famous religious assembly at Kannauj in 643 CE to honor the Chinese Buddhist scholar Xuanzang.
The grand quinquennial charity festival known as the "Mahamokshaparishad" was convened by Harsha at the holy confluence in Prayag (Prayagraj).
Banabhatta, the court poet of Harsha, was born near the banks of the Son river and composed the biographical classic Harshacharita and Kadambari.
Xuanzang described Kannauj as a strongly fortified, prosperous city with over 100 Buddhist monasteries, 200 Hindu temples, and lavish gardens.
Harsha's defeat on the Narmada river by Chalukya king Pulakeshin II is recorded in the Aihole Inscription authored by Ravikirti.
Harsha authored three classical Sanskrit dramas: Ratnavali, Priyadarsika, and Nagananda.
mains: Discuss the geopolitical and economic reasons for the emergence of Kannauj as the premier political capital of Northern India during the reign of Harshavardhana.
Analyze the accounts of Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang regarding the religious assemblies of Kannauj and Prayag, evaluating Harsha's secular policy.
Examine the political and cultural contributions of the Maukhari dynasty of Kannauj prior to its unification with Harsha's empire.

quickFacts: Kanyakubja, Prayaga, Kaushambi, Varanasi, Mathura, Sravasti, Ahichchhatra

periods.title: Gurjara-Pratiharas in Uttar Pradesh
periods.tagline: The Great Defenders of North India Against Arab Invasions
periods.overview: The national Early Medieval Period page describes a three-way 'tripartite struggle' for Kannauj among the Gurjara-Pratiharas, Palas, and Rashtrakutas at a necessarily abstract, empire-wide level; this page tells that same story from inside the winning side's own territory, since Kannauj — the actual prize being fought over — was the Pratihara capital for most of the dynasty's three-century run. What that regional vantage point makes vivid is the genuine strategic stakes: Nagabhata I and Nagabhata II's victories over Arab invaders at the Rajasthan frontier in the mid-8th century did not just defend Pratihara territory, they defended the entire Doab region this page covers from becoming the eastern edge of an expanding Arab conquest, a defensive achievement the source material explicitly credits with earning the dynasty their reputation as 'Defenders of North India'. Mihir Bhoja's reign, the dynasty's peak, shows what holding Kannauj actually enabled once secured: literary patronage (Bana's Harshacharita), administrative sophistication, and a cultural prestige that made Kannauj not just politically valuable but the acknowledged intellectual capital of North India for a generation — precisely the prize whose eventual loss to internal weakness and Chandella, Kalachuri, and Paramara pressure opens the next chapter of regional fragmentation this track goes on to cover.

phases.name: Rise of Power
points: Rise of Gurjara-Pratihara power in Rajasthan

phases.name: Nagabhata I
points: Emerges as a powerful ruler; defeat of Arab invaders (Muhammad bin Qasim's successors) at Rajasthan, c. 754–756 CE, protecting North India

phases.name: Vatsaraja & Nagabhata II
points: Vatsaraja (775–805 CE) extends territory; Nagabhata II (805–833 CE) defeats Arabs again, extends influence in North India

phases.name: Mihir Bhoja
points: The greatest Pratihara ruler; capital at Kannauj; resisted Palas and Rashtrakutas; patron of literature and art

phases.name: Mahendrapala I & Decline
points: Mahendrapala I (885–915 CE) — last powerful ruler of the early line, empire began to decline after him; 10th–11th century: decline due to internal weakness and rise of Chandellas, Kalachuris, Paramaras

Arab Invasions & the Pratihara Role.intro: This is the category that explains the dynasty's historical reputation: the specific victories described here, at the Rajasthan frontier in the mid-8th century, are what earned the Pratiharas their title as 'Defenders of North India' rather than simply one more regional power among several.
points: Arabs under Muhammad bin Qasim reached Sindh in 712 CE; successors attempted expansion into Rajasthan and western India; Nagabhata I and Nagabhata II defeated Arab forces near Jalore, Bhinmal and the Rajasthan frontiers (c. 754–756 CE)
This saved North India from further Arab expansion and marked the beginning of the Pratiharas' reputation as 'Defenders of North India'

Administration & Governance.intro: The Bhukti-Vishaya-Pattaka-Village hierarchy here should look familiar by now — it is the same basic administrative template this track has traced continuously from the Guptas through Harsha, refined slightly by each successive dynasty rather than reinvented from scratch.
points: Hereditary monarchy with strong central authority; empire divided into Bhuktis (provinces), Vishayas (districts) and Pattakas (sub-districts) and Villages; officials — Uparika (governor), Vishayapati, Dandapashika, Mahattaras, Bhogika and Sresthin (revenue officials)

Revenue system: land revenue as the main source, other taxes — trade tax, profession tax, fines etc.; strong cavalry, elephants and infantry; king supreme in justice, local officers maintained law and order

Society & Economy.intro: Note the specific claim that women's position was 'relatively better in elite families' — a more qualified statement than the broader Gupta-era description on an earlier page, suggesting genuine regional and class variation rather than a single uniform trend across the whole Early Medieval period.
points: Varna system continued; Brahmins enjoyed high status, many land grants; growth of municipalities and urban centres; artisans, traders, merchants and agriculturists contributed to the economy; position of women relatively better in elite families

Agriculture was the backbone of the economy; use of iron plough, irrigation tanks, wells and canals; active trade through land routes (Uttarapatha) and river routes; growth of towns like Kannauj, Mathura, Varanasi, Ahichchhatra, Prayag; guilds (shrenis) of artisans and merchants flourished

Religion & Culture.intro: Mihir Bhoja's patronage of the Harshacharita, referenced here, is a useful reminder that 'Harsha' as a name recurs in Indian history for reasons unrelated to the emperor Harsha covered earlier in this track — a common source of confusion worth clearing up explicitly.
points: Patronage to Hinduism — Shaivism, Vaishnavism, Shaktism; maintenance of temples, mathas and tirthas; tolerance towards Buddhism and Jainism continued; many grants to Brahmans and religious institutions

Patronage of Sanskrit literature and scholarship; famous works: Rajatarangini (later period), Harshacharita (Banabhatta — under Mihir Bhoja); development of art, sculpture and temple architecture; flourishing of learning centres in Kannauj, Kashi and Mathura

Pratihara Hegemony over Kannauj: Imperial consolidation: Nagabhata II captured Kannauj and made it the permanent imperial capital of the Gurjara-Pratiharas around 815 CE; celebrated as the bulwark of India for repelling early Arab invasions from Sindh.

Mihira Bhoja (r. 836–885 CE): Most illustrious Pratihara emperor; consolidated an empire stretching from the foothills of the Himalayas to the Narmada and from Bengal to Gujarat; assumed the titles "Adivaraha" and "Prabhas"; struck silver and copper coins bearing the boar incarnation of Vishnu; patron of learning; praised by Arab traveler Sulaiman as possessing the finest cavalry in India.

Culture & Rajasekhara: Mahendrapala I and Mahipala I patronized the great Sanskrit poet-playwright Rajasekhara, author of Kavyamimamsa, Karpuramanjari (written entirely in Sauraseni Prakrit), Balaramayana, and Viddhasalabhanjika; Arab geographer Al-Masudi visited Kannauj in 915 CE, calling the king "Baura" and describing his four vast armies guarding the four cardinal directions.

events.title: Defeat of Arab invaders
events.desc: Nagabhata I and Nagabhata II defeat Arab forces at the Rajasthan frontier, protecting North India from further Arab expansion.

events.title: Reign of Mihir Bhoja
events.desc: The greatest Pratihara ruler makes Kannauj the imperial capital and cultural heart of North India.

events.title: Decline of Pratihara power
events.desc: Internal weakness and the rise of the Chandellas, Kalachuris and Paramaras erode Pratihara control.

people.name: Nagabhata I
people.note: Defeated Arab invaders in Rajasthan.

people.name: Mihir Bhoja
people.note: r. c. 836–885 CE; capital at Kannauj; resisted Palas and Rashtrakutas.

people.name: Mahendrapala I
people.note: r. 885–915 CE; last powerful ruler of the early line.

prelims: The Gurjara-Pratihara emperor Mihira Bhoja assumed the title "Adivaraha" and minted silver coins depicting the Boar incarnation of Vishnu.
Nagabhata II made Kannauj the permanent imperial capital of the Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty in the early 9th century CE.
The celebrated Sanskrit poet and dramatist Rajasekhara was the court poet and guru of Pratihara king Mahendrapala I.
Rajasekhara composed Karpuramanjari, the only classical Sanskrit drama written entirely in Sauraseni Prakrit.
Arab traveler Al-Masudi visited Kannauj in 915 CE during the reign of Pratihara king Mahipala I, describing the kingdom as "al-Juzr" and the king as "Baura".
Arab chronicler Sulaiman (851 CE) praised Mihira Bhoja as the greatest enemy of Islam possessing India's most formidable cavalry.
Mahmud of Ghazni invaded and sacked Kannauj in 1018 CE, defeating the last major Pratihara ruler Rajyapala.
mains: Analyze the political and military role of the Gurjara-Pratiharas of Kannauj as the "defenders of the northwestern frontiers" against early Arab invasions.
Evaluate the reign and cultural achievements of Mihira Bhoja and Mahendrapala I, with specific reference to Rajasekhara's literary works.
Discuss the decline of the Gurjara-Pratihara empire and explain how its collapse led to the rise of regional Rajput polities in Northern India.

quickFacts: Repelled Arab invasions; made Kannauj a great imperial centre
10th–11th century, due to internal weakness and rise of regional powers

periods.title: Kalachuris & Chandellas in Uttar Pradesh
periods.tagline: Regional Powers, Temple Culture, Political Decentralisation and Cultural Florescence
periods.overview: This page zooms into the Bundelkhand region (ancient Jejakabhukti) that the national Early Medieval Period page mentions only as one of several regional power centres, and the zoom is worth it for one reason above all others: the Khajuraho temple complex, among the most architecturally and artistically significant religious sites anywhere in India, was built here under sustained Chandella royal patronage across the 10th and 11th centuries.
