What the regional focus reveals that a national-scale account cannot is how directly temple-building functioned as a form of dynastic legitimacy for both the Kalachuris and Chandellas — neither dynasty ever came close to Pratihara-level territorial reach, yet both invested surplus wealth in monumental religious architecture and Sanskrit and Prakrit literary patronage at a scale that rivalled far larger contemporary states. The Chandella ruler Vidyadhara's successful defence of the Kalinjar fort against Mahmud of Ghazni around 1022 CE also marks this region as an active site of the very Turkish-invasion pressure the national page describes only as a broader northern phenomenon — a reminder that the temple-building golden age this page celebrates and the beginning of sustained external military threat were happening here at almost exactly the same time.

phases.name: Rise of Regional Powers
points: Rise of regional powers in North India after decline of the Pratiharas; emergence of Kalachuris in Jejakabhukti (Bundelkhand region; parts of present U.P.)

phases.name: Rise of the Chandellas
points: Nannuka founds Chandella power; Yashovarman (925–950 CE) establishes independence from the Pratiharas

phases.name: Peak Power & Cultural Achievements
points: Period of greatest power and cultural achievements for both dynasties; Yuvarajadeva I of the Kalachuris (c. 915–945 CE) — titles Maharajadhiraja, Tribhuvanamalla, conquests in Bundelkhand; Dhangadeva and Gandharvavarman strengthen Chandella power

phases.name: Decline
points: Decline due to internal conflicts, attacks of Ghaznavids & Ghurids, and the rise of other powers; Vidyadhara (c. 1035–1050 CE) — greatest Chandella ruler, repelled Mahmud of Ghazni (c. 1022 CE) at Kalinjar, but the dynasty later declined

Administration & Governance.intro: Comparing the two dynasties side by side in this table, the Chandellas' more elaborate provincial hierarchy (Bhuktis, Vishayas, Pattakas, Grams with named officer categories) suggests a somewhat more developed bureaucratic apparatus than the Kalachuris managed to build in the same Bundelkhand region.
points: Kalachuris: monarchical rule with strong central authority, territories divided into provinces (Mandalas/Vishayas), officials (Mahasamantas, Uparika, Dandapashika), land revenue as the main source of income

Chandellas: well-organised administration, division into Bhuktis, Vishayas, Pattakas and Grams, officers — Vishayapati, Mahattaras, Dandadhikritas, Pustapalas; land revenue, tanks and wells were created; land grants to Brahmans, temples and officers

Society & Economy.intro: The temple-centred society described here is the direct social context for the monumental religious architecture discussed below — Khajuraho was not built in isolation but grew out of a broader regional culture in which temples functioned as economic and social hubs, not just places of worship.
points: Varna system continued; Brahmins and Kshatriyas enjoyed high status; growth of temple-based society; artisans, temple servants, dancers, musicians, traders flourished; women participated in religious and cultural life

Agriculture was the backbone; crops — rice, wheat, pulses, sugarcane, oilseeds; irrigation — tanks, wells, rivers, canals; trade & commerce flourished, use of coins; guilds (shrenis) of artisans and traders were active

Religion & Culture.intro: This category's claim that 'temple architecture reached its zenith' under these two dynasties is not exaggeration for effect — Khajuraho genuinely represents one of the peak achievements of medieval Indian temple-building, which is exactly why the next category treats it in such detail.
points: Hinduism was the dominant religion (Shaivism, Vaishnavism, Shaktism, all flourished); Jainism also patronised by both dynasties; temples were centres of religion, art, education, economy and culture; temple architecture reached its zenith under the Chandellas

Art, architecture & literature: Khajuraho temples — world famous for Nagara style architecture; temples at Kalinjar, Mahoba, Ajaigarh, Deogarh etc.; fine sculptures, erotic art, mythological themes; use of sandstone; patronage of poets — Rajasekhara (under Mahendrapala of the Chandellas); development of music, dance and drama

Legacy & Importance in U.P..intro: The phrase 'political decentralisation but cultural florescence' used here captures a pattern this entire Early Medieval section of the track keeps demonstrating: fragmented political power and vibrant regional culture were not opposites in this period but frequently went hand in hand.
points: Strengthened regional polity and administrative systems; patronised magnificent temple architecture (especially Khajuraho); promoted art, sculpture, literature and education; developed agriculture, irrigation and trade; U.P.'s Bundelkhand region became a great centre of culture and learning
Both dynasties contributed to political decentralisation but also cultural florescence in North India

Chandellas of Bundelkhand & Bundeli Valo: Chandellas of Jejakabhukti: Founded by Nannuka (9th cent); broke free from Pratihara suzerainty under Harsha and Yashovarman (built the Lakshmana Temple at Khajuraho); King Dhanga (built the Vishvanatha and Parshvanatha temples; shifted political capital to Mahoba while retaining Khajuraho as the sacred temple city); King Vidyadhara (1019–1022 CE; heroically resisted Mahmud of Ghazni twice at the impregnable Kalinjar Fort; built the soaring Kandariya Mahadeva Temple).
Kalinjar & Mahoba Fortresses: Impregnable military strongholds in Bundelkhand; Kalinjar withstood sieges by Mahmud of Ghazni, Qutbuddin Aibak, and later Sher Shah Suri (who died there in 1545).

Alha-Udal & Parmal: Reign of King Paramardideva (Parmal, r. 1165–1203 CE); defended Mahoba against Prithviraj Chauhan (1182 CE); celebrated in the heroic Bundeli folk ballad Alha-Khand (composed by court bard Jagnik), recounting the 52 epic battles of legendary warrior brothers Alha and Udal; Qutbuddin Aibak captured Kalinjar in 1203 CE.

Kalachuris of Dahala & Sarayupara: Kalachuri branch of Gorakhpur (Sarayupara) and Tripuri; King Gangeyadeva (assumed title Vikramaditya, struck Lakshmi-type gold coins widely imitated across North India) and Lakshmi-Karna.

events.title: Yashovarman establishes Chandella independence
events.desc: The Chandellas assert independence from the declining Pratiharas, beginning their rise as a major regional power.

events.title: Construction of the Khajuraho temples
events.desc: The Chandellas patronise the construction of the world-famous Khajuraho temple complex, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

events.title: Vidyadhara repels Mahmud of Ghazni
events.desc: The greatest Chandella ruler successfully defends Kalinjar against Mahmud of Ghazni's invasion.

people.name: Nannuka
people.note: Founded Chandella power.

people.name: Yashovarman
people.note: r. 925–950 CE; established independence from the Pratiharas.

people.name: Vidyadhara
people.note: r. c. 1035–1050 CE; repelled Mahmud of Ghazni; patron of art & architecture.

people.name: Yuvarajadeva I
people.note: c. 915–945 CE; greatest Kalachuri ruler.

prelims: The Chandella dynasty of Bundelkhand was anciently known as the rulers of "Jejakabhukti" (named after prince Jeja/Jayasakti).
The world-famous temples of Khajuraho were built between 950 and 1050 CE under the patronage of Chandella kings, notably Dhanga and Vidyadhara.
Chandella King Vidyadhara successfully resisted the invasions of Mahmud of Ghazni at the formidable Kalinjar Fort in 1019 and 1022 CE.
The folk ballad Alha-Khand, celebrating the martial exploits of warrior brothers Alha and Udal of Mahoba, was composed by court poet Jagnik.
Kalinjar Fort in Banda district of UP is one of the oldest and most impregnable hill fortresses of India, where Sher Shah Suri died in 1545.
The Kalachuri king Gangeyadeva issued gold coins bearing the seated image of Goddess Lakshmi, which became the standard coin type across Northern India.
Qutbuddin Aibak invaded Bundelkhand and captured Kalinjar Fort from Chandella king Paramardideva in 1203 CE.
mains: Trace the rise and political history of the Chandellas of Bundelkhand, analyzing their military resistance against Turkish invaders at Kalinjar.
Examine the folk and cultural significance of the Alha-Udal ballad tradition in the regional identity of Bundelkhand in Uttar Pradesh.
Analyze the architectural brilliance of the Khajuraho group of temples, focusing on temple layout, shikhara design, and sculptural iconography.

quickFacts: Internal conflicts, Ghaznavid/Ghurid attacks, rise of the Gahadavalas

periods.title: Gahadavalas in Uttar Pradesh
periods.tagline: Regional Power, Cultural Renaissance, and the Last Major Hindu Dynasty in North India Before the Ghurid Invasions
periods.overview: The Gahadavalas earn the description 'the last great Hindu dynasty of North India before the Delhi Sultanate' specifically because of where they ruled from — Kashi and Kanyakubja (Kannauj), the same two cities that had already anchored the Harsha and Gurjara-Pratihara stories earlier in this track — which makes this page as much a conclusion to the regional Kannauj-centred narrative as an introduction to what follows it. Govindachandra's reign, the dynasty's genuine peak, shows what a fully mature version of that Kannauj-Kashi power base could produce: patronage of the legal scholar Vijnaneshvara, whose Mitakshara became one of the most influential texts in the entire history of Hindu law, alongside sustained temple-building at Varanasi and a religious environment tolerant enough to support flourishing Vaishnava, Shaiva, Buddhist, and Jain communities simultaneously in the same cities. The dynasty's ending is where this page connects most directly to the national Delhi Sultanate story: Jayachandra's defeat by Muhammad Ghori at Chandawar in 1194 CE was not simply one more regional battle but the specific event that removed the last major Hindu power standing between Ghori's forces and unchallenged control of the Doab, opening the way for Qutb-ud-din Aibak's establishment of the Delhi Sultanate barely a decade later.

phases.name: Rise of Gahadavala Power
points: Rise of Gahadavala power in the Kashi region

phases.name: Chandradeva
points: Establishes the Gahadavala dynasty

phases.name: Expansion under Madachandra
points: Territorial expansion under Madachandra (c. 1030–1050 CE)

phases.name: Golden Age under Govindachandra
points: Greatest ruler; extended empire, promoted learning, religion & the arts; built temples, tanks & rest houses

phases.name: Decline & Defeat
points: Vijayachandra — last powerful ruler; 1194 CE: defeat of Jayachandra by Muhammad Ghori at Chandawar (near Etawah); early 13th century: decline and disintegration of the dynasty

Administration & Governance.intro: This is the same Bhukti-Vishaya-Pattaka structure this track has now traced across the Guptas, Harsha, the Gurjara-Pratiharas, and the Chandellas — by this point in the chronology it is worth noticing how remarkably stable this basic administrative vocabulary remained across four centuries of otherwise constant dynastic change.
points: Monarchical, hereditary kingship; empire divided into Bhuktis (provinces), Vishayas (districts) and Pattakas (sub-districts); officials — Uparika (governor), Vishayapati, Dandapashika, Mahattaras, Kayasthas and other officials

Land revenue was the main source; other taxes included trade tax, transit tax, fines and tributes; strong cavalry, infantry and elephants; king was supreme authority, Brahmanas consulted in judicial matters; maintained relations with neighbouring kingdoms, at times engaged in conflicts with Turko-Afghan invaders

Society & Economy.intro: The description of active local and long-distance trade here connects directly to the following page's focus on medieval city foundations — the same trade routes and economic activity described in this table are precisely what made new city foundations commercially viable under the Sultanate rulers who follow.
points: Varna system continued; Brahmanas enjoyed high status; growth of urban centres and market towns; artisans, traders, merchants and agriculturists formed important sections; women participated in religious, cultural and social life

Agriculture was the backbone of the economy; crops — rice, wheat, pulses, sugarcane, sesame; irrigation through tanks, wells, rivers and canals; active trade in local and long distance routes; land grants to Brahmanas, temples and scholars

Religion & Culture.intro: Vijnaneshvara's Mitakshara, mentioned here, deserves particular attention: it became one of the most influential legal texts in the entire history of Hindu law, meaning this relatively short-lived regional dynasty produced a genuinely lasting all-India intellectual legacy.
points: Vaishnavism, Shaivism and Shaktism were prominent; King Govindachandra was a great patron of all religions; tolerance towards Buddhism and Jainism continued; confluence of religious traditions in Kashi and Prayaga

Flourishing of Sanskrit literature and learning; important scholar Vijnaneshvara (author of Mitakshara on Hindu law) under Govindachandra; development of temples, tanks, rest houses (Dharmashalas) and ghats; promotion of art, sculpture, music and dance

Art & Architecture in U.P..intro: The temples described here at Varanasi and Kannauj are the last major flowering of specifically Hindu dynastic patronage this track will cover before the architectural vocabulary shifts decisively toward the Indo-Islamic styles introduced on the following pages.
points: Temples built in Nagara style; major centres — Varanasi, Kannauj, Ayodhya, Ghazipur, Prayaga and surrounding areas; examples — Vishwanath Temple (Varanasi, earlier structures), Bhairav Temple (Kashi), Madan Mohan Temple (Kannauj) etc.; fine stone sculptures of deities, dvarapalas, surasundaris influenced by earlier Pratihara-Chandella traditions

Legacy & Importance.intro: This category's framing of the Gahadavalas as 'the last great Hindu dynasty before the Delhi Sultanate' is the direct bridge to the next page — Jayachandra's 1194 defeat, detailed in the overview above, is the specific event this legacy statement is built around.
points: Gahadavalas were the last great Hindu dynasty in North India before the establishment of the Delhi Sultanate; promoted culture, learning, temples and urban development; strengthened Kashi and Prayaga as major religious and cultural centres; their period is important for understanding the transition from regional kingdoms to Sultanate rule

Gahadavala Hegemony & The Fall of Kannau: Dynastic establishment: Founded by Chandradeva (c. 1090 CE) following the chaotic collapse of the Pratiharas and Kalachuris; established dual capitals at Kannauj (political) and Varanasi (religious/cultural); assumed the imperial title "Parama-bhattaraka Maharajadhiraja Parameshvara".

Govindachandra (r. 1114–1155 CE): Greatest Gahadavala emperor; defended the Gangetic Doab against Ghaznavid invasions from Punjab; levied a specific defense war tax called "Turushkadanda" (tax to fight or tribute paid to the Turks); patron of learning: minister Lakshmidhara authored the monumental 14-volume legal compendium Krityakalpataru (defining medieval Hindu civil law and court procedure); Queen Kumaradevi (Buddhist princess of Pithi) built the Dharmachakra Jina Vihara at Sarnath.

Jaichand & The Battle of Chandawar (1194 CE): Last great sovereign; contemporary and rival of Prithviraj Chauhan (legendary swayamvara of daughter Sanyogita recorded in Prithviraj Raso); Muhammad Ghori invaded the Doab in 1194 CE; Jaichand confronted Ghori at the Battle of Chandawar (near Firozabad on the Yamuna river); struck in the eye by an arrow, Jaichand fell from his elephant and died; Ghori plundered Kannauj and Varanasi, destroying temples and ending independent Hindu monarchical rule in central UP.

events.title: Chandradeva founds the Gahadavala dynasty
events.desc: Establishes Gahadavala control over Kashi and surrounding regions.

events.title: Reign of Govindachandra
events.desc: The dynasty's golden age: extended empire, promoted learning, religion and the arts, and built temples, tanks and rest houses.

events.title: Defeat of Jayachandra at Chandawar
events.desc: Muhammad Ghori defeats Jayachandra (Vijayachandra's successor) at Chandawar, near Etawah, marking the end of Gahadavala power and opening the way for the Delhi Sultanate.

people.name: Govindachandra
people.note: r. 1114–1154 CE; golden age of the dynasty.

people.name: Vijayachandra (Jayachandra)
people.note: r. c. 1170–1203 CE; defeated by Muhammad Ghori at Chandawar (1194 CE).

people.name: Vijnaneshvara
people.note: Author of Mitakshara, a landmark legal text, under Govindachandra.

prelims: The Gahadavala dynasty ruled over Kannauj and Varanasi from the late 11th century until their defeat in 1194 CE.
The "Turushkadanda" was an extraordinary war tax levied by Gahadavala rulers like Govindachandra to maintain defenses against Ghaznavid Turkish invasions.
Lakshmidhara, the chief minister of Gahadavala king Govindachandra, compiled the celebrated encyclopaedic legal digest Krityakalpataru.
Queen Kumaradevi, the Buddhist wife of Gahadavala king Govindachandra, constructed the Dharmachakra Jina Vihara monastery at Sarnath.
The Battle of Chandawar took place in 1194 CE near modern Firozabad, where Muhammad Ghori defeated and killed Gahadavala king Jaichand.
The Gahadavala rulers were devout Vaishnavas and Shaivas who styled themselves protectors of holy shrines in Varanasi, Ayodhya, and Gaya.
The romantic episode of the abduction of Jaichand's daughter Sanyogita by Prithviraj Chauhan is recounted in Chand Bardai's Prithviraj Raso.
mains: Evaluate the political, military, and administrative achievements of King Govindachandra Gahadavala, with specific reference to the Turushkadanda tax and the Krityakalpataru.
Analyze the geopolitical causes and consequences of the Battle of Chandawar (1194 CE) in sealing the fate of Turkish hegemony across Northern India.
Examine the patronage extended by the Gahadavalas to both Brahmanical learning and Buddhism at Varanasi and Sarnath.

quickFacts: Defeat of Jayachandra by Muhammad Ghori, 1194 CE (Battle of Chandawar)

periods.title: Foundation of Cities in Medieval Period in Uttar Pradesh
periods.tagline: Urbanisation, Trade, Administration and Culture in Medieval Uttar Pradesh
periods.overview: This page steps outside the dynasty-by-dynasty narrative the rest of this track otherwise follows to ask a more structural question the national account never poses directly: how did medieval Uttar Pradesh's actual cities — as opposed to its ruling houses — come into being, and why there rather than elsewhere? The answer the source material lays out is consistently pragmatic across four centuries of city-founding, whether under the Delhi Sultanate (Sambhal, Badaun, Etawah, Ghaziabad, Jaunpur) or the Lodis and Mughals (Agra, Fatehpur Sikri, Allahabad): strategic and military considerations, control of trade routes, proximity to rivers and fertile land, and religious or cultural patronage that drew population and investment together. Read alongside the individual dynasty pages elsewhere in this track, this page functions as connective infrastructure — Agra, founded here by Sikandar Lodi in 1504, becomes the Mughal imperial capital the up-mughal-period page covers in depth; Allahabad, founded by Akbar as Ilahabas in 1583, becomes the administrative and, much later, freedom-struggle centre that recurs across the British-era pages further along this track. In other words, this page explains the urban stage on which most of the rest of this track's political drama actually took place.

phases.name: Rise of Towns Under Regional Powers
points: Rise of important towns under Gurjara-Pratiharas and regional powers

phases.name: Growth Under Gahadavalas & Chandellas
points: Growth of religious, trade and administrative centres under the Gahadavalas and Chandellas

phases.name: Sultanate City Foundations
points: Establishment of new cities by Delhi Sultanate rulers for strategic and military considerations: Sambhal (founded by Shihabuddin Ghori's general, Kutubuddin Aibak's time, 13th c.), Badaun (Alauddin Khalji, 13th c.), Etawah (Khilji rulers, 13th c.), Ghaziabad (Ghazi-ud-din, 13th c.), Jaunpur (Malik Sarwar/Sharqi rulers, 14th c.)

phases.name: Mughal & Regional State Foundations
points: Foundation of cities under Mughals and regional states, cultural and economic flourishing: Fatehpur (Sikandar Lodi, 1482 CE), Agra (Sikandar Lodi, 1504 CE), Fatehpur Sikri (Akbar, 1571 CE), Allahabad (Akbar as Ilahabas, 1583 CE), Azamgarh (Akbar, 16th c.), Sikandra Rao (Akbar, 16th c.)

phases.name: Modern Transition
points: Modern cities emerge; colonial influence begins

Factors Behind Foundation of Cities.intro: This list of motives — strategic, commercial, administrative, religious — is worth keeping in mind while reading every subsequent dynasty-specific page in this track, since it explains why so many of the same city names (Agra, Jaunpur, Allahabad) keep reappearing across otherwise very different political regimes.
points: Strategic & military considerations (frontiers, defence); control over important trade routes; proximity to rivers, fertile land and markets

Administrative needs — provincial capitals, garrisons; religious & cultural centres attracted population; patronage of rulers, nobles, Sufis and merchants; growth of craft production and urban economy

Functions & Characteristics of Medieval.intro: Notice how many distinct functions a single medieval city was expected to combine — administrative, military, economic, and religious all at once — which is exactly why capturing or founding a city like Kannauj or Agra mattered so much more than simply gaining farmland.
points: Administrative centres: provincial headquarters, court, revenue offices; military centres: fortress, garrisons, arsenals; economic hubs: trade, markets (bazaars), craft production
Cultural & religious centres: mosques, madrasas, temples, khanqahs, libraries; urban amenities: sarais, wells, tanks, bridges, roads, gardens

Economy & Urban Life.intro: The specific trade routes listed here (Delhi–Badaun–Kannauj–Jaunpur–Bengal, for instance) are the actual commercial arteries that the following Delhi Sultanate and Mughal-era pages assume already exist when they discuss regional trade and revenue.
points: Active participation in regional and long-distance trade; products — textiles, metalware, ivory, pottery, leather, sugar, spices; guilds (shrenis), artisans, weavers, metalworkers, carpenters flourished; use of copper/silver coins, monetised economy; growth of moneylenders, merchants and bankers
Important trade routes: Delhi–Badaun–Kannauj–Jaunpur–Bengal; Delhi–Etawah–Gwalior–Central India; Agra–Allahabad–Varanasi–Bengal; Northwest (Punjab)–Sambhal–Ganga Plain

Administration of Cities.intro: The Shahna–Muhtasib–Kotwal structure described here is specifically an urban administrative layer, distinct from (though coordinated with) the broader provincial Iqta system the following Delhi Sultanate page describes — cities needed their own dedicated market and law-and-order officials that rural provinces did not.
points: Shahna (Governor) or Iqtadars controlled the city and surrounding area; Muhtasib supervised markets, weights & measures, public morals; Kotwal maintained law & order; revenue collection through taxes on trade, land, houses and professions; strong fortification in many cities

Architectural & Cultural Heritage.intro: Jaunpur's description here as 'Shiraz-i-Hind' is a preview of a claim the dedicated Jaunpur Sultanate page will explore in far more depth — worth flagging now so the connection is clear when you reach that page later in this track.
points: Architectural features: fortresses, city walls & gates (e.g. Badaun, Jaunpur), mosques with arches, domes, minarets; sarais, bridges, tanks, gardens; blend of Indo-Islamic and local styles
Cultural contributions: Jaunpur — 'Shiraz-i-Hind' (centre of learning, music, literature); patronage of art, architecture, calligraphy, Persian literature; growth of Sufi centres and khanqahs

Medieval Urban Foundations in UP: Agra (1504 CE): Founded by Sultan Sikandar Lodi as a forward military outpost against Rajput rulers and to control trade routes through the Doab; transferred the capital from Delhi to Agra in 1506 CE; transformed into the grand imperial metropolis "Akbarabad" by Akbar, Jahangir, and Shah Jahan.

Jaunpur (1359 CE): Founded by Sultan Firuz Shah Tughlaq along the Gomti river, named in loving memory of his cousin Muhammad bin Tughlaq (whose original name was Fakhruddin Jauna Khan); flourished as the capital of the Sharqi Sultanate (1394–1479 CE), celebrated as the "Shiraz of the East".
Firozabad (1354 CE): Founded by Firuz Shah Tughlaq on the Yamuna; evolved into India's premier hub of glassmaking, bangles, and chandeliers ("Suhag Nagari").

Fatehpur Sikri (1571 CE): Founded by Emperor Akbar atop a rocky ridge near Sikri village to honor Sufi saint Shaikh Salim Chishti; planned imperial capital with red sandstone palaces, public halls, and Buland Darwaza.

Other major medieval foundations: Sambhal, Badaun (cultural and administrative centre under Iltutmish and Sayyid kings), and Shahjahanpur (founded in 1647 by Diler Khan and Bahadur Khan under Shah Jahan).

events.title: Jaunpur founded/rises as Sharqi capital
events.desc: Jaunpur emerges as one of medieval U.P.'s greatest centres of learning, music and literature — the 'Shiraz-i-Hind'.

events.title: Sikandar Lodi founds Agra
events.desc: Agra rises on the Yamuna, later becoming the imperial Mughal capital.

events.title: Akbar founds Fatehpur Sikri
events.desc: A planned city built as Akbar's capital for about 14 years.

events.title: Akbar founds Allahabad (Ilahabas)
events.desc: Built at the strategic confluence of the Ganga, Yamuna and Saraswati, becoming an important administrative and military centre.

people.name: Sikandar Lodi
people.note: Founded Agra (1504) and Fatehpur (1482).

people.name: Akbar
people.note: Founded Fatehpur Sikri (1571), Allahabad (1583), Azamgarh and Sikandra Rao.

prelims: Sikandar Lodi founded the city of Agra in 1504 CE and shifted his imperial capital there in 1506 CE.
The city of Jaunpur was founded on the banks of the Gomti river in 1359 CE by Firuz Shah Tughlaq in memory of his cousin Jauna Khan (Muhammad bin Tughlaq).
Firozabad was established by Firuz Shah Tughlaq and is historically renowned as India's glassmaking and bangle manufacturing capital ("Suhag Nagari").
Akbar founded his planned capital city of Fatehpur Sikri in 1571 CE in gratitude to the Sufi saint Shaikh Salim Chishti.
Badaun was an illustrious medieval administrative centre where Iltutmish served as governor before becoming Sultan of Delhi.
Jaunpur was renowned throughout the medieval Islamic world as the "Shiraz-i-Hind" (Shiraz of the East) for its Islamic colleges and architecture.
The historic Grand Trunk Road (Sadak-e-Azam) rebuilt by Sher Shah Suri traversed through major medieval urban hubs in UP including Chunar, Varanasi, and Agra.
mains: Analyze the strategic, geopolitical, and commercial reasons behind the foundation of medieval cities in Uttar Pradesh, with special focus on Agra and Jaunpur.
Examine the urban planning, water architecture, and cultural significance of Fatehpur Sikri as Akbar's planned capital.
Discuss how urban foundations during the Delhi Sultanate and Mughal era reshaped trade routes and regional craft production across the Ganga-Yamuna Doab.

quickFacts: Agra, Fatehpur, Fatehpur Sikri, Allahabad, Azamgarh
Laid the foundation for later urban growth in the colonial period

periods.title: Delhi Sultanate Period in Uttar Pradesh
periods.tagline: Establishment, Expansion and Administration of the Delhi Sultanate in U.P.
periods.overview: The national Delhi Sultanate overview, and its five dedicated dynasty pages, describe an empire-wide institution — the Iqta system, the five ruling houses, the slow evolution of Indo-Islamic administration and architecture; this page asks the more specific question of what all of that meant for the region that was, in practical terms, the Sultanate's core home territory rather than a distant province. Every one of the five dynasties covered nationally left a direct, datable mark here: Sambhal and Badaun developed under the Mamluks and Khaljis, Alauddin Khalji's conquests brought Awadh, Kannauj, and Varanasi under direct central control, Firuz Shah Tughlaq's Doab canal system was a genuine piece of regional infrastructure rather than an abstract policy, and Sikandar Lodi's foundation of Agra in the dynasty's final decades set up the city that would become the Mughal Empire's first great capital. What this regional lens adds to the national account is a concrete sense of continuity across dynastic change: regardless of which of the five houses held power at Delhi, the same Doab cities — Sambhal, Kannauj, Koil, Varanasi, Chunar — kept functioning as the Sultanate's actual administrative and military backbone, a continuity the national dynasty-by-dynasty narrative, focused on Delhi-centred political change, does not have space to show.

phases.name: Establishment
points: Establishment of the Delhi Sultanate by Qutb-ud-din Aibak

phases.name: Mamluk Consolidation
points: Iltutmish consolidates power in North India including U.P.

phases.name: Khalji Expansion
points: Alauddin Khalji conquers most of U.P.

phases.name: Tughlaq Rule
points: Administrative reforms; growth of towns

phases.name: Sayyid Decline
points: Decline of central authority; local chiefs grow in power

phases.name: Lodi Rule
points: Last Afghan dynasty before the Mughal invasion

Important Sultans and Their Connection w.intro: This ruler-by-dynasty table is the single most useful quick-reference item in this section of the track — use the 'Contribution/Impact in U.P.' column specifically to distinguish what each of the five Sultanate dynasties actually did in this region, since the national Delhi Sultanate pages cover the same rulers at empire-wide scale without this regional breakdown.
points: Mamluk (Slave) Dynasty: Qutb-ud-din Aibak (1206–1210) laid the foundation of Sultanate power in U.P.; built mosques, consolidated control; Iltutmish (1211–1236) consolidated rule in North India including U.P.; Sambhal, Badaun developed
Khalji Dynasty: Jalal-ud-din Khalji (1290–1296) captured strategic forts in U.P.; Alauddin Khalji (1296–1316) conquered Awadh, Kannauj, Varanasi, Jalaun; introduced market reforms

Tughlaq Dynasty: Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq (1320–1325) strengthened administration in the Doab; Muhammad bin Tughlaq (1325–1351) undertook reforms, revenue measures, attempted capital shift, agricultural expansion; Firoz Shah Tughlaq (1351–1388) built canals in the Doab, developed cities, mosques, madrasas

Sayyid Dynasty: Khizr Khan (1414–1421) had weak control in U.P., local chiefs grew; Lodi Dynasty: Bahlul Lodi (1451–1489) reorganized administration in U.P.; Sikandar Lodi (1489–1517) developed Agra, encouraged agriculture, trade & arts; Ibrahim Lodi (1517–1526) defeated by Babur in 1526

Administration & Governance.intro: The Iqta system described here as the backbone of Sultanate administration is identical to the system the national Delhi Sultanate page discusses, but this table shows specifically how it operated across the Doab, Awadh, and Rohilkhand regions that made up the Sultanate's regional core.
points: Centralised Sultanate with the Sultan at the head; Iqta System — land revenue assignments to nobles in exchange for military service; provinces (Iqtas) headed by Iqtadars; strong revenue administration especially under Alauddin Khalji
Qazi, Muhtasib, Barid — important officials; development of a police & intelligence system; urban administration in major towns & cities

Society & Economy.intro: The description of a genuinely composite society — Turks, Afghans, and local Hindus interacting within the same urban economy — is the social backdrop against which the Sufi-driven cultural synthesis discussed in the next category actually took place.
points: Composite society: interaction of Turks, Afghans and local Hindus; growth of urban middle class — artisans, traders, soldiers, officials; emergence of new occupational groups — weavers, dyers, metal workers; Sufism played a unifying role; social mobility through service, trade & religious movements

Agriculture — mainstay; revenue improvement under Khaljis & Tughlaqs; canal construction (especially under Firoz Shah Tughlaq); growth of towns and trade centres — Kannauj, Varanasi, Koil, Sambhal, Badaun; development of crafts — textile, metal, pottery, leather, arms; active internal & external trade via land routes

Religion, Culture, Art & Architecture.intro: Note that Sufism is described here as playing a 'unifying role' rather than simply a religious one — this is a recurring theme across the whole Sultanate period in U.P., and it directly explains why so many of the architectural sites listed (Chunar Fort, Jaunpur's tombs) sit close to identifiable Sufi shrine networks.
points: Islam became dominant among the ruling class; construction of mosques, madrasas, tombs, khanqahs; Sufis — Khwaja Muinuddin Chishti (Ajmer, connected with U.P. travel), Nizamuddin Auliya visits the region; Hindi language & literature saw growth; Indo-Islamic architecture developed; cultural synthesis and syncretic traditions

Mosques: Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque (Sambhal), Adhai Din ka Jhonpra (influence in region); tombs: Tomb of Iltutmish (Delhi, influence), Sharqi & Lodi structures in Jaunpur; forts: Chunar Fort, Etawah, Kalpi; Persian was the official language; Hindi/Sanskrit literature continued; Amir Khusrau's cultural influence extended to the region

Legacy & Impact.intro: This category's claim that the Sultanate 'prepared ground for emergence of independent kingdoms (Jaunpur) and later the Mughals' is the explicit bridge to the next several pages in this track, each of which picks up one thread of that legacy in turn.
points: Delhi Sultanate laid the foundation of political unification in North India; development of administration, revenue system and law & order; growth of cities, trade, crafts and agriculture; Indo-Islamic culture flourished in U.P.; Sufism promoted social harmony; prepared the ground for emergence of independent kingdoms (Jaunpur) and later the Mughals

The Doab as Fiscal Core & Rebellions: Geopolitical significance: Uttar Pradesh and the fertile Ganga-Yamuna Doab formed the economic backbone of the Delhi Sultanate; prime source of agrarian land revenue (Kharaj).

Administrative centres: Kara-Manikpur (on the Ganga near Prayagraj) served as the vital strategic provincial headquarters where Alauddin Khalji governed and murdered Jalaluddin; Badaun, Sambhal, Koil (Aligarh), Kannauj, and Baran (Bulandshahr) were major Iqta centres.

Agrarian resistance: Rebellions of the Hindu agrarian gentry (Khuts and Muqaddams) in the Doab were crushed ruthlessly by Balban (who cleared the Mewat and Katehr forests) and Alauddin Khalji (who confiscated tax-free lands and raised revenue to 50%); severe famine in the Doab under Muhammad bin Tughlaq triggered wide peasant flight and uprisings.

events.title: Establishment of the Delhi Sultanate
events.desc: Qutb-ud-din Aibak founds the Delhi Sultanate, bringing U.P. under Turkish rule for the first time.

events.title: Alauddin Khalji conquers most of U.P.
events.desc: Awadh, Kannauj, Varanasi and Jalaun come under direct Khalji control, alongside major market reforms.

events.title: Firoz Shah Tughlaq's canals and cities
events.desc: Canal construction in the Doab and the development of new towns mark a period of infrastructure growth.

events.title: Defeat of Ibrahim Lodi
events.desc: Babur defeats Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat, ending the Delhi Sultanate's control over U.P. and beginning Mughal rule.

people.name: Qutb-ud-din Aibak
people.note: Laid the foundation of Sultanate power in U.P.

people.name: Alauddin Khalji
people.note: Conquered Awadh, Kannauj, Varanasi and Jalaun.

people.name: Muhammad bin Tughlaq
people.note: Undertook major reforms affecting the Doab region.

people.name: Sikandar Lodi
people.note: Developed Agra; encouraged agriculture, trade and arts.

prelims: Kara-Manikpur (near Prayagraj, UP) was the strategic provincial governorship from where Alauddin Khalji launched his raid on Devagiri and murdered Sultan Jalaluddin in 1296 CE.
Badaun in Western UP was one of the most prestigious governorships in the Delhi Sultanate; Iltutmish served as its governor before ascending the throne.
Balban deployed his "Blood and Iron" policy to ruthlessly suppress rural uprisings and bandits in the forests of Katehr (Rohilkhand) and the Doab.
The famous Jama Masjid of Badaun (Shamsi Jama Masjid) was constructed by Shamsuddin Iltutmish in 1223 CE.
Muhammad bin Tughlaq introduced agricultural relief measures (Diwan-i-Kohi and Takkavi loans) following devastating famines and rebellions in the Ganga-Yamuna Doab.
Ziauddin Barani, the author of Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi, hailed from Baran (modern Bulandshahr in Western Uttar Pradesh).
Firuz Shah Tughlaq excavated canals from the Yamuna to irrigate agricultural tracts in the upper Doab and Haryana.
mains: Examine the strategic, fiscal, and agrarian importance of the Ganga-Yamuna Doab for the sultans of Delhi from Iltutmish to Muhammad bin Tughlaq.
Analyze the role of Kara-Manikpur as a nodal military base for Sultanate expansion into Central and Southern India.
Discuss the peasant unrest in the Doab during the reign of Muhammad bin Tughlaq and evaluate the state's agricultural response through the Diwan-i-Kohi.

quickFacts: Doab (between Ganga-Yamuna), Awadh, Rohilkhand, Benares region
Defeat of Ibrahim Lodi by Babur, 1526 CE

periods.title: Jaunpur Sultanate in Uttar Pradesh
periods.tagline: A Powerful Regional Sultanate that Made Jaunpur a Centre of Politics, Learning, Architecture and Indo-Islamic Culture
periods.overview: Jaunpur is the one genuinely independent kingdom in this entire track's medieval section — founded in 1394 when the Tughlaq governor Malik Sarwar simply declared independence from a Delhi Sultanate too weakened by Timur's coming invasion to stop him, and surviving as a fully sovereign Sharqi state for eighty-five years before Bahlul Lodi's 1479 annexation folded it back into Delhi's orbit. That independence is exactly what makes this page worth reading against the surrounding Delhi Sultanate and Sayyid-Lodi pages rather than as a simple regional footnote to either: while Delhi itself passed through the chaos of the late Tughlaqs and the weak Sayyids, Jaunpur built its own flourishing centre of Indo-Islamic learning, architecture, and Persian literary culture, earning the title 'Shiraz-i-Hind' — the Shiraz of India — a level of cultural prestige the contemporary Delhi Sultanate, mired in political weakness during exactly these same decades, simply could not match. The Atala Masjid and Lal Darwaza that survive from this period stand as physical evidence of a genuinely distinct regional power, not merely a provincial administrative unit, briefly rivalling Delhi itself for cultural leadership in North India before its eventual reabsorption.

phases.name: Foundation
points: Malik Sarwar (founder), the governor (nawab) of Jaunpur under the Tughlaqs, declares independence from Delhi

phases.name: Consolidation
points: Mubarak Shah (1398–1434) and Ibrahim Shah Sharqi (1434–1440) consolidate the Sharqi kingdom

phases.name: Peak & Cultural Flourishing
points: Mahmud Shah Sharqi (1440–1457) presides over Jaunpur's peak as a centre of politics, learning and architecture

phases.name: Decline & Annexation
points: Muhammad Shah Sharqi (1457–1479); constant wars with the Delhi Sultanate and Gujarat Sultanate weaken the kingdom; after the death of the last ruler, Jaunpur is annexed by Bahlul Lodi in 1479 CE, marking the end of the Sharqi dynasty

Administration.intro: Compare this table's Diwan-Ariz-Qazi-Kotwal structure to the Delhi Sultanate's own administrative vocabulary on the previous page — the near-identical terminology shows that Jaunpur, despite its political independence, continued running on essentially the same Turkic-Persian administrative model it had inherited before declaring independence.
points: Sultan was the supreme authority; kingdom divided into parganas and villages; Iqta system prevailed; efficient revenue system based on land revenue
Officials: Diwan (finance), Ariz (military), Qazi (judicial), Kotwal (police chief); strong emphasis on law and order and public works

Military Power.intro: The description of frequent conflict with the Delhi Sultanate, Gujarat Sultanate, and other neighbours here underlines a point easy to miss: Jaunpur's eighty-five years of independence were not peaceful by default but had to be actively defended on multiple fronts simultaneously.
points: Maintained a strong army with cavalry and infantry; fortified the capital Jaunpur; built forts and defensive structures; often in conflict with the Delhi Sultanate, Gujarat Sultanate and other neighbours

Society & Economy.intro: The 'multi-religious and composite' society described here, with Hindus and Muslims living and trading together, is the same social pattern the previous Delhi Sultanate page documents at wider scale — Jaunpur's political independence did not translate into any distinct social model.
points: Society was multi-religious and composite; Hindus and Muslims lived together, cultural synthesis developed; agriculture was the main occupation; development of irrigation and canals; trade and crafts flourished, with Jaunpur an important trade centre on the Ganga

Religion & Culture.intro: This category's description of Jaunpur as a centre of learning and scholarship is precisely what earns it the 'Shiraz-i-Hind' title referenced on the earlier Foundation of Cities page — the connection between religious tolerance, Sufi presence, and genuine intellectual output is treated here as a single interconnected phenomenon rather than three separate facts.
points: Islam was the state religion; Sufism flourished with the presence of many Sufi saints; promotion of religious tolerance and coexistence; Persian was the court language; development of literature, poetry and music; Jaunpur became a great centre of learning and scholarship

Art & Architecture.intro: The Atala Masjid and Lal Darwaza described here represent a genuinely distinct 'Jaunpur style' rather than a simple provincial copy of Delhi's architecture — worth noting for any question that asks you to distinguish regional Sultanate-era architectural styles from one another.
points: Jaunpur style of architecture is distinct and grand; use of red sandstone and bricks; arches, domes, minarets and strong fortifications; blend of Islamic and local (Hindu) architectural elements

Major monuments: Atala Masjid — one of the largest mosques in Jaunpur; Jami Masjid; Lal Darwaza — famous for its grand gateway; Shahi Bridge (over the Gomti River); Jhanjhari Masjid; Maqbara of Malik Sarwar; Rampur Fort

The Sharqi Dynasty & Shiraz of the East: Foundation (1394 CE): Malik Sarwar, a noble of Firuz Shah Tughlaq, appointed "Sultan-us-Sharq" (Ruler of the East) by Nasiruddin Mahmud Tughlaq; established the independent Sharqi Sultanate of Jaunpur; spanned modern Eastern UP and Western Bihar (Kanpur to Tirhut).

Golden Age under Ibrahim Shah Sharqi (r. 1402–1440 CE): Promoted Islamic scholarship, literature, and arts; attracted celebrated scholars, theologians, and Sufis fleeing Timur's devastation of Delhi, earning Jaunpur the title "Shiraz-i-Hind" (Shiraz of the East).

Sharqi Architectural Style: Distinctive monumental style discarding the traditional minaret; characterized by massive, steeply sloping propylons (screen walls with central arched pylon) fronting the central dome; blend of Hindu beam-and-bracket construction with Islamic arches; prominent monuments: Atala Masjid (built 1408 on site of Atala Devi temple), Jami Masjid (built 1478 by Husain Shah Sharqi), Lal Darwaza Masjid (built 1450 by Bibi Raji), and the historic Shahi Bridge (Akbari Bridge over Gomti built by Munim Khan in 1568).

Fall of Dynasty: Perpetual wars with the Lodi Sultans of Delhi; Sultan Bahlul Lodi annexed Jaunpur in 1479 CE, defeating the last Sharqi Sultan Husain Shah Sharqi, though Sharqi culture and Hindustani classical music (Jaunpuri Todi, Khayal) endured.

events.title: Malik Sarwar declares Jaunpur's independence
events.desc: Founds the Sharqi dynasty and the independent Jaunpur Sultanate.

events.title: Mahmud Shah Sharqi's reign
events.desc: Jaunpur reaches its peak as a centre of politics, learning and grand Indo-Islamic architecture.

events.title: Annexation by Bahlul Lodi
events.desc: After the death of the last Sharqi ruler, the Jaunpur Sultanate is absorbed into the Lodi Sultanate.

people.name: Malik Sarwar
people.note: r. 1394–1398; declared independence from Delhi.

people.name: Ibrahim Shah Sharqi
people.note: r. 1434–1440; patron of learning.

people.name: Mahmud Shah Sharqi
people.note: r. 1440–1457; peak of Jaunpur's power and culture.

prelims: The Sharqi dynasty of Jaunpur was founded in 1394 CE by Malik Sarwar, who assumed the title "Sultan-us-Sharq" (King of the East).
Jaunpur was hailed across medieval Asia as "Shiraz-i-Hind" (Shiraz of the East) due to its flourishing colleges, arts, and Islamic scholarship.
The Atala Masjid at Jaunpur, completed in 1408 CE by Ibrahim Shah Sharqi, is famous for its massive central sloping pylon and absence of minarets.
Sharqi architecture is unique for using towering screen facades (propylons) in front of domes and combining Hindu trabeate brackets with arcuate arches.
The Shahi Bridge (Akbari Bridge) across the Gomti river in Jaunpur was built by Mughal governor Munim Khan in 1568 CE.
Husain Shah Sharqi, the last ruler of Jaunpur, was a master composer of Hindustani classical music who created the Raga Jaunpuri and popularized Khayal singing.
Bahlul Lodi annexed the Jaunpur Sultanate into the Delhi Sultanate in 1479 CE, ending the Sharqi dynasty.
mains: Critically evaluate the architectural innovations of the Sharqi style of Jaunpur, with specific reference to the Atala Masjid and Jami Masjid.
Analyze the cultural and intellectual flourishment that earned Jaunpur the moniker "Shiraz-i-Hind" during the 15th century.
Examine the geopolitical conflict between the Sharqi rulers of Jaunpur and the Lodi Sultans of Delhi leading to the annexation of Jaunpur in 1479.

quickFacts: 1479 CE, annexed by the Lodi Dynasty

periods.title: Delhi Sayyid & Lodi Dynasties in Uttar Pradesh
periods.tagline: Weaker Central Power Followed by Stronger Afghan Administration in U.P.
periods.overview: Where the national Sayyid Dynasty and Lodi Dynasty pages describe these two houses at the scale of the whole Delhi Sultanate, this page examines them specifically as rulers of the region that was, by this point, their most direct and consistently governed territory — and the contrast between the two dynasties' effectiveness is, if anything, sharper when viewed at this regional scale. The Sayyids' control over U.P.'s nobles and provinces was genuinely weak throughout their thirty-seven-year run, a regional reflection of the broader institutional collapse the national Sayyid Dynasty page describes following Timur's devastating invasion; the Lodis who followed, by contrast, visibly strengthened regional administration, with Sikandar Lodi's reforms to land measurement, agriculture, and trade producing concrete, datable improvements across the same U.P. territory the Sayyids had struggled to hold together. Sikandar Lodi's foundation of Sikandra near Agra during this period also connects directly forward to the next page in this track: the city infrastructure the Lodis built in U.P. is precisely what Babur inherited, and largely built upon, once his 1526 victory at Panipat ended Lodi rule and opened the Mughal era.

phases.name: Sayyid Dynasty
points: Founded by Khizr Khan in 1414 CE; claimed descent from Prophet Muhammad (Sayyids); rose to power after the decline of the Tughlaqs; weak central power and challenges from nobles and regional rulers

phases.name: Lodi Dynasty Founded
points: Founded by Bahlul Lodi in 1451 CE; Afghan (Pashtun) dynasty; stronger administration than the Sayyids but faced noble opposition

phases.name: Lodi Consolidation
points: Sikandar Lodi's effective administration, coinage reforms, promotion of agriculture; built cities (Agra, Sikandra near Agra)

phases.name: End of Lodi Rule
points: Ibrahim Lodi alienated the nobles but was defeated by Babur at the First Battle of Panipat (1526 CE); ended the Lodi rule

Important Rulers.intro: The stark contrast this table draws between the weak Sayyid rulers and the more effective Lodis, especially Sikandar Lodi, is the organising idea for this entire page — read the rest of the categories below with that contrast specifically in mind.
points: Sayyid Dynasty (1414–1451 CE): Khizr Khan (1414–1421) — consolidated Sayyid rule in Delhi and adjacent regions; Mubarak Shah (1421–1434) — coinage reforms, shift of capital within Delhi; Muhammad Shah (1434–1445); Alauddin Alam Shah (1445–1451)

Lodi Dynasty (1451–1526 CE): Bahlul Lodi (1451–1489) — centralised authority to a degree, laid foundation for stable administration; Sikandar Lodi (1489–1517) — effective administrator, promoted agriculture, built cities (Agra, Sikandra); Ibrahim Lodi (1517–1526) — alienated nobles, defeated by Babur

Administration & Governance.intro: Notice how explicitly this table states that central authority was 'weaker in the Sayyid period, improved under the Lodis' — this is a rare case in the source material of a direct, comparative judgement about relative dynastic competence rather than a neutral list of features.
points: Central authority was weaker in the Sayyid period, improved under the Lodis; U.P. divided into Iqtas, governed by governors (muqtis); land revenue (kharaj) was the main source, with improved measurement under Sikandar Lodi
Army mainly Afghan cavalry with foot soldiers; Qazi courts and Sharia law, with Sikandar Lodi ensuring impartial justice; public works: construction of mosques, sarais, roads, tanks and gardens

Society & Economy.intro: The 'kharaj' land revenue described here as the main source of income, with improved measurement specifically credited to Sikandar Lodi, is the direct forerunner of the far more famous Mughal-era Zabt system the next-but-one page in this track will describe in detail.
points: Afghans were the dominant nobility; agriculture was the backbone; use of iron plough, Persian wheel and better irrigation; growth of towns and markets; interaction between different communities continued; development of trade routes connecting Delhi–Agra–Jaunpur–Bengal; crafts like weaving, pottery, metal work flourished

Religion & Culture.intro: Sufi khanqahs are described here as established 'in many parts' of the region — this continues the same pattern of Sufism as a social unifying force that the earlier Delhi Sultanate and Jaunpur pages already established, now specifically under Sayyid and Lodi patronage.
points: Islam was the state religion; Sufism flourished, khanqahs established in many parts (Jaunpur, Delhi, Agra etc.); saints like Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti and Nizamuddin Auliya influenced the region

Use of Persian as the court language; development of literature, history writing and music; architecture saw continuance of Indo-Islamic style, including the development of Afghan-style architecture (arches, domes, thick walls, sloping buttresses)

Art & Architecture in U.P..intro: Sikandar Lodi's construction of Sikandra near Agra, noted here, is worth remembering specifically because Agra itself — founded by the same ruler — is about to become the setting for the entire next chapter of this track under the Mughals.
points: Important buildings: Tomb of Khizr Khan — Delhi (early Sayyid); Sikandra (Agra) — built by Sikandar Lodi; Atala Masjid — Jaunpur (Lodi period); sarai buildings and forts in various towns
Sources: Tarikh-i-Mubarak Shahi (by Mubarak Shah's court), Tabaqat-i-Akbari (important for the Lodi period); coins — silver Tanka and copper Jital were in circulation

Lodis in UP & The Foundation of Agra: Sayyid retirement in Badaun: Last Sayyid Sultan Alauddin Alam Shah voluntarily abdicated Delhi in 1451 CE and retired to Badaun (UP), where he lived peacefully until his death in 1478 CE.

Sikandar Lodi & Agra Capital: Sikandar Lodi recognized that controlling the central Doab and neutralizing hostile Rajput chiefs required moving imperial headquarters south; founded Agra in 1504 CE and officially shifted the imperial capital there in 1506 CE; introduced Gaz-i-Sikandari; laid layout of modern Agra city.
End of Sultanate: Ibrahim Lodi ruled from Agra; after his death at the First Battle of Panipat (1526), Babur dispatched Humayun directly to secure the royal treasury and palaces of Agra.

events.title: Khizr Khan founds the Sayyid Dynasty
events.desc: Establishes weak but formal control over Delhi and adjoining U.P. regions after the decline of the Tughlaqs.

events.title: Bahlul Lodi founds the Lodi Dynasty
events.desc: Begins a stronger Afghan administration in the region.

events.title: Sikandar Lodi's city-building programme
events.desc: Sikandar Lodi's administrative reforms and city foundations (Agra, Sikandra) mark the high point of Lodi rule in U.P.

events.title: Defeat of Ibrahim Lodi
events.desc: Babur's victory at the First Battle of Panipat ends Lodi rule over the region.

people.name: Sikandar Lodi
people.note: r. 1489–1517; effective administrator; built Agra & Sikandra.

people.name: Ibrahim Lodi
people.note: r. 1517–1526; defeated by Babur.

prelims: The city of Agra was established in 1504 CE by Sikandar Lodi to maintain strategic control over the Rajput borders and the Doab.
Sikandar Lodi shifted the imperial capital of the Delhi Sultanate from Delhi to Agra in 1506 CE.
The last Sayyid ruler, Alauddin Alam Shah, surrendered the throne of Delhi to Bahlul Lodi in 1451 CE and lived out his life in Badaun, UP.
The standard land measurement rod "Gaz-i-Sikandari" of 32 units was introduced in Uttar Pradesh by Sikandar Lodi.
Following the First Battle of Panipat (1526), Babur immediately dispatched Prince Humayun to seize the imperial treasury at Agra Fort.
Sikandar Lodi constructed the Baradari building at Sikandra near Agra, which was later converted into the burial site of Akbar.
Ibrahim Lodi resided primarily at Agra during his confrontation with rebellious Afghan sardars and Rana Sanga of Mewar.
mains: Examine the strategic and political considerations that prompted Sikandar Lodi to found Agra in 1504 and make it the imperial capital.
Analyze the transition of power from the Sayyids to the Lodis in Uttar Pradesh, focusing on the regional roles of Badaun and Jaunpur.
Examine the administrative, agrarian, and architectural contributions of the Lodi dynasty in Uttar Pradesh with special reference to the Gaz-i-Sikandari and the Sikandra Baradari.

quickFacts: Delhi, Agra, Sambhal, Etawah, Prayagraj, Ghazipur, Badaun

periods.title: Mughal Period in Uttar Pradesh
periods.tagline: U.P. as the Political and Cultural Heartland of the Mughal Empire
periods.overview: This page exists because Uttar Pradesh was not simply one province among the Mughal Empire's many territories, as the national Mughal Empire overview and its individual emperor pages might suggest at first glance, but the empire's literal political and cultural centre of gravity for well over a century: Agra served as Akbar's imperial capital from 1556 to 1571, Fatehpur Sikri was purpose-built as his subsequent capital, and Shah Jahan's Taj Mahal — the single most recognisable structure the national Shah Jahan page discusses — physically stands in Agra rather than in any other Mughal city. Reading this page alongside the individual national emperor pages reveals a consistent pattern: Akbar's conquest and administrative integration of Awadh, Jahangir's development of Allahabad into a major administrative centre, and Aurangzeb's continued reliance on U.P. bases even while personally leading Deccan campaigns all show a dynasty that, whatever territory it held elsewhere, never stopped treating this specific region as its home ground. The Taj Mahal, Agra Fort, and Allahabad Fort that survive from this period are not incidental Mughal monuments that happen to be located in U.P.; they are, in a real sense, the physical core of what the wider Mughal story was actually built around.

phases.name: Babur
points: First Battle of Panipat (1526) near Panipat (in present U.P. region's proximity)

phases.name: Humayun
points: Stayed in Agra; reorganisation of territories

phases.name: Akbar
points: Foundation of Fatehpur Sikri (1571); conquest & consolidation of Awadh; administrative reforms

phases.name: Jahangir
points: Allahabad (Prayagraj) becomes an important administrative centre; growth of trade and culture

phases.name: Shah Jahan
points: Construction of the Taj Mahal (Agra), Jama Masjid (Agra), Shahi bridges, gardens and sarais

phases.name: Aurangzeb
points: Long Deccan campaigns; administration continued from U.P. centres like Allahabad, Banaras

Administration & Governance.intro: The Zabt revenue system and Mansabdari nobility structure described here are the same institutions the national Akbar the Great page discusses at empire-wide scale — this table's value is showing specifically how they were administered through the Subah Allahabad and Subah Awadh provinces that covered most of present-day U.P.
points: Territorial system: province of Subah (Sarkar); U.P. was part of Subah Allahabad and Subah Awadh; revenue system: Zabt system under Akbar, land revenue assessment through measurement (Todar Mal)

Mansabdari System: nobility system based on rank (Mansab) and salary; local administration: Pargana and Mahal system, Qanungos, Patwaris, Amin were important officials; law & order: Qazi (judicial) and Kotwal (police chief) maintained order in towns; public works: construction of roads, sarais, bridges, gardens, tanks and canals

Economy & Society.intro: The list of major trade centres here — Agra, Banaras, Allahabad, Lucknow, Jaunpur, Etawah, Kannauj — is essentially a roll call of cities this track has already introduced under earlier dynasties, showing a striking continuity of urban economic importance across nearly a millennium of political change.
points: Agriculture was the backbone of the economy; main crops — wheat, rice, sugarcane, indigo; development of irrigation, use of Persian wheel and tanks; growth of trade and crafts — textiles, metal work, carpets, jewellery, pottery
Major trade centres: Agra, Banaras, Allahabad, Lucknow, Jaunpur, Etawah, Kannauj; society was composite — Hindus, Muslims, Jains, Sikhs lived together; local zamindars and merchants played key roles

Religion & Culture.intro: Note the explicit contrast drawn here between Akbar's and Jahangir's tolerance, Shah Jahan's continued but less expansive tolerance, and Aurangzeb's more orthodox but still regionally variable practice — the same nuanced picture the national Aurangzeb page presents, now grounded in specifically U.P.-based examples.
points: Religious policy: Akbar followed Sulh-i-Kul (universal peace) and respected all religions; Jahangir and Shah Jahan continued a policy of tolerance; Aurangzeb was orthodox but allowed Hindu practices in various contexts

Cultural developments: flourishing of music (Tansen — linked with Akbar's court); miniature painting, calligraphy, silk weaving, carpet making; composite culture and syncretism of Indo-Islamic traditions; growth of the Sufi tradition, influenced by the Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti (Ajmer) connection

Art, Architecture & Literature.intro: The Taj Mahal listed here is this page's single most important entry — while the national Shah Jahan page discusses it as the era's defining monument, this table is a reminder that it is, quite literally, a U.P. building, standing in Agra rather than in any other Mughal city.
points: Architecture: Agra Fort (Akbar), Fatehpur Sikri (Akbar), Taj Mahal (Shah Jahan), Itimad-ud-Daulah's Tomb (Agra), Jama Masjid (Agra), Shahi Bridge (Allahabad), Shahi Qila (Allahabad Fort), gardens — Ram Bagh (Agra), Shalimar Bagh (Allahabad)
Literature: Akbarnama (Abul Fazl), Ain-i-Akbari, Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri (Jahangir), Padshahnama (Abdul Hamid Lahori); Persian was the court language

Important Mughal Rulers & Their Contribu.intro: Use this ruler-by-ruler breakdown specifically to distinguish U.P.-focused achievements (Akbar's conquest of Awadh, Jahangir's development of Allahabad) from the same rulers' better-known empire-wide achievements covered on their own dedicated national pages elsewhere on this site.
points: Akbar (1556–1605): conquered Awadh (1564), brought it under Mughal rule; founded Fatehpur Sikri (1571) near Agra; reorganised administration and revenue system
Jahangir (1605–1627): made Allahabad (Prayagraj) an important administrative centre; encouraged art and natural history
Shah Jahan (1628–1658): built the Taj Mahal, Jama Masjid (Agra), Moti Masjid; developed cities, gardens, sarais and roads
Aurangzeb (1658–1707): administered the empire from U.P. centres during Deccan campaigns; built many mosques and sarais

Uttar Pradesh as Imperial Mughal Epicent: Agra as the Mughal Capital (Akbarabad): Served as the primary imperial seat for Babur, Akbar, Jahangir, and Shah Jahan; Babur created Aram Bagh (1526); Akbar rebuilt Agra Fort in red sandstone (1565–1573 with over 500 stone structures including Jahangiri Mahal); Shah Jahan added the white marble Moti Masjid, Khas Mahal, Diwan-i-Aam, and Musamman Burj.

Fatehpur Sikri: Built by Akbar (1571–1585) in Agra district; unique fusion of Rajput and Persian architectural traditions: Buland Darwaza (176 ft gateway), Jodha Bai Palace, Panch Mahal, Diwan-i-Khas with ornate central lotus bracket, Tomb of Shaikh Salim Chishti with white marble jali screens.

The Taj Mahal (Agra): Built by Shah Jahan (1631–1648) on the Yamuna bank; peak of Mughal architecture using Makrana white marble, Pietra Dura inlay, double dome, and four minarets; world heritage monument.

Other monumental heritage in UP: Akbar's Tomb at Sikandra (unique 5-tier open-air top pavilion without a dome), Tomb of Itmad-ud-Daula at Agra (built by Nur Jahan, "Baby Taj"), Allahabad Fort built by Akbar at the Sangam (1583 CE, housing the Ashoka Pillar and Patalpuri temple).

events.title: First Battle of Panipat
events.desc: Babur's victory establishes Mughal rule in North India, with lasting effects on the U.P. region.

events.title: Second Battle of Panipat
events.desc: Akbar defeats Hemu, consolidating Mughal control that will extend deeply into U.P.

events.title: Foundation of Fatehpur Sikri
events.desc: Akbar builds his new capital near Agra, a landmark of Mughal urban planning and architecture.

events.title: Construction of the Taj Mahal
events.desc: Shah Jahan builds the Taj Mahal at Agra, the defining monument of the Mughal period in U.P.

people.name: Akbar
people.note: r. 1556–1605; founded Fatehpur Sikri; conquered Awadh.

people.name: Jahangir
people.note: r. 1605–1627; developed Allahabad.

people.name: Shah Jahan
people.note: r. 1628–1658; built the Taj Mahal at Agra.

people.name: Aurangzeb
people.note: r. 1658–1707; administered the empire from U.P. centres.

prelims: Akbar founded his imperial capital at Fatehpur Sikri in Agra district in 1571 CE to honor Sufi saint Shaikh Salim Chishti.
The Buland Darwaza at Fatehpur Sikri was constructed by Akbar in 1601 CE to celebrate his victorious conquest of Gujarat.
The Taj Mahal in Agra was commissioned by Shah Jahan in 1631 CE as a mausoleum for Mumtaz Mahal and designed by chief architect Ustad Ahmad Lahori.
The tomb of Itmad-ud-Daula in Agra, constructed by Nur Jahan between 1622 and 1628 CE, is the earliest Mughal monument featuring extensive Pietra Dura on white marble.
Akbar constructed the massive red sandstone Allahabad Fort at the confluence of the Ganga and Yamuna in 1583 CE.
Akbar's tomb at Sikandra near Agra was planned by Akbar and completed by Jahangir in 1613 CE, notable for its tier-stacked design without a central dome.
The Ram Bagh (originally Aram Bagh) in Agra is the oldest surviving Mughal garden in India, laid out by Babur in 1526 CE.
mains: Critically evaluate the architectural evolution of Mughal monuments in Uttar Pradesh from Akbar's red sandstone at Fatehpur Sikri to Shah Jahan's white marble at the Taj Mahal.
Analyze the planning, symbolic geometry, and defensive engineering of the Allahabad Fort built by Akbar at the holy confluence (Sangam).
Examine the influence of Rajput architectural elements in the palaces of Fatehpur Sikri and the Agra Fort.

periods.title: Later Mughals in Uttar Pradesh
periods.tagline: Decline of Mughal Power & Rise of Regional Powers — Crucial for Understanding the Transition to Colonial Rule
periods.overview: The national Later Mughal Empire page traces imperial collapse at the scale of the whole subcontinent — Nadir Shah's invasion, Ahmad Shah Abdali's raids, the rise of the Marathas and Sikhs; this page narrows that same 1707–1803 story to what filled the vacuum specifically in U.P., and the answer is remarkably concrete: the Nawabs of Awadh, beginning with Saadat Khan Burhan-ul-Mulk in 1722, who built a genuinely autonomous regional state that outlasted meaningful Mughal central authority by decades while nominally still deferring to Delhi. Asaf-ud-Daula's decision to shift the Awadh capital from Faizabad to Lucknow in the 1770s is the direct origin of Lucknow's later reputation as a centre of Mughal-derived courtly culture, Urdu poetry, and distinctive Nawabi architecture — a cultural inheritance that would matter enormously when Lucknow became one of the most fiercely contested centres of the 1857 Revolt covered later in this track. Shuja-ud-Daula's participation in, and defeat at, the 1764 Battle of Buxar also marks this page as the direct hinge point between Mughal-successor regional autonomy and the beginning of serious British political and revenue control over the region — a transition the following British-era pages in this track pick up directly.

phases.name: Onset of Decline
points: Death of Aurangzeb; decline of Mughal power begins; rise of regional powers, weak centre, administrative disintegration and foreign invasions

phases.name: Rapid Succession of Emperors
points: Bahadur Shah I (1707–1712), Jahandar Shah (1712–1713), Farrukhsiyar (1713–1719), Rafi-ud-Darajat (1719), Rafi-ud-Daula/Shah Jahan II (1719–1748), Ahmad Shah Bahadur (1748–1754), Alamgir II (1754–1759), Shah Alam II (1759–1806, nominal)

phases.name: Rise of Awadh's Nawabs
points: Saadat Khan Burhan-ul-Mulk (1722–1739) founds Awadh's autonomy; Safdar Jang (1739–1754) strengthens administration; Shuja-ud-Daula (1754–1775) defeated at the Battle of Buxar (1764); Asaf-ud-Daula (1775–1797) shifts the capital to Lucknow

phases.name: Colonial Encroachment
points: Diwani rights granted to the British by the Mughal Emperor (Allahabad Treaty, 1765); continued Awadh autonomy under Wajid Ali Shah's predecessors even as British influence grows

Administration & Governance.intro: The description here of emperors as 'figureheads' with real power resting with 'nobles, wazirs and regional governors' is the same structural collapse the national Later Mughal Empire page describes at empire-wide scale — this table's contribution is naming the specific U.P.-based nobles (the Nawabs of Awadh) who filled that vacuum locally.
points: Weak central authority: emperors were figureheads, real power was with nobles, wazirs and regional governors; Subah system — U.P. was part of Subah Awadh and Subah Allahabad

Revenue system: Zabt system continued but revenue farming increased, with the Ijara system becoming common; Nawabs of Awadh (Saadat Khan, Safdar Jang, Shuja-ud-Daula, Asaf-ud-Daula, Wajid Ali Shah) became the de facto rulers; law and order deteriorated, zamindars became powerful in rural areas; Mughal army weak and undisciplined, reliance on provincial forces

Society & Economy.intro: Notice the continuity of trade centres named here — Agra, Allahabad, Banaras, Shahjahanpur, Moradabad — with almost every previous page in this track; even as political authority fragmented and weakened, the same underlying urban economic geography persisted largely unchanged.
points: Agriculture remained the main occupation; irrigation through canals and wells; growth of commercial crops — indigo, opium, sugarcane; trade centres — Agra, Allahabad, Banaras, Shahjahanpur, Moradabad
Crafts and industries — textiles, metal work, pottery, glass, carpets, arms; society: influence of Persian culture continued, composite culture flourished

Religion & Culture.intro: Shah Waliullah's influence, noted here as extending into the Awadh and Banaras region, is a useful reminder that major religious-intellectual figures based elsewhere in India (in his case, Delhi) still shaped the specifically regional religious culture this track has been tracing throughout.
points: Islam remained the state religion, but tolerance continued; growth of Sufi centres — Chishti, Qadri orders; development of Urdu language; patronage to literature, music, painting (Mughal miniature style declined but provincial styles developed)
Important scholars: Shah Waliullah (born in Delhi, influence in the Awadh & Banaras region)

Art, Architecture & Literature.intro: The Lucknow-centred monuments listed here — the Rumi Darwaza, Asafi Imambara — mark a genuine stylistic departure from the Agra- and Delhi-centred Mughal architecture of the previous page, reflecting Awadh's real cultural and political independence even under nominal Mughal suzerainty.
points: Architecture: blend of Mughal and regional styles; important monuments — Imambara, Rumi Darwaza (Lucknow), Asafi Imambara (Lucknow), Chhota Imambara, Dilkusha Kothi (Constantia, later colonial influence)

Literature & arts: Urdu poetry by Wali Dakhini, Mir Taqi Mir (Banaras connection); Persian literature continued; music and dance patronised at the Awadh court; painting declined in imperial centres but provincial schools like Awadh style flourished

Important Nawabs of Awadh (Impact on U.P.intro: This is the page's most important table: the Nawabs listed here are not minor regional governors but the actual rulers of what had become, by this point, U.P.'s single most powerful and consequential political entity — worth remembering each name and reign in sequence.
points: Saadat Khan Burhan-ul-Mulk (1722–1739): founder of Awadh's autonomy
Safdar Jang (1739–1754): strengthened administration, controlled U.P., Bihar
Shuja-ud-Daula (1754–1775): defeated Mughals & Marathas; participated in the Battle of Buxar (1764)
Asaf-ud-Daula (1775–1797): shifted capital to Lucknow, built many monuments
Wajid Ali Shah (1797–1856): last Nawab, deposed by the British in 1856; Awadh became the most powerful state in U.P. during the Later Mughal period

Nawabs of Awadh & Lucknow Composite Cult: Rise of the Awadh Nawabi: Saadat Khan Burhan-ul-Mulk appointed Subahdar of Awadh in 1722 by Muhammad Shah; founded autonomous dynasty; succeeded by Safdarjung (1739–1754, who also served as imperial Wazir).

Shuja-ud-Daula (r. 1754–1775): Fought alongside Ahmad Shah Abdali at Third Battle of Panipat (1761); formed confederacy with Mir Qasim and Shah Alam II against the British, defeated at Battle of Buxar (1764); signed Treaty of Allahabad (1765), paying 50 lakh indemnity and ceding Kora and Allahabad to the Company.

Asaf-ud-Daula & Shift to Lucknow (1775): Shifted capital from Faizabad to Lucknow in 1775; commissioned the monumental Bara Imambara (Asafi Imambara, 1784) during a devastating famine as food-for-work relief; world's largest unsupported vaulted central hall without pillars or beams; built the Bhulbhulaiya (labyrinth) and Rumi Darwaza (modeled on the Sublime Porte of Istanbul).

Wajid Ali Shah & The Twilight of Awadh: Last Nawab (r. 1847–1856); celebrated patron of music, dance, and poetry; developed Kathak dance and Thumri; authored Indar Sabha (first musical opera in Urdu); deposed by Lord Dalhousie in February 1856 on the pretext of misgovernance, and exiled to Metiabruz near Calcutta.

events.title: Death of Aurangzeb
events.desc: Marks the beginning of rapid Mughal decline and the disintegration of central authority across U.P.'s subahs.

events.title: Saadat Khan founds Awadh's autonomy
events.desc: Begins the rise of the Nawabs of Awadh as the de facto rulers of a major part of U.P.

events.title: Battle of Buxar
events.desc: Shuja-ud-Daula's defeat, alongside Mughal and Bengal forces, marks a decisive step toward British ascendancy in the region.

events.title: Diwani rights granted to the British
events.desc: The Allahabad Treaty grants the British East India Company revenue rights, deepening colonial encroachment on the region.

people.name: Shuja-ud-Daula
people.note: r. 1754–1775; defeated at the Battle of Buxar (1764).

people.name: Asaf-ud-Daula
people.note: r. 1775–1797; shifted the capital to Lucknow.

prelims: Saadat Khan Burhan-ul-Mulk founded the autonomous principality of Awadh in 1722 with its original capital at Faizabad.
Nawab Asaf-ud-Daula shifted the capital of Awadh from Faizabad to Lucknow in 1775 CE.
The Bara Imambara in Lucknow was built in 1784 CE by Nawab Asaf-ud-Daula as a famine relief project, renowned for its vaulted roof without supporting pillars and the Bhulbhulaiya labyrinth.
The Rumi Darwaza in Lucknow was constructed by Asaf-ud-Daula in 1784 CE, modeled after the historic Bab-i-Humayun (Sublime Porte) gateway in Constantinople / Istanbul.
The Treaty of Allahabad was signed in August 1765 between Robert Clive, Nawab Shuja-ud-Daula of Awadh, and Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II.
Nawab Wajid Ali Shah was a celebrated patron of the Lucknow Gharana of Kathak dance, under whose patronage classical Thumri blossomed.
Lord Dalhousie annexed the Kingdom of Awadh on 7 February 1856 on the pretext of "gross maladministration" based on the Outram report, exiling Wajid Ali Shah to Calcutta.
mains: Analyze the political, diplomatic, and territorial consequences of the Treaty of Allahabad (1765) for the Nawab of Awadh and the British East India Company.
Examine the distinctive architectural and cultural features of the Nawabs of Awadh in Lucknow, with special reference to the Bara Imambara, Rumi Darwaza, and Chhota Imambara.
Discuss the development of the "Ganga-Jamuni Tehzeeb" (composite culture), Urdu poetry, and Kathak dance under the patronage of the Nawabs of Awadh.

quickFacts: Decline of Mughals & Rise of Regional Powers
prelimsFacts: Bara Imambara & Bhool Bhulaiya (1784, Lucknow): Architectural masterpiece commissioned by Nawab Asaf-ud-Daula as a royal food-for-work famine relief project; features a colossal 50-meter unsupported central vaulted hall built without timber or iron columns, enveloped by the world-famous Bhool Bhulaiya (labyrinthine maze of 489 identical interlocking arched doorways) and flanked by the monumental Rumi Darwaza.

Sharqi Architectural Propylon Screens of Jaunpur: The Atala Masjid (1408 CE) and Lal Darwaza Masjid constructed by the Sharqi rulers of Jaunpur featured massive sloping propylon archways concealing the rear domes, symbolizing Jaunpur's status as 'Shiraz of the East' (Shiraz-i-Hind).

Kalinjar Fort & Death of Sher Shah Suri (1545 CE, Banda district): Historic Bundelkhand stronghold where Sher Shah Suri suffered fatal burns from an exploding artillery rocket (Ukka) during a military siege.

periods.title: British Rule and Administration in Uttar Pradesh
periods.tagline: A Mix of Exploitation and Modernisation — Laying the Base of Modern U.P.
periods.overview: This page and the national British Colonial Rule and British Administration pages describe the same broad transformation — Company trading post to full territorial administration — but from opposite ends of the telescope: where the national pages explain the system's general architecture, this page shows exactly how that system was built and operated in the specific territory that became, first, the North-Western Provinces (1835) and then, merged with annexed Oudh, the United Provinces (1902). The land revenue systems described here in regional detail — Permanent Settlement in western U.P., Mahalwari across Rohilkhand, Agra, and Bareilly, and the distinctive Taluqdari system in Oudh — are the concrete, on-the-ground version of the extractive colonial economy the national pages describe more abstractly, and the resulting exploitation of taluqdars and peasants under this specific revenue regime is not incidental background but a direct, documented cause of the 1857 Revolt this track covers next. The 1866 establishment of the Allahabad High Court and the region's early railway and educational infrastructure also show the other half of the colonial ledger the national pages discuss: genuine institutional modernisation, built for imperial administrative convenience but leaving structures — courts, universities, railways — that would outlast British rule entirely.

phases.name: Early British Power
points: British power in U.P. began with the Battle of Buxar (1764); Diwani rights of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa granted to the East India Company in 1765; after the Regulating Act (1773), administration became more organised; Permanent Settlement introduced in some parts (not in U.P.) in 1793

phases.name: Formation of the North-Western Provinces
points: Charter Act (1833) — centralisation of administration; U.P. (then North-Western Provinces) officially formed in 1835; Lord William Bentinck reorganised territories; Agra and Allahabad Presidencies were merged; elite landlords and taluqdars given a share in administration

phases.name: Annexation of Oudh
points: Annexation of Oudh by Lord Dalhousie, a key grievance behind the 1857 revolt

phases.name: Consolidation & Reform
points: British rule brought administrative centralisation, revenue reforms, modern infrastructure, education and law & order systems; Local Boards Act (1884) introduced local self-government

phases.name: Bifurcation
points: The North-Western Provinces and Oudh were bifurcated into: (i) the United Provinces of Agra and Oudh, and (ii) Oudh (Chief Commissioner's Province)

Administrative Structure.intro: The Governor–Commissioner–Collector–Tehsil hierarchy described here is the direct British successor to, and in some ways a more rigidly bureaucratic version of, the Subah–Sarkar–Pargana structure the Mughals used on earlier pages in this track — worth comparing the two systems directly.
points: Governor (Lieutenant Governor after 1858) — head of the province; Executive Council assisted the Governor; Commissioners headed divisions (Agra, Allahabad, Bareilly, Lucknow etc.)
District Collector — key officer, responsible for revenue, magisterial and administrative functions; Tehsil & Police System ensured law and order

Land Revenue Systems.intro: This table's three systems — Permanent Settlement, Mahalwari, Taluqdari — are not simply administrative trivia; the specific grievances they generated, especially under the Taluqdari system in Oudh, are a direct, documented cause of the 1857 Revolt covered on the very next page.
